claim: Match the lead to market stage: clueless market, open on a felt symptom and educate; aware market, attack existing options; saturated market, only a new mechanism or messenger works.
body: Craig Clemens (Golden Hippo) illustrates the three stages with his own probiotic ads. Clueless (around 2010 to 2014): almost nobody knew the word probiotic, so ads opened on what people already cared about, digestion and irregularity, then explained hidden sugars and sweeteners in 'healthy' food, the microbiome, and only then the product. That long educational video reportedly reached over 100 million views in about four months, and category searches for 'probiotics' spiked when it ran and dipped when it was pulled from Google. Curious (by about 2018): buyers had heard of probiotics and many owned one, so the headline intercepted that knowledge: a doctor saying to throw your probiotics in the trash because most lack enough strains. Saturated (now): the category is commoditised; he would not launch another probiotic without a strongly new mechanism or a recognised personality (his later brand ran education through Dr Gundry, and searches tracked campaign flighting). How to apply: search your category term and ask a few buyers what they already believe. If the term means nothing, lead with the symptom; if they own an alternative, lead with what is wrong with it; if every claim is taken, change the mechanism or the messenger, not the adjectives. A useful check is whether Google Trends for the category term moves when your campaigns run.
conditions: Consumables and supplements sold with long-form video or advertorial funnels; categories moving from unknown to crowded over several years.
fails_when: Regulated claims (health, medical) where 'doctor says' or disease framing breaches ad policy or law; markets where a cheap, simple direct-response offer outsells education; misreading the stage (educating buyers who already know bores them).
numbers: Educational probiotic video: claimed 100 million+ views in ~4 months
Problem-led ads 2013 to 2014; contrarian 'throw your probiotics in the trash' headline ~2018

claim: Tie a consumable to something buyers already do every day (morning coffee, breakfast, brushing); a daily ritual drives repeat use and daily word of mouth that one-off use cannot.
body: Clemens lists changing a daily behaviour as the hijack that creates the biggest brands, and distinguishes two routes. Hijack an existing ritual: Bulletproof got people to add MCT oil or butter to coffee they already drank every morning; a 1920s campaign recast breakfast as a hearty meal with bacon. Create a new daily ritual: his probiotic brands asked people to take something every day; Hal Elrod's morning routine book got readers journaling each morning. The mechanism he gives is conversation: people talk about what they are doing now, not what they bought last year. A daily behaviour produces daily mentions ('I just did my morning routine', 'I put this in my coffee'), long after the purchase, which he calls a viral effect nothing else matches. It also builds repeat purchase into the product's use. How to apply: name the exact moment in the day the product attaches to, put that moment in the product name, instructions, packaging and ad creative, and size packs to a daily dose so running out is predictable. Piggybacking on an existing habit is easier than creating a new one, because the cue already exists. This is a practitioner's framing with historical examples, not a measured result.
conditions: Consumables, supplements, food, personal care; products with a natural daily dose; DTC brands relying on repeat purchase.
fails_when: Products used occasionally by nature (seasonal, durable goods); a ritual so effortful buyers drop it within weeks; health claims tied to a daily routine that regulators treat as therapeutic claims.

Our supplement gets bought once and forgotten. How do we fix repeat purchases?

claim: Running founder ads as partnership ads through the founder's own handle beats the brand page by about 5 to 30%, but only if that profile has relevant content.
body: The host says he has almost never seen the brand-page version of a founder ad beat the same ad run as a partnership ad through the founder's personal handle. The lift is moderate, roughly 5% to 30%, and depends on the founder's credibility and profile. His own agency sits at the top of the range because its company page is nearly empty while his personal Instagram posts every couple of hours. The lift comes from the profile a viewer lands on: a personal page full of content tied to the founder story adds trust; a personal page of dog-in-the-park photos adds nothing. Trade-offs: running through the founder builds association with the person rather than the brand, and if founder ads come to carry most spend, that dependency can become an issue in an exit term sheet. How to apply: check the founder's profile first; if it has regular, relevant posts, test the partnership version against the brand-page version on the same creative; if not, keep founder ads on the brand page. Most brands, he says, should just stay on the brand page.
conditions: Meta partnership ads (formerly branded content or whitelisting) with the founder's Instagram or Facebook profile; founders who post regularly about the brand.
fails_when: Founder profile is empty, private or off-topic; brands planning an exit where key-person dependency hurts valuation; accounts where the founder may leave.

claim: At $30-100/day, test a focused batch with a per-ad impression cap (about 1,000, cut to 800 when CPM ran $50-70) so every ad gets equal exposure within 1-2 weeks.
body: Small accounts that upload 20 or 30 new ads a week rarely learn anything: Meta pushes most spend to one ad, the rest get almost no delivery, and the team decides the new creative does not work, or crowns the one ad that got all the spend. The agency's fix is to match test volume to budget and force an apples-to-apples read. In a $30 a day account they launched 13 ads and capped each at a set number of impressions so delivery could not snowball onto the early favourite, starting at 1,000 impressions per ad. Because the new pixel had little data and CPMs were averaging $50 to $70, they lowered the cap to 800 to finish the test without burning budget. The goal is a readable answer within the first one to two weeks; then cut the worst performers and make the next brief from the winner (more of the winning angle, the winning hook with new bodies, or more of the winning format). How to apply: budget per test equals ads times cap times CPM divided by 1,000 (13 ads x 800 impressions x $60 CPM is about $625); if that exceeds two weeks of spend, test fewer ads. Change one meaningful variable between ads (for example the same angle as UGC versus carousel) so the result teaches something.
conditions: Meta accounts spending roughly $30 to $100 a day on prospecting, especially new pixels with high CPMs.
fails_when: Larger accounts where Advantage+ creative testing or enough budget lets the algorithm allocate spend; 800 impressions per ad is too few to judge purchase rate, so it reads only top-of-funnel signals and needs a follow-up with more spend on survivors.

claim: Launch each 4-8 ad batch as its own avatar-grouped ad set with a 7-day minimum spend of 1x target CPA (max 20% of budget), then remove it.
body: An agency running Meta for about 100 DTC brands describes a modular 'pack' structure inside one prospecting campaign with campaign-level budget. Every new round of creative goes into a new ad set (a pack); packs are grouped by avatar, so ads aimed at one need (hair) never share an ad set with ads aimed at another (weight). The sweet spot is 4 to 8 ads per pack: enough angles to test, not so many that spend fragments. To stop the algorithm starving new ads in favour of old winners, they set an ad set minimum spending limit equal to one times the target CPA (target $50, minimum $50) for the first 7 days. If $50 would be more than about 20% of the daily budget, cap the minimum at 20%. After 7 days, delete the minimum and let the pack compete: winners keep spending above it, losers fade. How to apply: write the avatar and launch date in the ad set name, keep existing packs running, and judge packs on cost per purchase after the 7-day window. Practitioner method; no account-level results shown.
conditions: Meta prospecting with campaign budget optimisation, enough budget that 1x CPA per new pack is affordable, and a steady flow of new creative.
fails_when: Very small budgets where even 20% minimums starve existing winners; accounts with only one avatar and few creatives; minimum spend left on after 7 days forces spend on losers.

claim: Pick ads to iterate from Meta's 'compare attribution settings' incremental column, ranking by incremental revenue and ROAS, then make big-swing variations of those winners.
body: The same agency chooses which ads to iterate not by default 7-day click attributed ROAS but by Meta's incremental attribution view: in the ads view, set columns to compare attribution settings and add incremental attribution. This estimates revenue that would not have happened without the ad, which filters out ads that mainly collect credit from buyers who were coming anyway (retargeting-like behaviour inside broad campaigns). Then rank prospecting ads by incremental revenue and incremental ROAS and produce variations of the top ones. Their definition of an iteration is a substantial swing on a proven angle (new opener, new format, new creator, new visual) rather than changing one word in a headline; what would once have counted as a new ad is now treated as a variation of a winning concept. How to apply: 1) open the main prospecting campaign at ad level; 2) add the incremental attribution comparison; 3) shortlist the top ads by incremental ROAS with meaningful spend; 4) brief 3 to 5 bold variants per winner into a new pack. Availability of the incremental column depends on Meta's current rollout.
conditions: Meta accounts where the incremental attribution comparison is available and ads have enough spend for stable estimates.
fails_when: Low-spend ads where incremental estimates are noisy; accounts without the feature; treating Meta's model as ground truth without a holdout or survey check.

claim: Give each batch of 4 to 8 new creatives its own ad set in the prospecting CBO, with a daily minimum of 1x target CPA, removed after 7 days.
body: In a CBO campaign, older proven ads tend to take most of the budget, so new ads can sit for weeks without enough spend to judge them. The Moonlighters agency (over 100 brands) launches every new batch of creatives as a new ad set, or 'pack', inside one prospecting CBO campaign; the account shown was up to pack 76. Four to eight ads per pack is their usual range. In the ad set's budget settings they add an ad set spending limit, switch it to a dollar value, and set the daily minimum equal to one times the target cost per acquisition (target CPA $50, minimum $50). They set a reminder and never leave a minimum on for more than seven days. After seven days they decide: a winner usually keeps spending above that level once the minimum is removed; a loser drops back when the floor goes. Removing the floor is the default, because leaving it on keeps forcing spend into ads that may not deserve it. This shortens the waiting period so the account finds winners faster. Agency practice shown on account screens, no controlled comparison against other setups.
conditions: Meta prospecting with Advantage campaign budget (CBO), a known target CPA, and enough budget for several packs each spending 1x CPA a day for a week; brands launching new creative weekly.
fails_when: Total daily budget is too small to fund 1x CPA per active pack alongside proven ads; very high CPA products where 7 days at 1x CPA is a large share of budget; accounts using ABO testing campaigns already.

claim: Pick creatives to iterate by sorting ads by spend under Meta's incremental attribution column and keeping every concept above your incremental ROAS floor, not just the highest-ROAS ad.
body: The agency's analysis step: in the prospecting campaign, use 'compare attribution settings' to add the incremental attribution column, then sort all ads by spend, highest first. Look for ads with high spend and results above the brand's own threshold. In the 14-day example shown, the campaign spent about $97,000 at 1.42 ROAS on standard attribution and 1.23 on incremental. This brand's break-even new-customer incremental ROAS is about 1.1. One ad took over 25% of spend (about $26,000) at 1.46; others sat at 1.38 to 1.5; ads at 1.13 to 1.16 were left alone. The high-spend winners become the next round's source concepts for variants and iterations. The speaker's wider point: a concept returning 2.2x on $50,000 adds more profit than one returning 10x that can only spend $500, so under Meta's Andromeda delivery you run every concept that clears the profit floor rather than chasing the top ROAS. How to apply: set the floor from your own margin and new-customer economics first, then judge on incremental, not default, attribution. One account, one period.

fails_when: Low spend where ad-level numbers are noise; the brand has no margin-based ROAS floor so 'above threshold' is undefined; incremental attribution not available on the account or objective.

claim: Do not switch off low-ROAS ads in an ad set that is hitting KPI; Meta sequences ads across views, so add or cut ads only in underperforming ad sets.
body: Meta's delivery learns which sequence of ads leads to a purchase, using views and multiple clicks, but Ads Manager credits the sale to the last-clicked ad. So within one ad set, ad three might show 6x ROAS and ads one and two 2x and 1.4x, while ads one and two were the earlier touches that made the sale possible. Turning them off breaks the sequence. The agency's rules: structure each testing ad set around one concept (persona, angle, offer), with at least three ads; to validate a new concept properly, launch at least 10 ads and ideally about 20, given a typical 5 percent hit rate. If an ad set is hitting its KPI, leave it alone, because adding ads resets learning and reshuffles the sequence. If it is missing KPI, add, remove and change freely. At ad level, use the amount spent as the signal of what Meta values, since spend follows its multi-touch view. Do not mix conflicting personas (men and women) in one concept ad set.
conditions: Meta accounts using consolidated, concept-based ad sets with several ads each.
fails_when: Ads with clear policy, brand or offer errors should be removed regardless; tiny ad sets with one or two ads have no meaningful sequencing to protect.

claim: Dynamic product ad ROAS is inflated by existing customers; Meta's incremental attribution view can halve it (5x to 2.5x), and moving budget there starves prospecting.
body: Dynamic product ads retarget people who viewed products and usually show the best attributed ROAS in an account, which tempts brands, especially in fashion, to shift budget into them. The agency calls this a death spiral: much of that ROAS comes from existing customers and from people who would have bought anyway. In Ads Manager you can add incremental attribution via the columns, compare attribution settings option; Meta holds out about 10 percent of the audience and compares conversion rates. In their example, 2 percent of exposed people convert versus 1 percent of the holdout, so only half the sales are caused by ads and a 5x DPA ROAS is really about 2.5x. They have seen DPA spend work at about $1,000 a day on cold audiences but never scale to $50,000 a day. Shifting budget from prospecting to DPAs shrinks the pool of new visitors that DPAs feed on, and overall ROAS then falls. Rough split: 70 to 90 percent top of funnel, about 20 percent middle, 5 to 10 percent bottom, now steered mostly by the share of creative made for each stage.
conditions: Meta accounts running catalogue or dynamic product ads alongside prospecting, especially apparel and large catalogues.
fails_when: Large catalogue retailers with high repeat purchase, where DPAs to past customers are a deliberate retention channel measured separately; when the incremental attribution option is unavailable, use a holdout test instead.

claim: Partnership ads, run through a creator's handle, take up to 40 percent of spend in some agency accounts because delivery uses both the brand's and creator's audience data.
body: Partnership (collaborator) ads appear under the creator's profile, the brand's, or both, and Meta can now test those combinations automatically. The agency explains their strength two ways. First, targeting draws on both handles' audiences, so a relevant creator's followers and lookalike signals help find new buyers on cold traffic, not just warm. Second, a post from a person reads as content rather than an ad, so it meets less resistance. In some accounts they manage, up to 40 percent of total spend runs through partnership ads, and they call the format one of the most underused in 2026 while warning that the advantage is shrinking as more brands adopt it. How to apply: choose creators whose audience matches your buyer, secure usage and partnership permissions in the creator agreement, run their content as partnership ads in prospecting, and compare against brand-handle versions of the same asset. Recheck the edge every few months, since the arbitrage is time-limited.

fails_when: Creators whose audience does not match the buyer, which pulls targeting the wrong way; categories where creator partnerships face disclosure or claim restrictions; once the format is saturated in a category.

claim: Set how hard to push a winning ad by inventory and cash: squeeze it when stock must sell, or hold it near $100 a day to last months, not weeks.
body: Every ad has a maximum daily spend it can hold and a total lifetime spend before it fatigues. You can push a winner hard and burn its capacity in weeks, or hold it at a modest budget, the agency's example being $100 a day, and let it run for months at better efficiency. Which is right depends on the business, not the ad account. If there is excess inventory to sell this month, squeeze winners even at worse efficiency. If stock is short, a reorder is pending, or growth is outrunning the cash conversion cycle, pushing hard makes no sense. The agency warns that agencies optimise the P&L (efficiency and contribution) by default and can leave the balance sheet worse: their example is a business showing $2 million profit while holding $3 million of unsold inventory, effectively $1 million down in cash. The fix is to restructure campaigns and make creative around the slow stock, accepting lower ROAS to free cash. How to apply: share inventory position and cash targets with whoever runs media every month, and set ad-level spend caps accordingly.
conditions: Inventory-holding DTC brands with an agency or in-house media buyer, especially over $50k a month spend.
fails_when: Made-to-order or print-on-demand brands with no inventory risk; brands with ample cash where maximum short-term growth is the goal.

claim: Too few live ads can cap an account: one spending $350k a month on about 15 ads cut CAC 20 to 30 percent after relaunching old winners to reach 60.
body: When an account has little creative to work with, media buyers compensate with structure: the agency inherited an account spending about $350k a month (AUD) on Meta with only about 15 live ads, split across many campaigns with bid caps and cost caps, and CAC worsening for two years. Their diagnosis was that creative volume was the bottleneck, not buying. With no new production, they relaunched and lightly reworked past strong performers to reach about 60 live ads and simplified the structure; spend rose by about $40k a month while CAC fell 20 to 30 percent, and new-customer revenue grew roughly 28 percent. Because the founder refused to fund new production, those ads fatigued and performance slid back over the following months. Their proposed fix: move $10k of media to production for about 40 new assets, roughly doubling live ads, which they estimated would lift efficiency at least 5 percent, worth about $17.5k a month at that spend. How to apply: if spend per live ad is very high and the account is heavily segmented, audit past winners, relaunch them and redirect a slice of media to production before touching bids.
conditions: Meta accounts with high spend relative to the number of active ads, typically $100k+ a month.
fails_when: Accounts whose problem is offer, landing page or tracking; relaunching old ads only buys time if new production does not follow.

claim: Under campaign budget optimisation about 4 percent of ads end up holding about 64 percent of spend; that maximises short-term efficiency but leaves the account exposed when those ads fatigue.
body: Spend in ad accounts follows a compounding 80/20 pattern: 20 percent of ads take 80 percent of spend, and within that group the same split repeats, so roughly 4 percent of ads hold about 64 percent of spend and revenue. The agency says this shows up in every account they have analysed. Campaign budget optimisation leans into the pattern, which usually gives the best near-term ROAS, but concentrates the business on a handful of ads that will all fatigue, and can also concentrate sales on a few products, hurting sell-through on the rest of the range. Ad-set budgets (manual allocation) spread risk across more ads and products at a slightly lower expected return. How to apply: use CBO when you need a quick efficiency recovery, and set budgets across concepts when you want a steady, diversified portfolio of working ads, or when inventory across several products needs to sell through. Check the share of spend held by your top 5 percent of ads each week; if it creeps toward two-thirds or more with no backups, build replacements before those ads decline.
conditions: Meta accounts with many ads and multiple products, typically over $50k a month spend.
fails_when: Single-product brands with small accounts, where concentration risk is unavoidable and CBO's efficiency gain matters more; accounts in a short-term cash crunch that need ROAS now.

claim: In Meta's audience segments set engaged as 30-day site visitors plus 90-day add-to-carts and existing customers as 180-day purchasers, then exclude existing customers from prospecting.
body: The Moonlighters' core prospecting campaign: buying type auction, objective sales, CBO with a daily budget of at least one times target CPA (start where you already spend; do not use setup as a reason to raise spend), bid strategy highest volume or value, no budget scheduling. Audience segment reporting: engaged audience = anyone who visited the site in the last 30 days plus anyone who added to cart in the last 90 days; existing customers = purchasers in the last 180 days, not all-time purchasers. Ad sets: customer lifecycle goal set to acquire new customers, existing customers excluded, website single conversion event, purchase event only. Performance goal: maximize number of conversions for single-product brands or catalogs at one price point; maximize value of conversions when product prices vary. Attribution: 7-day click, 1-day engaged-view, 1-day view. No dynamic creative, no placement exclusions, no other targeting. Retargeting, retention and scale campaigns are built separately. How to apply: copy these settings into a new prospecting campaign, check the segment windows in the ad account's audience settings, and keep existing customers out so new-customer CPA is readable.

fails_when: Long purchase cycles or high-AOV products where 30-day and 90-day windows are too short; low-volume pixels where value optimization lacks data; when Meta changes segment or attribution options (verify against current Ads Manager).

claim: Launch every new creative batch into its own ad set ('pack') named pack number, avatar and angle inside one CBO prospecting campaign; 30 to 100 ad sets is acceptable.
body: Rather than adding new ads into an existing ad set, the agency launches every batch into a new ad set it calls a pack, duplicated from the same settings. The naming convention is pack number, then avatar, then angle, with the funnel role spelled out (for example 'Pack 2 - GLP-1 users - bottom of funnel - warranty'). Each pack holds one avatar-and-angle concept: problem-and-solution ads for top-funnel packs, objection ads for bottom-funnel packs. Some of its accounts run 30, 40, 50 or even 100 ad sets in a single CBO campaign; the host says this gives control, because instead of pausing ads they can use value rules and ad-set spend minimums or maximums. Over time the campaign becomes dozens of packs, and the naming makes it easy to see which concepts and funnel roles take spend. Expect top-funnel packs to take more budget at lower ROAS and bottom-funnel packs to post higher ROAS on less spend. Later additions include interest-based ad sets built around proven winners and a separate scale campaign. How to apply: adopt the naming format before the next launch, keep one concept per pack, and review spend share by pack weekly.

fails_when: Small budgets where many ad sets fragment spend and none exits learning; Advantage+ shopping campaigns that do not use ad sets this way; teams that duplicate concepts across packs, blurring the read.

claim: Track creative hit rate: ads that spent over 5% of campaign budget at target CPA, divided by ads launched; about 5% is a normal rate.
body: The Moonlighters agency (about $500M in Meta and Google spend over 11 years, $100M+ in the last year) argues that ad count means nothing and only the number of winners matters. Its metric is creative hit rate: winners divided by total ads launched, times 100. A winner is defined in advance as an ad that both spent more than 5% of the campaign's total budget and hit the target CPA. Launch 100 ads and see 5 dominate, and the hit rate is 5%, which the host calls solid and fairly normal. At a stable hit rate, volume scales winners: 1,000 ads at 5% should yield about 50. The catch is quality: the host claims that flooding an account with sloppy ads sends unqualified clicks that bounce or abandon, and that these 'negative events' train the pixel badly; treat that mechanism as his view, not Meta's documentation. How to apply: fix the winner definition (spend share plus CPA target) before testing; compute hit rate per month and per creative source (AI, UGC, in-house); raise volume only from sources whose hit rate holds; if hit rate falls as volume rises, cut volume and raise the quality bar.
conditions: Meta sales campaigns with CBO or Advantage+ where spend share signals delivery preference; accounts launching dozens of ads a month.

claim: About 60% of readers read only the headline; in a 2,500-ad study full-headline readership fell from 87.3% at 3 words or fewer to 77.9% at 13 or more.
body: Two numbers sit behind Whitman's rule to put the biggest benefit in the headline. First, about 60% of people who see an ad read the headline and nothing more (no source given beyond agency lore), so whatever the headline omits most people never learn. Second, Harold Rudolph's study of 2,500 ads in the Saturday Evening Post (1939 to 1940) measured how many readers finished the headline: up to 3 words, 87.3%; 4 to 6 words, 86.3%; 7 to 9, 84%; 10 to 12, 82.5%; 13 or more, 77.9%. The shortest headlines were read about one-seventh better than the longest, with the steepest drop past 12 words. Rudolph himself warned that content matters more than length, and Ogilvy found longer headlines often sold more. Whitman's resolution: always put the biggest, most specific benefit in the headline; if two headlines are equally strong, choose the shorter. Specific beats vague ('boost your tips by 512% or your money back' over 'learn the tricks of the trade'). How to apply: for ad headlines, hero sections and email subject lines, lead with the concrete benefit; trim beyond about 12 words unless the extra words add a specific.
conditions: Any headline slot: paid social primary text first line, landing page hero, email subject and preview; the data are from print magazine ads.
fails_when: Long-form direct-response pages where long headline and subhead stacks deliberately pre-qualify readers; platforms that truncate at fixed character counts, where the limit decides; when a short headline loses the specific benefit.

claim: When every rival claims 'lowest prices', a disclosed, checkable figure (such as 'our net profit is 3 percent') persuades where superlatives no longer register.
body: Hopkins' case: a mail-order clothing seller used 'lowest prices in America' for years; rivals copied it, then everyone guaranteed to undersell competitors, and the claims became background noise. On advice, the seller switched to stating its net profit was 3 percent. Readers could reason that no business runs on less, so its prices had to be near the floor, and the next year sales rose sharply. A car advertiser did the same when the public believed margins were excessive: it stated a 9 percent profit and itemised $735 of hidden costs in a $1,500 car. The general mechanism is that a superlative is assumed to be puffery and discounted entirely, while a precise figure implies it was measured and can be challenged, so it is believed (he gives 'three and one-third times the light' beating 'more light', and 'reduced 25 percent' beating 'prices reduced'). How to apply: when your category's price or quality claims have converged, replace the superlative with one verifiable number buyers can sanity-check, such as your markup, cost breakdown, test result or time saved, and keep it true, because a specific false figure is easier to expose than a vague one.
conditions: Price-competitive categories where rivals' claims have converged; brands willing to disclose cost or margin data; markets that distrust markups.
fails_when: Disclosing margin invites competitors to undercut, or contradicts a premium positioning; the figure cannot be substantiated under advertising law (comparative and price claims are regulated); buyers who do not care about price.

claim: Size paid spend on existing customers in dollars: frequency (4 to 7 a month) x customers x CPM / 1,000, with a CPA target about half the new-customer target.
body: Paid ads are mainly an acquisition tool, but the presenter changed his earlier view that existing customers should get no spend. Fashion is the clear exception: weekly drops need surfacing to past buyers, and email and SMS miss many of them, so a dedicated new-arrivals campaign to existing customers is incremental. Rules for that spend. Set its CPA target well below new-customer CPA, for example $20 or lower against a $40 new-customer target, because warm audiences should convert cheaply. Expect steep diminishing returns: in his example, cutting existing-customer spend from $1,000 to $700 a day only dropped conversions from 50 to 47, so the last $300 a day bought three orders at $100 each. Budget it as a dollar amount, not a percentage of spend: monthly budget equals desired frequency (4 to 7 impressions a month) times the number of existing customers times CPM divided by 1,000. Test cutting existing-customer spend while watching conversions; most brands overspend here and can move the savings to acquisition.

claim: Budget existing-customer ads as customers x desired monthly frequency x CPM / 1,000, not a percentage; 7-day frequency above 8 on existing customers signals overspend.
body: Ad platforms like spending on existing customers because those conversions attribute easily, yet existing customers are the least incremental audience. Large brands often ask what share of budget should target them; the speaker says a percentage is the wrong frame. Instead compute it: number of existing customers, times how many times a month you want them to see an ad, times the CPM for that audience (from Meta's audience segment breakdown), divided by 1,000. His example: 300,000 existing customers shown three ads a month at an illustrative $2.50 CPM is $2,250 a month. Real CPMs will be higher, but even brands with millions of customers usually need only around $10,000, at most $30,000 to $40,000, a month to reach them three to six times, while he sees small businesses spending $40,000 a month on them. Check the frequency column for existing customers over the last seven days; above about eight means you are over-serving and paying for purchases that would have happened anyway. claim: Maximize-conversions bidding sends spend to the lowest-CPA product, not the highest contribution; segment campaigns by product economics when CPA and contribution diverge.
body: Default bidding on Meta, Google and TikTok minimises cost per acquisition, so spend flows to whichever product or ad converts cheapest, regardless of profit per sale. The speaker's example: a $90 hoodie with $21 cost (gross margin $69) at $45 CPA leaves $24 contribution per sale; a cheaper t-shirt with $27 gross margin at $15 CPA leaves $12. The platform will push budget to the t-shirt because its CPA is lower, even though each hoodie sale contributes twice as much. Switching to maximise conversion value does not fix it here either, because the t-shirt also has the better ROAS. The fix is structural: separate campaigns or ad sets by product group based on product-level contribution economics, so budget can be set deliberately. A second question follows: if the t-shirt converts that cheaply, would it sell anyway without paid support (organic demand, retail stores)? If so, pull spend from it, lift its contribution from $12 to about $27, and reallocate to products that need paid media to sell through. How to apply: build a sheet per product or category with price, true gross margin, recent CPA and contribution per sale, and review it before choosing campaign structure.
conditions: Multi-product catalogues on conversion-optimised campaigns where products differ widely in margin and conversion cost.
fails_when: Single-hero-product brands; very low budgets where splitting campaigns starves learning; when the cheap product is a strong entry point whose buyers go on to high-margin repeat purchases.

claim: Tie ad targets to stock: when a SKU has fewer days of inventory than its reorder lead time, raise its ROAS target or pause its ads; discount aged stock.
body: A media buyer told to hit a blended ROAS target will push the best-selling SKUs hardest regardless of stock. Holiday's rule ties media to days of inventory outstanding. When a SKU is about to sell out before a new order can arrive (his example: 30 days of stock left, 80 days to reorder), either raise the efficiency target on it sharply so each remaining unit earns maximum margin, or turn its ads off; the worst outcome is paying a high acquisition cost to sell through stock that will be gone anyway. In the other direction, grade inventory A to D by how long it has sat or how many days of stock remain. The deeper the overhang (he cites SKUs reaching 1,000 days of inventory after demand dipped), the more discount or lower ad efficiency you should accept to turn it back into cash, and aged stock that is not moving should be liquidated to fund better bets, even below cost; buyers of the business will not value two-year-old stock at retail anyway. The ideal is that days of stock equal production lead time, so a PO placed today lands as stock runs out. Hold a weekly inventory meeting between the media buyer and operations.
conditions: Multi-SKU brands with variant and colour/size inventory risk (apparel especially) and long reorder lead times.
fails_when: The SKU is the brand's hero product and going dark would cost ranking, audience learning or customer acquisition that matters more than batch margin; pre-orders or backorders are available to keep selling through a stock gap.

Audience segment breakdown (existing customers, engaged audience, new audience): about half the ad's budget was going to existing customers, and ROAS on new audiences was about 5. Attribution comparison (Columns, compare attribution settings: 7-day click, 1-day view, incremental): on new audiences the incremental figure was 1.71. Mechanism: with 7-day click plus 1-day view optimisation and no audience limits, Meta pushes spend toward whatever earns attributed purchases most easily, which is existing customers and view-through conversions, so the ad ranking stops reflecting new-customer performance. The cost is double: wasted spend, and a creative team told to make more of a concept that is not actually working, while a better new-customer ad sits underfunded. The symptom at account level: every attempt to scale raises CAC while new-customer counts stay flat (this brand's pattern for two years). How to check: run both breakdowns on your top five spenders before briefing more creative in the same style.

He shows Meta's incremental attribution only as a breakdown column, not as the optimisation goal, because he understands it as a modelled estimate built from other advertisers' lift studies rather than a measurement of your account; check Meta's own documentation on how it is computed, and use a Conversion Lift test (a true holdout) when you need real incrementality. 2) Audiences: exclude existing customers from cold scaling campaigns. claim: Cap dynamic product ads well below the roughly 70% of spend auditors often find; DPAs mostly reach bottom-funnel buyers and are rarely incremental.
body: A common audit finding in the creative pillar is that most of the account's spend goes into dynamic product ads (catalog ads). The agency's view is that DPAs sit at the bottom of the funnel and are mostly not incremental: they serve to people already close to buying, so attributed ROAS looks strong while new-customer revenue per ad dollar does not move. They can spend on cold audiences and do acceptably there, so they are not banned, but an account with about 70% of spend in DPAs is a red flag. How to apply: check the share of spend in catalog or DPA ads; compare their reported ROAS with the first-order acquisition MER from the store; if DPAs dominate spend and the gap is large, shift budget to concept-led prospecting creative and judge DPAs with incremental attribution or a holdout. claim: Fix ad account bottlenecks in this order: data integrity first, account structure second, creative third; creative has more impact than structure but takes longest to change.
body: The agency's audit has three pillars: data integrity (do platform numbers track business numbers), technical account structure, and creative (volume, concept diversity, quality). It works top-down from Shopify revenue and new-customer revenue to platform, campaign, ad set and ad until it finds the single current constraint, then orders fixes by commercial impact and time to fix, as a 90-day roadmap. Data integrity always comes first and is usually quickest: if platform ROAS is far from acquisition MER, every creative or structure decision is being made on wrong numbers. In impact, creative ranks second, but it is slowest because it often needs a bigger or better creative team or a new agency, so in practice account structure is fixed second (it can be changed fast) and creative third. claim: Judge spend on existing and engaged audiences by 30-day frequency, not budget share: around 30 on existing customers or 14 on engaged audiences means overspend.
body: Rather than asking what percentage of budget goes to new, engaged and existing customers, the agency checks 30-day frequency in each group, using Meta's audience-segment definitions (which must be set up, a common error when missing). Their examples of warning levels: frequency around 30 on existing customers means you are overspending on people who already buy, often because existing-customer spend is not ring-fenced in a dedicated campaign and bleeds into every campaign; frequency around 14 on engaged audiences means too much middle-of-funnel creative. The speaker calls this one of the biggest current mistakes: content that is not top-of-funnel enough, so delivery piles onto warm people. Fixes: define new, engaged and existing segments; exclude existing customers properly from cold campaigns; control existing-customer spend in one place; and shift creative toward broader, colder concepts. Pair it with the aMER check, since existing-customer overspend is one of the main reasons platform ROAS looks much better than new-customer revenue per ad dollar.

claim: Start from one cold campaign; add campaigns only for business complexity (countries, sub-brands, categories), not spend: accounts at $1M to $5M a month often run 4 to 5.
body: The agency's premise is that every campaign must have a purpose you can defend, and the ideal is one campaign. Audit method: list every campaign in a sheet, write its purpose in the next column, and check its settings (exclusions, objective, audience). Typical finding: about half the campaigns duplicate each other, for example two cold creative-testing campaigns or a separate add-to-cart objective campaign with no reason to exist; consolidate them and performance usually improves. Spend level is not a reason to add campaigns; they audit accounts spending $1M to $5M a month that run four or five. Business complexity is a reason: selling in several countries, several sub-brands, a fast-changing product range, or categories the business wants to push independently (if dresses underperform, you need a lever for dresses). Their Australian example: smaller brands combine Australia and New Zealand in one campaign, while large retailers split them so they can move budget into New Zealand separately. The same exercise applies to Google: write each campaign's purpose and roll up any you cannot justify.

claim: Move ads that got no spend in a CBO but still deserve a test into a separate 'zombie' ad set; one large advertiser recovers about 20% more winners this way.
body: When many variations sit in one Advantage campaign budget (CBO) campaign, Meta shifts spend toward a few early leaders and many ads get little or no delivery. That is the system's early guess, not a test, so some good ads are never judged. The speaker, who says he has spent over $300 million on Meta, collects the ads that got no spend but that he still has strong conviction about, puts them together in their own ad set (a 'zombie campaign'), and launches it so they are forced to get delivery. He reports that about 20% of those revived ads turn out to be winners. The process it sits inside: take a winning ad, have an AI tool write many close variations in the same voice for specific segments (body copy first, then headlines, then creative), put them all in a CBO and let spend flow to the best. Then sweep the unspent ones into the zombie set. How to apply: after 5 to 7 days, list ads with near-zero spend, keep only those with a clear reason to believe in them (proven angle, new segment), and give them their own budget for a fixed test window.

claim: On Meta, name the target segment in the ad copy instead of interest targeting: duplicate a winner, insert the niche word, run broad, compare CPA after 7 days.
body: Since Meta's Andromeda delivery system, the ad itself (image, copy, offer and landing page) is what Meta reads to decide who sees it, so the creative now does the targeting. A generic winning ad finds one pocket of buyers; the same ad with a segment named in the headline or body tells the system to look for a different pocket. The speaker calls this word an identity trigger. His method: take your best ad, find which segments make up the 20% of customers producing 80% of revenue, and duplicate the ad once per segment with that word inserted ('lead' becomes 'dental lead', 'lawyer lead'), or with a demographic named (a 25-year-old woman versus a 30-year-old woman). He also favours long-form copy, because more text gives Meta more context about who the ad is for. To prove it, run your interest-stacked winner side by side with the same ad on country-only targeting for 7 days and compare cost per acquisition; he expects broad to win. For a store, the segments might be use cases, gift recipients or life stages taken from order and review data.

body: A high platform ROAS on a small budget usually means you are under-spending: the cheapest buyers are being reached and more are available at a higher but still profitable cost. body: Many small accounts size ad-set budgets with the '50 conversions in 7 days' rule, which forces far more budget than the business can afford. This agency back-calculates instead. Step 1, test budget: multiply target CPA by three. At a $50 CPA, spend $150 on the new concept's ads; three or more purchases, keep it running; two, a yellow light, allow roughly another CPA of spend; zero or one, cut it. Their preferred rule, if the client accepts it, is five times CPA ($250) with no yellow light, because early spend is partly the system learning whom to show the ads to. Step 2, test duration: do not burn the whole test budget in one day. Weekday performance varies, and buyers often need several impressions over three to four days before purchasing; kill a top-of-funnel ad after one day and its warmed-up viewers convert later through retargeting ads, crediting the wrong creative. Divide the test budget by the number of days you are willing to wait for an answer to get the daily ad-set budget. Read results on 7-day click attribution, with existing customers excluded from the test, so returning buyers do not make a concept look better than it is. Step 2, incrementality: going from a frequency of 10 to 20 might add something, so run a Meta conversion lift experiment (Experiments tab) on the existing-customer campaign over about 30 days. claim: Scale on marginal, not average, CAC: adding 25% spend moved average CAC from $337 to $392, under a $400 limit, while the extra customers cost about $1,000 each.
body: Averages hide the return on the last dollar. Blue Sense Digital's worked example: baseline CAC for new customers is $337. Adding 25% more spend, $80,000, raises average CAC to $392, still under a $400 CAC tolerance, so it looks fine. But that $80,000 bought only 76 more customers, a marginal CAC of about $1,000, far above tolerance. Their rule is to keep adding spend only while contribution margin after marketing (CM3) keeps rising, and stop when it flattens. CM3 peaks where marginal ROAS equals break-even ROAS, which is 1 divided by gross margin (gross margin after discount, fees and fulfilment, as a share of revenue). How to apply: in the pacing sheet, compute incremental spend, incremental new customers and incremental CM3 between budget levels rather than daily blended numbers; also watch the 1-day to 7-day click ratio, which flattens when you stop creating demand and are only harvesting. claim: Write Black Friday scaling rules in advance: scale on 3-day rolling marginal CM3, cut after two poor reads, and use spend elasticity only to cut, never to scale.
body: Blue Sense Digital's pacing rules for November: on a three-day rolling basis, if marginal contribution margin after marketing (CM3) is improving, increase budget; if not, hold; after two consecutive poor reads, decrease. They also compute a spend elasticity: log of day-two revenue over day-one revenue, divided by log of day-two spend over day-one spend, read as roughly 0 to 2 (under-spending, about right, or room to push), retrospectively or with a three-to-four-day lag. The warning: this number is observational, not causal. You raise spend on days when demand is already high (Black Friday itself), so it overstates headroom and can lead to severe overspend. Use it only as a reason to cut. claim: At zero-to-one, run a $10-50/day Meta test campaign adding 1-3 creatives every few days; judge first whether an ad gets spend, then whether it returns money.
body: On a small budget, Meta's delivery system tells you two separate things about each creative. Whether it gets spend shows if people engage with it and the algorithm can find an audience; whether that spend returns revenue shows if the ad and landing page actually sell. Reading them in order gives a diagnosis: spend with no return means the creative entertains but does not explain the product or does not match the landing page; no spend means nobody cares, so replace the concept rather than tweak it. Structure for a simple catalogue: one test campaign at $10 to $50 a day, adding one to three new creatives every few days (seeded from organic posts that performed), and one scale campaign for proven ads. Expect it to take time: at $10 a day on a $150 product, validation may take about two weeks. When an ad holds a positive return, double the budget in steps ($50, $100, $200 a day) and stop doubling when the return ratio falls, then work out whether it is creative fatigue (needs new ads) or limited demand. A founder can validate a product this way for roughly $300 in ad spend before committing more.
conditions: New brands or new products spending under about $10,000 a month on Meta with a simple product set; physical products in the roughly $30 to $200 range.
fails_when: Doubling budgets fails at six-figure monthly spend, where smaller increments and broader structures are needed; very low budgets on low-priced products may never exit learning, and high-ticket products need more spend per conversion to read results.

claim: On broad Meta targeting, exclusions, minimum age, location and language are hard controls; age bands, gender and interests are treated as suggestions, so exclude existing customers.
body: Meta now places users in a very high-dimensional space built from their paid and organic interactions rather than tagging them with interest labels. Broad targeting sprinkles spend across that space, finds clusters that respond to the creative, and narrows onto them. The catch the presenter flags: the cluster most likely to convert is often your warm and existing customers, so delivery drifts there and prospecting budget gets spent on people who would have bought anyway. According to the presenter, the inputs Meta still obeys are exclusions (customer lists, recent purchasers), minimum age, locations and languages; age bands, gender and interests are taken only as suggestions. He says interest and lookalike targeting as a primary method is obsolete. How to apply: run prospecting broad with existing-customer and recent-purchaser exclusions kept up to date via customer list sync, set locations and language deliberately (never worldwide by default), and judge prospecting by new-customer metrics. Keep campaign and ad set splits only where audiences or categories genuinely differ (his example: ice baths versus saunas), and otherwise consolidate so conversion data is not split across many under-funded ad sets.

claim: The 'never raise Meta budget more than 20%' rule has no Meta documentation behind it; a big raise looks bad because new audiences take days to convert.
body: Blue Sense Digital says it routinely raises budgets by more than 20% at a time without problems and that Meta's documentation contains no such rule. What makes a sharp increase look like it 'broke learning' is a timing effect: extra spend reaches people further from your core buyers, and many of them need to see several ads over days before purchasing, so revenue lags spend. Triple the budget today and same-day revenue will not triple, but some of that spend converts later. How to apply: when scaling, judge the change over a window long enough to cover your typical time to purchase (several days to a couple of weeks for considered products), compare cohort or blended results rather than same-day ROAS, and do not roll back after one or two weak days. Separately, remember that broad delivery tends to drift toward warm and existing-customer clusters because they convert most easily, so keep existing customers excluded from prospecting so the extra budget buys new customers. Ratchet budgets in steps you can afford to hold through the lag rather than in tiny daily increments chosen to dodge a rule that does not exist.

fails_when: Very low daily budgets or small audiences near saturation, where a large raise mainly raises frequency; accounts still in early learning with few conversions, where volatility is high regardless.

claim: Your Meta bid is your unit economics: a competitor with higher AOV, gross margin or LTV can win auctions with weaker creative and account structure.
body: In the auction, the advertiser who can sustainably bid more wins more placements and more scale. What decides a sustainable bid is not a platform setting but the business: price, cost of goods, units per order, first-order gross profit and 365-day lifetime gross profit. The presenter's point is that a brand with better economics can run worse creative, worse structure and worse measurement and still out-scale you, simply by paying more per customer. So platform tactics have a ceiling set by the offer and margin. He also notes that Meta's own algorithm updates aim at small platform-wide gains (Meta claimed about 3% more conversions and 5% higher CTR from its adaptive ranking update) that Meta then recovers through higher CPMs, so advertisers should expect efficiency to hold steady, not improve, from updates. How to apply: before changing campaigns, rebuild first-order unit economics and 365-day LTGP, then work the levers that raise the affordable bid: post-purchase upsells, bundles and units per order, stronger front-end offers and retention. Audits should start with economics, not with the ad account.
conditions: Competitive Meta auctions in ecommerce; brands whose CAC is being pushed up by rivals.
fails_when: Brands whose problem is clearly broken tracking or creative (zero delivery, policy rejections), where economics work will not fix delivery; categories with little competition for the audience.

claim: Group Meta ad sets by concept (persona plus angle plus offer), not by launch date or mixed audiences, because each ad set learns its own audience.
body: In the source's model of Meta's Andromeda-era delivery, each ad set goes out and learns its own audience; most of the targeting learning sits at ad set level, not ad level. If an ad set holds one concept, it finds the people that concept resonates with. A concept is a persona plus an angle plus an offer; change one and it is a new concept. Creatine gummy example: people who hate creatine powder; beginners starting at the gym; wellness-focused professionals; brain support. Each becomes an ad set with as many ads as you can make under it, and the ad set result tells you whether the concept works, with a reliable attributed number. The common structure that breaks this is ad sets named by launch batch (the March 7 creatives, the March 9 creatives), each mixing several personas and angles: the ad set has no clear audience to learn, so delivery goes broad and performance drops. A sportswear example: putting men's and women's ads in one ad set leads to ads serving across genders with no clear split. Use campaign-level splits for business units (product categories with different margins or budgets) and concept splits inside them.

claim: Judge Meta creative at the ad set level, not the ad level: ROAS gets less reliable down the structure because ad-level credit goes to the last click.
body: The operator's reasoning: Meta optimises delivery across a sequence of ads (one ad warms a cold viewer, another later gets the click), but reports conversions on the last click. Campaign-level ROAS on 7-day click tracks the business's real acquisition numbers fairly well; ad set level is less reliable; ad level is very unreliable. That is why the highest-spending ad in an ad set often shows lower ROAS than a smaller one: it may be doing the opening work while a follow-up ad takes the credit. Debating which ad to turn off produces opinions, not answers. Instead, put a group of related ads (5, 10 or 20) in one ad set, let Meta distribute spend, and ask one question: is this ad set at its KPI? If yes, raise its budget. Inside it, use spend as the signal of what is working (often about four of 20 ads take most of the spend) and brief more ads like those. Avoid judging ads after $1 or $2 of spend, and avoid spreading budget across so many campaigns that nothing reaches a readable level. The goal is a loop where account data reliably tells the creative team what to make next.
conditions: Meta accounts running many creatives per month with conversion optimisation; most relevant above about $10k a month in spend.
fails_when: Very small accounts where each ad set cannot reach enough conversions to read; brands with incrementality tests that show ad-level effects directly.

claim: Split Meta ad sets by format (images, video, catalogue ads) only in new accounts; once spending about $10k a month, the split adds little.
body: When an ad set or campaign is new, Meta has no conversion data, so the source says it leans on soft signals such as CPM, click-through rate, cost per click, hook rate and hold rate to choose which ads to spend on. Mixed into one ad set, static images tend to win spend because their CPMs are low, and dynamic product ads tend to win because they automatically find warm, high-intent audiences and convert early. Spend then swings toward those formats for reasons that do not reflect real performance, and new video concepts never get a fair read. For a brand-new account it therefore makes sense to give formats their own ad sets so each gets budget. For most accounts at roughly $10,000 a month or more, the operator does not recommend format splits: concept-based ad sets give more useful learning. Splitting by landing page is also possible, but conversion rate by landing page can be read in Shopify, so it rarely justifies its own ad sets unless testing a custom page. Splitting by product category works when categories have different margins, for example dresses at 70% gross margin can run at a lower ROAS target than tops at 55%.

fails_when: Accounts with steady conversion volume, where format splits dilute budget and concept splits produce better learnings.

claim: When one concept takes about 80% of Meta spend, either shift creative output toward it (120 ads versus 40) or cap it near 40% of spend and rotate new concepts.
body: With four concept ad sets and 50 new creatives each, the structure absorbs about 200 new ads a month. The operator expects Pareto to show up: one or two concepts will barely spend and one will outperform, until about 80% of spend sits in one ad set (by manual budget moves or automatically under campaign budget optimisation). Two responses. First, double down: move creative production toward the winner, for example about 120 new ads for it and about 40 for each other concept, so more spend can flow to what works. Second, protect the business from over-reliance: put a maximum spend limit on the winning ad set, around 40% of spend, and keep launching new concept ad sets, let each spend enough to read, and rotate out the losers, so a fallback exists when the main angle fatigues. The source warns concentration is a real risk: when a dominant concept stops working there is nothing behind it, and a winning funnel can also bring customers with poor lifetime value, which is another reason to segment. Choose based on how dependent revenue already is on one angle.
conditions: Meta accounts producing high creative volume (around 200 new ads a month) across several concepts.
fails_when: Small accounts that cannot fund several concept tests at once; brands whose single winning angle is the core product promise and not a fatiguing hook.

claim: Size TikTok ad group budgets at about 2x target CPA rather than TikTok's suggested ~10x, aiming for 25 conversions within the 7-day learning phase; $20/day is the minimum.
body: TikTok's learning phase, in which delivery is volatile while the system finds buyers, settles after about 25 campaign results or seven days. TikTok's own guidance, as the host reads it, suggests a daily budget of roughly ten times CPA ($100 a day at a $10 CPA, $400 at $40), which he considers too high for most advertisers. His rule: start at about two times your current or expected CPA per day ($20 a day at a $10 CPA, $60 a day at $30), the level that has a chance of getting 25 results inside the seven days. TikTok enforces a $20 a day minimum; at that floor, expect a long learning phase. Leave target CPA blank on a new account until you have data. At $20 a day, run one prospecting campaign with one broad ad group and several creatives, then move winners into a separate campaign to scale. With more budget, test broad against interest-based ad groups, and use campaign budget optimization only once you are scaling proven ads. Retargeting starts with one audience of site visitors in the last 30 days excluding purchasers, then expands to 7-day visitors and 30-day add-to-carts as budget grows. Broad targeting usually beats granular manual targeting now, in his tests.

claim: Below about $1,000 a day of Meta spend, wild day-to-day ROAS swings are normal; judge on at least 7 days and ignore Meta's automated suggestions and opportunity score.

At spends from about $50 a day up to about $1,000 a day, results that rise and fall like a sine wave are normal, and even larger accounts see swings. A day at 3x ROAS followed by an unprofitable day on $100 of spend tells you almost nothing. His rule is to zoom out to at least seven days and the largest spend sample available before changing anything. He also warns against accepting Meta's in-platform recommendations that promise, for example, an 11% lower cost per result, and says the account opportunity score is not a performance measure: he shows a highly profitable account with an opportunity score of zero and an Event Match Quality around 9.8 to 9.9, while seeing no direct link between EMQ and profit. He judges purchases with third-party attribution rather than Meta's reported CPA. claim: Daily test budget = target conversions x expected CPA / test days: 20 conversions at $100 over 14 days is $143 a day, versus $714 to hit Meta's 50-in-7-days rule.
body: To set a creative or concept test budget, Blue Sense Digital asks two questions: how many conversions will you accept as a readable result, and how fast do you need the answer? Then: daily test budget = target conversions x expected cost per acquisition / test duration in days. Example: a threshold of 20 conversions, $100 expected CPA, 14 days gives about $143 a day for that ad set. They argue Meta's guidance of 50 conversions in 7 days to exit the learning phase is unworkable for most brands: the same maths gives $714 a day per test, so five to ten concept tests would cost $3,500 to $7,000 a day just for testing. body: CBO (Advantage campaign budget) lets Meta move money to the best ad sets, which usually gives the best ROAS, but it concentrates spend roughly 80/20 on a few ads, so new creative, an expensive shoot or a paid partnership ad may get no spend. ABO forces spend through each ad set. Blue Sense Digital's preferred setup for large accounts: CBO, with minimum and maximum ad set spend limits that direct about 60% of the budget, and about 40% left for Meta to place freely; that 40% is still spent, it is not a reserve. It needs a lot of oversight, which is worth it only at large spend; for an account around $10,000 a month they call it overkill and say to run plain CBO or ABO depending on your appetite for risk versus efficiency. They have seen both ABO and CBO work at very high spend, so it is a preference about whether you want spend forced through every new creative. Related: when a winner emerges, raise its budget where it is; do not turn it off to relaunch it in a scaling campaign.
conditions: Meta accounts with several ad sets of new creative competing with proven ones; large budgets with active daily management.
fails_when: Small accounts (management cost outweighs gain); teams without capacity to adjust limits regularly; accounts where all new creative already gets spend.

overkill at about $10k a month spend

claim: Set existing-customer Meta spend in dollars, not percent: customer count x CPM / 1,000 x the monthly frequency you want on them.
body: Brands often target a percentage of budget for existing customers, such as 20%. Blue Sense Digital calls that a bad metric because the right share depends on the size of your customer list and on how much you spend on acquisition, both of which change. The same 20% might mean a frequency of 50 a month on a small list, which is wasteful, or a frequency of 1 on a large list, which is underspending. Instead calculate a dollar budget: number of existing customers (in the audience Meta can reach) times your CPM divided by 1,000 times the frequency you want each month. Example: 100,000 reachable customers at a $10 CPM with a target frequency of 4 a month is about $4,000 a month. Then check the actual 30-day frequency in Meta's audience-segment breakdown. They often see about 50% of account spend going to existing and engaged audiences, which mostly supports sales that would happen anyway rather than adding new customers.
conditions: Meta accounts with customer lists uploaded and audience segments defined; brands with meaningful repeat purchase.
fails_when: Customer lists with low match rates (reachable audience much smaller than the list); campaigns where existing customers cannot be separated; launch periods where heavier frequency on customers is deliberate.

illustration: 100,000 customers x $10 CPM x 4 = about $4,000 a month

claim: In a Meta catalog, sale_price must be below price.
body: Without sale_price_effective_date an item stays on sale until the sale price is removed; images must be JPEG or PNG, at least 500 x 500 and up to 8 MB; a changed image needs a new URL. Meta's catalog fields reference sets the data that catalog ad overlays read. price is a number, a space and a three-letter ISO currency code (9.99 USD), with a period as decimal and no symbols. sale_price is the discounted price, must be less than the full price, uses the same format, and should be removed after the sale ends. sale_price_effective_date gives the start and end date, time and time zone; if it is missing, items with a sale_price stay on sale until the sale price is removed. image_link must be JPEG or PNG, at least 500 x 500 pixels and up to 8 MB, and if an image changes later the new image needs a different URL or the change is not picked up. A shipping field allows a shipping-related overlay. So any price, strikethrough or percent-off overlay is only as true as these fields; set the effective date for every sale so a badge cannot outlive the offer.
conditions: Meta catalogs used for Advantage+ catalog ads, Shops and dynamic overlays.
fails_when: A Shopify channel app or feed tool may write these fields for the store; check what it sends.

claim: New Advantage+ sales campaigns no longer take the existing-customer budget percentage; Meta's documented way to cap that spend is two ad sets, one for existing customers with a spend cap and one excluding them.
body: Meta's Marketing API guide for Advantage+ campaigns says the existing_customer_budget_percentage field is not available for new Advantage+ campaigns, and that old Advantage+ shopping campaigns using it will be paused at API version 26.0 unless migrated in Ads Manager. For new campaigns the guide suggests two ad sets under one Advantage campaign budget. The first includes a custom audience that defines existing customers, with targeting relaxation set to zero so the audience is a hard rule, and a daily spend cap (and optionally a daily minimum spend target) on that ad set. The second is a copy of the first that excludes the same custom audience. A campaign counts as Advantage+ sales only when three levers are on: budget set at campaign level, an Advantage+ audience (or no targeting beyond location) in at least one ad set, and no ad set level placement targeting or exclusions. The guide also notes that legacy campaigns with more than 50 ads in one ad set cannot be migrated. How to apply: write the existing-customer audience definition (for example a customer list plus purchasers from the last 180 days) and the cap in money per day into the launch sheet, check the campaign still shows as Advantage+ after the second ad set is added, and read new-customer results from the excluding ad set.

claim: Once a creator accepts a brand's account-level partnership ad permission in the Instagram app, the brand can run ads from the creator's handle without an existing post, and can revoke it later.
body: Meta's partnership ads documentation describes two permission models, account level and post level. For account level, the brand (or an app acting for it) sends a request to the creator's Instagram account; the creator accepts it inside the Instagram app. After acceptance the brand can create partnership ads from the creator's handle without an existing post, can promote the creator's existing posts that tag the brand (paid partnership label, mentions, people or product tags, or Collabs), and can choose to include or exclude the creator's audience. Each permission has a status such as approved, revoked or pending, and the brand can revoke it. The documentation does not state an expiry, so the end date of usage belongs in the written creator agreement. Separately, a creator can make a partnership ad code for a post they own and share it with the brand, which uses it in Ads Manager; the creator can remove that code. How to apply: get the written usage terms first, then the platform permission, then record the permission status and the code per creator in one sheet before any ad is built.

claim: Meta reviews each ad's image, video, text, targeting and landing page, usually within 24 hours; a rejected ad can be edited (it is then reviewed as new) or sent for another review in Account Quality.
body: Meta's Advertising Standards say review is mostly automated with some manual review, and covers images, video, text, targeting information and the ad's landing page or other destination. Review usually ends within 24 hours, and ads can be reviewed again after they go live. When an ad breaks a standard it is rejected, and the ad account, Page or business portfolio and its assets may be restricted; a restricted account or asset cannot be used to advertise across Meta technologies. Advertisers usually get the chance to edit a rejected ad, and the edited ad is treated as a new ad and reviewed again. If the advertiser believes an ad, account, Page or business portfolio was wrongly rejected or restricted, they can request a review in Account Quality. Meta also says it monitors advertiser behaviour and may restrict accounts that keep breaking the standards. How to apply: treat every rejection as a signal about the account's record, fix the cause across all similar ads rather than resubmitting one, and use Account Quality, not a new account, for appeals.

fails_when: Special ad categories and regulated goods carry extra rules and authorisations beyond the general review process.

claim: A Meta catalog item needs id, title, description, availability, condition, price, link and image_link plus one of brand, GTIN or MPN; out-of-stock items stop appearing in ads.
body: Meta's catalog field reference lists the required fields for a product: id, title, description, availability, condition, price, link and image_link, and at least one of brand, gtin or mpn. Missing or badly formatted required fields can stop products from uploading. Price is a number, a space and a three-letter ISO currency code with a full stop as the decimal mark and no currency symbol (for example 499.00 INR or 24.99 USD). Availability takes in stock or out of stock; items marked out of stock show as sold out in a shop and do not appear in ads. Links must start with http or https, be valid and sit on the business's own website domain, not a Facebook Page. How to apply: check these fields on every item before building catalog ads, keep availability synced with the store at a frequency that matches how fast stock moves, and spot-check that the feed price equals the live page price, because the field reference itself does not enforce that match.

claim: Google disapproves ad text with misused capitals, punctuation or symbols, gimmicky repetition or spacing, a phone number in the text, or no clear name of the business or product.

claim: India's ASCI Code requires verifiable claims to be substantiated on demand, cited research to show its source and date, permission to refer to people, 'free' only when nothing but delivery is charged, and an ad label on social posts.
body: Chapter I of the ASCI Code says claims about objectively verifiable facts must be substantiated, and advertisers must produce that proof when ASCI asks. If an ad cites independent research, the source and date should appear in the ad. Ads must not distort facts or mislead by implication or omission, and must not be so exaggerated that they cause grave or widespread disappointment; obvious humour or hyperbole is allowed. Referring to a person, firm or institution needs permission. A product may not be called free if the buyer pays anything beyond delivery, freight or postage, and that cost must be stated. In buy-one-get-one-free offers, the price of the item bought must be no more than its usual price without the offer. 'Prices from as low as' claims must not mislead about availability. Ads on social media must carry a clear label at the start, such as Ad, Sponsored, Partnership or Collaboration. Special care applies to health claims. How to apply: keep a proof file per claim and check every 'free', BOGO and 'from' line against the real price.
conditions: Advertising seen in India, including digital and social ads.
fails_when: Category rules (food, cosmetics, health, finance) and the Consumer Protection Act add further limits; check those for regulated products.

claim: ASCI treats drip pricing, bait and switch, false urgency and disguised ads as misleading from 1 September 2023; for 'limited stock' claims the advertiser must show the stock really was that low.
body: ASCI's Guidelines for Online Deceptive Design Patterns in Advertising (15 June 2023, applicable from 1 September 2023) apply Chapter I of the code to digital ads and e-commerce. Drip pricing: quoted prices must include non-optional taxes, fees and charges that apply to all or most buyers, rather than revealing them at the end. Bait and switch: an ad that implies one outcome but delivers another, such as a product shown at a price that is then only available at a higher one, or an attractive product later found out of stock with an alternative pushed. False urgency: stating or implying quantities are more limited than they are is misleading, and on a complaint the advertiser must show the stock position when the message appeared justified it. Disguised ads: content formatted like editorial or organic posts, including influencer posts and paid reviews, must clearly say it is an ad. How to apply: show all-in prices, keep stock evidence for any scarcity line, and label creator and advertorial-style ads.
conditions: Digital advertising and e-commerce in India.
fails_when: The government's own 2023 dark patterns guidelines under the Consumer Protection Act list more patterns; check them for checkout and site design, not just ads.
numbers: applicable from 1 September 2023

claim: If Meta ads are meant to drive retail sales, run them in a separate ad account and measure with a geo-lift test, because in-store purchases cannot feed Meta's purchase optimisation.
body: Gorilla Mind's energy drink sells mostly in stores, and Meta cannot see those store sales as conversions. Mixing retail product ads into the main account means they compete for budget with products that send purchase events, and Meta will starve them or learn the wrong things. Blue Sense's setup if a brand wants Meta to grow retail: 1) Put retail-product ads in their own ad account so they do not interfere with purchase optimisation for DTC products. 2) Run them only in selected US states and keep other states as a control. 3) Use a model built from past data to predict what retail sales in the test states would have been without ads, compared with the control states. 4) Increase spend as a test and see whether retail sales in test states rise beyond the prediction. This needs store sales data by region from retailers or a data provider. Without such a test, retail-focused Meta spend cannot be judged.
conditions: Brands with retail distribution across many regions, access to sell-through data by region, and budget to run a multi-week geo test.
fails_when: Retail sales data is not available by region or arrives too late, or spend is too small to move regional sales above normal noise.

claim: Point DTC ads at products that ship well online and leave heavy, low-price goods to retail: Gorilla Mind gives its canned drink 3.7% of Meta ads and its powders and gummies 71.7%.
body: Gorilla Mind sells in Vitamin Shoppe, GNC, Walmart, 7-Eleven and QuikTrip, but the product in those stores is mainly the canned energy drink. On the website, cans get no free shipping and each order is limited to two cases, because cans are heavy and cheap relative to shipping cost. Of 272 Meta ads Blue Sense pulled, only 10 (3.7%) feature the drink, while creatine gummies, two pre-workouts and the Sigma testosterone booster take 71.7%. Powders and gummies are light, high value and consumable, which suits DTC and subscriptions. The lesson Blue Sense draws for any brand: decide which products are retail products and which are DTC products before planning paid social. Do not spend Meta budget trying to sell cans or bulky low-margin goods online, and protect your margin with shipping rules (exclude from free shipping, cap quantities) where you must list them. How to apply: for each product, work out shipping cost as a share of order value and gross margin after shipping; products where shipping eats most of the margin belong in retail or in bundles, not in cold ads.
conditions: Brands with both retail distribution and a DTC store, or with products that vary a lot in weight and price per unit.
fails_when: A brand has no retail channel for heavy products, or can bundle heavy items into high order values where shipping is a small share; then they can still work online.
