claim: A cold prospecting campaign at 2x ROAS is usually worth more than existing-customer retargeting at 7x; almost every account overspends mid and bottom of funnel, and moving 30% of budget down starves growth.
body: Bottom-of-funnel and existing-customer campaigns show high ROAS because they reach people who were already likely to buy. The business only grows when spend at the top brings new people in efficiently, and those people feed the middle and bottom campaigns later. Blue Sense often sees teams take 30% of budget from cold campaigns and put it into middle or bottom of funnel because ROAS looks better there; growth then fades. A cold Meta prospecting campaign with existing customers excluded and top-of-funnel creative, running at 2x, is doing harder and more valuable work than retargeting at 7x. Overspend on dynamic product ads and on existing-customer campaigns are both recurring audit findings, driven by their flattering ROAS. How to apply: cap retargeting and existing-customer spend at a small share of budget; put increases into cold prospecting and, at scale, upper-funnel channels such as YouTube or TikTok; and judge the whole funnel on new-customer revenue and acquisition MER.
conditions: Meta accounts with separate prospecting and retargeting or existing-customer campaigns.
fails_when: A large engaged customer base plus a launch or event where retargeting truly drives extra sales, or prospecting creative so weak that extra cold spend is wasted.

claim: Around March or April 2026 Meta limited 7-day click to outbound clicks and moved likes, comments, shares and page clicks into 1-day engaged-view, so click ROAS fell overnight; keep engaged-view in reports.
body: Before the change, any click on an ad counted as a click for attribution, including a like, a comment, a share or a click to the page, which few advertisers realised. After it, only outbound clicks count in 7-day click, and the interactions that used to count now sit in 1-day engaged-view. So 7-day click ROAS dropped for everyone with no change in real sales. Blue Sense keeps 1-day engaged-view in its preferred setting because it restores the old meaning of a click, and someone who engaged with an ad and then bought probably has some causal link to it. How to apply: when comparing 2026 results with earlier periods, do not read the fall in 7-day click ROAS as a performance decline. Compare 7-day click plus 1-day engaged-view now with 7-day click before the change, and mark the change date on your reports and dashboards.

Its feed shows many tiles at once, so one ad among them is enough to claim the purchase, and at modest budgets it tends to serve warm audiences who visited the site in the last few days and would probably have bought anyway. Moving budget from Meta to Pinterest because 7 beats 2.5 rewards the platform that claims credit most generously. TV sits at the other extreme: zero attributed ROAS, real impact. claim: If a TikTok test at 25% of Meta budget shows only 1x to 2x while Meta's mid-funnel campaign jumps from 4x to 12x, the jump is TikTok traffic being retargeted, so do not raise Meta budgets on it.
body: New channel tests are easy to misread because their effect shows up somewhere else. Blue Sense's example: a brand launches TikTok at about a quarter of its Meta budget. On TikTok's own numbers it looks unscalable at 1x to 2x. At the same time a middle-of-funnel Meta campaign climbs from 4x to 12x. Most teams credit Meta, raise mid-funnel budgets, and often raise cold Meta budgets too because Meta overall looks strong. That extra spend is largely wasted, because the improvement came from TikTok visitors being picked up by the Meta pixel and retargeted. How to apply: when you add or scale a channel, hold budgets elsewhere steady for the test window, and track total new customers and acquisition MER for the whole business, plus each channel's retargeting results. If retargeting ROAS spikes at the same moment, credit the new channel, and consider a geo or holdout test before deciding its long-term budget.

claim: Report Meta on 7-day click plus 1-day engaged-view and drop 1-day view; in Blue Sense's audits 30 to 50% of reported ROAS often comes from view-throughs alone.
body: Meta's default is 7-day click, 1-day view and 1-day engaged-view. The 7-day click window credits sales within a week of an outbound click. Engaged-view credits sales within a day after someone watched 3 seconds or more, liked, commented or otherwise interacted without clicking through. The 1-day view window credits a sale within 24 hours of an ad simply being served, with no watch or click, which is where most over-attribution sits, especially for past visitors and customers who would buy anyway. Running 1-day view across all campaigns and reporting on it is the first of nine recurring patterns in Blue Sense's audits. How to apply: set new campaigns to 7-day click and 1-day engaged-view, or, for reporting only, open Columns, choose Compare attribution settings and add 7-day click results. These track much more closely to acquisition MER in the business. Know the other platforms' defaults too: Google commonly uses a 30-day click window plus view and engaged windows, and TikTok and Pinterest have their own, so their numbers are not comparable with Meta's.

claim: Small budgets on Snapchat, Pinterest or Reddit report high ROAS because low spend goes to warm pixel audiences, and traffic or reach campaigns at 3% of budget can never be measured; test both or cut them.
body: Recurring audit patterns from Blue Sense's portfolio. Tertiary channels at a tiny share of spend report excellent ROAS but add no new growth, because at low budgets the platform serves the warm visitors its pixel already knows. Meta traffic or reach campaigns run on an assumption: asked how their impact is measured, teams usually say they added one at about 3% of budget during Black Friday and that month went well. At 3% it cannot have a measurable effect, and a before-and-after read across a peak proves nothing, so the money is spent on something nobody can judge. Over-segmentation, with too many campaigns for the spend level or the business, fragments conversion data and makes results harder to read. And many accounts have no testing structure at all. How to apply: list every campaign and channel that takes a small slice of spend, and next to each write how its incremental impact is measured. Where there is no answer, either set up a holdout or geo test with enough budget to read, or switch it off and move the budget to proven campaigns.
conditions: Accounts running several small channels or awareness objectives beside conversion campaigns.
fails_when: The small channel reaches a distinct audience and a test shows real lift, or an awareness push runs with a geo test in place.

claim: Two campaigns with the same 4x ROAS and $10K of revenue can differ in profit, say full-price retention against discount-code entry, so rank campaigns on profit contribution, not ROAS.
body: Revenue is not all equal. One campaign might sell full-price products to existing customers; another might push a discount code or lower-margin lines. Their ROAS can match while their gross margin, and so their profit contribution, differs a lot. In Blue Sense's example the two worked out at 3 and 4 on a profit contribution basis, so the second deserved more budget even though they looked identical in the ad account. How to apply: tag each campaign by the offer and product group it pushes; apply that group's real gross margin, after discount and delivery costs, to its attributed revenue; subtract spend; and rank campaigns on contribution dollars per dollar spent. Tagging COGS on every Shopify product is what makes this possible; without it, every campaign is assumed to carry the store's average margin and discount campaigns look better than they are.
conditions: Accounts running mixed offers, discount codes or product groups with different margins.
fails_when: All campaigns sell similar products at the same price and margin.

Profit contribution 3 versus 4

claim: A product with a suspiciously low CAC may sell without ads; test pulling its paid spend, keep the full margin (the tee's contribution would rise from $12 to $27), and move budget to products that need paid help.
body: Very cheap acquisition can mean the product has its own pull: word of mouth, a viral moment, strong product market fit, or store foot traffic. If people would buy it anyway, the ad spend is paying for sales you already had. In Blue Sense's example, the tee's $15 CAC was the warning sign. If paid spend on it stops and sales hold, each tee earns its full $27 of gross margin instead of $12, and the budget can move to the hoodie, which does not sell on its own and needs paid traffic to reach its sell-through target. How to apply: take the products with the lowest CAC, pause or sharply cut their dedicated spend for a few weeks (or exclude them from catalogue ads), and watch total units sold of that product across every channel, including stores. If units barely drop, keep spend low and reinvest in slower sellers. Blue Sense says this matters most for omnichannel and large brands, where organic and store demand are big.
conditions: Larger or omnichannel brands with strong organic demand on some products.
fails_when: The low CAC comes from a genuinely efficient ad rather than organic demand, which a pause test shows as a sales drop; small brands with little organic demand.
numbers: Tee CAC $15; contribution $12 with ads vs $27 gross margin without

claim: For some large retail brands, more TikTok spend lifts Meta and Google ROAS while TikTok's own ROAS stays weak, so a C-suite cutting TikTok on its ROAS removes the demand the other channels harvest.
body: TikTok often reaches new people who never click off the app, or who view a product page and leave. Meta then retargets them through the pixel, and the rest later search the brand on Google and buy. So when TikTok spend goes up, Meta and Google ROAS go up and TikTok's does not. Blue Sense was seeing this in large retail accounts at the time of recording and notes it may change. The danger is leadership reading channel ROAS and moving budget from TikTok to Meta and from Meta to Google, which strips out the top of the funnel to feed the bottom; the bottom stops working once nothing fills it. How to apply: before cutting an upper-funnel channel on its attributed ROAS, check what happened to Meta retargeting and branded search conversions while it ran; judge it on total new customers and acquisition MER over the period, or with a geo or holdout test; and report to leadership on those, not on channel ROAS.
conditions: Large retail or fashion brands running TikTok, Meta and Google together.
fails_when: Small brands where TikTok reach is minor, or brands whose test shows TikTok does not lift other channels.
asks: TikTok ROAS is bad, should I cut it?
Why does Meta ROAS go up when we spend more on TikTok?

Is Google really driving the sales it reports?

claim: Maximise-conversions bidding sends spend to the lowest-CPA product even when another earns more per sale; Blue Sense's $90 hoodie made $24 contribution at a $45 CAC, the $50 tee $12 at $15.
body: Default bidding on Meta, Google and TikTok optimises for the cheapest conversion. Example: hoodie at $90 with $21 COGS, $69 gross margin, $45 CAC and $24 contribution; t-shirt at $50 with $23 COGS, $27 gross margin, $15 CAC and $12 contribution. The tee wins the auction on CPA, so the algorithm gives it most of the budget, though each hoodie sale earns twice as much. Switching to value bidding does not fix it, because the tee also has the better ROAS (about 3.3 against 2.0). The fix is segmentation: split campaigns into product groups by contribution per sale and set budgets by contribution, not platform efficiency. How to apply: keep a sheet per product or category with price, COGS, gross margin, current CAC or CPA and contribution after ad cost; group products with similar economics into their own campaigns; give more budget to the higher-contribution group; and judge the result on total contribution, not blended ROAS.
conditions: Catalogues whose products differ widely in price and margin, with enough spend to fund separate campaigns.
fails_when: Products earn similar contribution per sale, or spend is too low to split without starving each campaign of conversions.
numbers: Hoodie: $90 price, $21 COGS, $45 CAC, $24 contribution, ROAS 2.0
Tee: $50 price, $23 COGS, $15 CAC, $12 contribution, ROAS about 3.3

claim: Scale each main channel until its marginal acquisition MER reaches break-even, then stop; add new channels only once your three primary channels all sit at that profit frontier.
body: Part of this section is missing from the transcript, so this card keeps to the rule as stated. For each channel, find the point where the next dollar of spend only just breaks even on new-customer contribution. Below that point more spend adds profit; past it, each extra dollar loses money even if blended numbers still look fine. Keep every primary channel pushed to that point all the time, and only then add a fourth or fifth channel, because opening new channels before the main ones are maxed spreads budget and attention for a lower return. How to apply: for each channel, use months of daily spend and new-customer revenue to estimate how acquisition MER falls as spend rises; compute break-even acquisition MER from first-order gross margin (break-even is 1 divided by the gross margin on new orders); raise budget while the marginal acquisition MER is above that line and hold once it reaches it.
conditions: Brands with enough spend history on each channel to see diminishing returns.
fails_when: A new channel reaches a market the main ones cannot (a new country or audience), or proven repeat purchase justifies acquiring below first-order break-even.
numbers: Three primary channels before adding more

claim: Use paid media to turn grade C and D stock back into cash at break-even or a small loss, through an isolated funnel, whitelisted creator pages, or a new country where heavy discounts will not cheapen the home brand.
body: Example: a launch sold $100,000 of a $1M order (at sell value) and now has about 400 days of stock on hand. Owners and CFOs tend to tackle this alone, but paid media can clear it. Options Blue Sense uses: give the product its own ad funnel and landing page, separate from the main site, and run it at break-even or slightly below; push it through whitelisted creator or partner pages; or, as they did for one client, take grade D stock into a new country they expected to suit it, discount hard there, and keep the main market's prices and brand intact. The obstacle is incentives. An agency judged only on profit or ROAS will send every dollar to grade A products, and B, C and D stock never gets the budget it needs. How to apply: share stock grades and days on hand with the ad team monthly, agree a separate clearance budget with a target of cash recovered rather than ROAS, and stop the push once stock reaches the agreed level.
conditions: Brands with slow stock worth clearing and an audience or market that would buy it.
fails_when: The stock is so unwanted that even break-even ads cannot move it (liquidate or write it off), or luxury brands where any visible discounting harms the brand.

About 400 days of stock on hand

claim: When unsold November stock and a rising MER hit in February, do not cut media 40%; a short lift in MER from about 30% to 35%, aimed at C and D stock, can restore cash faster.
body: Example P&L: cost of delivery 30%, marketing 25%, opex 15%, profit 30%. In February revenue dips, MER climbs to 30% and profit falls to 25%, with November stock in grades C and D still unsold. The typical CFO move is to cut marketing by 40% to save cash. Two problems. If paid media is driving most of the revenue, the cut lowers revenue too, MER does not improve, and more cuts follow in a downward spiral. And the leftover November stock needs more selling, not less. Blue Sense's alternative: accept a temporary MER of about 35%, with the extra 5 points spent only on moving C and D stock, even at little or no profit, so the stock turns back into cash and the business can get back to its normal revenue level. How to apply: separate the efficiency problem (is the core spend inefficient?) from the cash problem (is stock stuck?); fix efficiency within the core spend, and fund a time-limited clearance budget with its own cash-recovered target.
conditions: Seasonal brands with post-peak overstock where paid media drives most revenue.
fails_when: Marketing really is inefficient at the margin, or the extra spend cannot move the stock near break-even.

claim: A home-market ad with over $200,000 in lifetime spend will very likely win in the US; one brand doing $13M to $14M took its five-plus such winners there, and the US became 75% of the business.
body: Blue Sense says most brands doing $10 million or more online in Australia have at least five Meta ads that each spent over $200,000, and an ad that wins in one big English-speaking market (Australia, UK, Canada, NZ) tends to win in the others. The brand in the case was spending about $300,000 a month in Australia, where Blue Sense says it is very hard for an e-commerce brand to spend more than about $500,000 a month before reaching everyone every 30 days and frequency soars. Their advice was to skip the long checklist: set up Shopify Markets for the US, ship from Australia to validate, localise the site so it does not read as Australian, and launch the winners. A few months later the US was 75% of the business, which Blue Sense estimates is now $30 million to $40 million, and more profitable than Australia, an outlier. How to apply: list your ads by lifetime spend; if you have five or more over $200,000 and your home market is near its ceiling, test them in the US.
conditions: Brands over about $10M a year online at home with several high-spend winning Meta ads and a home market near saturation.
fails_when: Smaller brands without proven high-spend winners; Blue Sense stresses most brands are not in this position.

claim: Launch US-wide unless one of three things holds: strong seasonality, a small budget (around $10,000 a month), or retail presence in a few states, in which case concentrate spend by state.
body: Blue Sense has run successful US launches both ways, nationwide and state by state with a rollout. Pick state-level targeting when: 1) the product is seasonal, for example summer fashion, which should not go to cold-winter states (though US-wide targeting tends to drift toward the right states anyway, so this is mainly about cost); 2) the budget is small, since spreading $10,000 a month across the whole US is thin and concentrating it in a few likely states gives clearer reads; 3) you have retail presence in specific states, often the case for fashion brands that win a few stockists, so spend reinforces those stores. If none of these apply, with a big budget, no strong seasonality and no local stores, a US-wide launch is fine. Keep sales tax in mind when you concentrate spend in a few states.
conditions: Brands launching paid social into the US for the first time.
fails_when: Products that only sell in certain regions for legal or climate reasons; very large budgets that can test both approaches.

claim: Blue Sense sees CPMs track the action rate of the optimisation event: lead magnet pages converting 30% to 70% run around $25 CPM, while book-a-call pages at 3% to 6% sit near $100.
body: Stepping outside e-commerce to make the point, Blue Sense compares two funnels that fire the same lead event. A book-a-call page converts 3% to 6% of visitors and its CPMs are around $100. A free lead magnet page converts 30% to 70% and its CPMs are around $25, roughly four times cheaper. Their hypothesis: Meta's estimated action rate for the event drives CPM, so when most visitors complete the event Meta lowers the price, and when few do it charges more. Meta may also infer that a booked call is worth more, but they cannot prove how it would know, since the event is the same. If action rate is the driver, it can be used: design the step you optimise for so that a high share of visitors complete it. For a store, that suggests testing a landing page or optimisation event with a higher completion rate when CPMs are crippling, while watching that the cheaper event still leads to purchases. Treat this as a practitioner's hypothesis, not documented fact.
conditions: Accounts able to test different landing pages or optimisation events; most relevant for lead-generation and high-ticket funnels.
fails_when: Optimising a store for a cheap upper-funnel event (add to cart, lead) that does not lead to purchases; lower CPMs then buy the wrong people.

claim: Campaigns and ad sets exist to wall off data, each learning on its own model, so only split them for truly different buyers (ice baths versus saunas); low-spend, hyper-segmented accounts starve every model.
body: Every major platform (Meta, Google, TikTok, Pinterest, Snapchat) uses the same campaign, ad set, ad hierarchy, and Blue Sense argues it is not there for your reporting convenience. It is how you tell the algorithm that some ads should learn separately. Two campaigns do not share conversion data; each trains its own machine learning model on its own results. That is right when the products resonate with different people: a brand selling both ice baths and saunas may want separate campaigns so each model learns its own buyer. It is wrong when an account with modest spend is split into many campaigns and ad sets with few ads each, so conversion data is spread so thin that nothing learns well. Their rule across Meta, Google and TikTok: consolidate wherever there is no clear reason to separate, because pooling conversion data improves performance. Summary of their algorithm advice: go broad with exclusions, feed diverse concepts, keep EMQ high, fix the economics, and consolidate.
conditions: Meta, Google and TikTok accounts of any size; matters most for accounts with limited weekly conversions.
fails_when: Businesses with genuinely different products, countries or sub-brands needing separate budgets and learning, where merging blurs who buys what.

claim: Every Meta impression passes retrieval (Andromeda narrows tens of millions of ads to a few thousand), ranking, then the auction within about 200 milliseconds; GEM made retrieval multimodal, which is why creative diversity now matters.
body: Blue Sense sources this to Meta's engineering material. Stage one, retrieval: from tens of millions of eligible ads, the system shortlists a few thousand relevant to the person about to see one. Stage two, ranking: using that person's history with ads and organic content, it picks the hundreds most likely to convert. Stage three, the auction among those. Each update hits one stage. Lattice (2023) consolidated ranking. Sequence learning (November 2024) let Meta optimise across sequences of ads in a buyer's journey, which is when the one-ad-per-ad-set setup stopped making sense. Andromeda (December 2024) rebuilt retrieval so the system reads your creative to decide who it is relevant to. GEM gave Andromeda multimodal ability, so it watches video and hears audio and can group near-identical ads; GEM, more than Andromeda, is the reason similar ads now collapse together. Then an adaptive ranking model that tunes compute per impression and speeds up relevance: Meta claims about 3% more conversions and 5% more clicks, and users now see a page's ads almost as soon as they engage with its organic posts.
conditions: Meta advertising as described in Meta's published engineering material up to mid 2026.
fails_when: Meta changes the system again; treat names and dates as a snapshot and recheck against current documentation.
numbers: whole process about 200 milliseconds
tens of millions of ads narrowed to a few thousand, then hundreds
Lattice 2023; sequence learning Nov 2024; Andromeda Dec 2024
adaptive ranking claim: +3% conversions, +5% CTR

claim: Expect Meta algorithm upgrades to raise CPMs rather than your ROAS: the platform converts better, charges more for it, and a well-run account's efficiency should stay roughly flat.
body: Meta's updates are not designed to hurt advertisers. Each one aims for a small lift in total conversions across the platform, a few percent, and Meta then captures that value by letting CPMs rise, which grows its earnings. Blue Sense's read: after billions in investment for a 3% lift, Meta taking much of the gain is to be expected. The practical consequence for a brand is that ROAS should not climb as the platform improves, and it should not fall either; it should move sideways as long as you adapt your account to each change (broad targeting, diverse concepts, consolidated structure). So if ROAS drops after an update, the cause is more likely your account failing to adapt (too few distinct concepts, fragmented structure) than the update itself. How to apply: when reviewing a year of performance, read rising CPMs with flat ROAS as normal, and treat a sustained ROAS decline as a signal to check creative diversity and structure.
conditions: Meta accounts compared over periods that include major algorithm changes.
fails_when: Periods of unusual auction pressure (Black Friday, elections, new competitors) where CPM shifts have causes other than Meta's own updates.
numbers: Meta claims about 3% conversion lift from one update

claim: Meta now places each user in a vector space of tens of thousands of dimensions; broad targeting sprinkles spend across it and homes in on whoever buys, so creative, not interests, chooses the audience.
body: Old Meta targeting tagged people with labels: interact with a pets post in any way, even a hostile comment, and you get a pets interest. Advertisers stacked labels (pets plus cat owner plus family plus city) to narrow down, but that was hard to measure without big budgets and fatigued small audiences fast. Today every interaction nudges a user's position in a huge vector space, so people with similar behaviour cluster together. When you go broad, Meta spends a little across many regions of that space, sees who engages and buys, then concentrates delivery around those clusters. Broad does not mean everyone sees your ads; it means Meta finds the buyers based on how they react to your creative. That is why Blue Sense says broad beats interest targeting on large data sets over time, and why the content of the ad (who it speaks to, what problem it names) is now the main targeting lever. How to apply: stop building interest stacks for purchase campaigns, go broad with exclusions, and change who you reach by changing the creative.
conditions: Meta purchase-optimised campaigns with enough conversion volume for the system to learn, typically tens of purchases a week or more.
fails_when: Very new pixels with almost no conversion data, or niche B2B-style products where a tiny audience means broad delivery wastes early spend.
numbers: vector space of tens of thousands of dimensions

claim: Meta's auction ranks bid times estimated action rate (expected CTR times expected conversion rate) plus ad quality, so a competitor bidding 50 cents can beat your $1 bid by being more relevant.
body: At the final stage each ad's total value is roughly bid multiplied by estimated action rate, plus an ad quality score. Estimated action rate is expected click-through rate multiplied by expected conversion rate for that person. Because relevance multiplies the bid, two advertisers showing the same product to the same person can win at very different prices. The cheapest way to lower costs is therefore to be more relevant, not to bid more. Two cautions from Blue Sense. First, Meta describes estimated action rate and ad quality as diagnostics of past performance used to adjust your bid per user, not dials you can turn in the live auction; think rear-view mirror, not steering wheel. Second, you cannot optimise relevance in the abstract, because an ad is relevant to some people and not others; the practical route is more diverse concepts so more people find one relevant. In their experience estimated action rate seems closely tied to CPMs. Quality score tricks are, in Nathan's words, the star signs of Meta ads: unmeasurable, so do the basics and move on.
conditions: Meta auctions for any objective; the formula is Meta's published model.
fails_when: Treating the diagnostics as levers, for example chasing CTR with clickbait that lowers conversion rate and so lowers estimated action rate overall.

claim: Missing conversions shrink Meta's view of your action rate: if it sees 70 of 100 sales, a real 3% conversion rate reads as about 2%, which lowers your auction value and raises costs.
body: Signal quality is a hidden lever on CPMs because it feeds estimated action rate in the bid formula. Blue Sense's example: your ads drive 100 conversions, but pixel and Conversions API only report 70 back. Meta then believes your conversion rate is about 2% when it is actually about 3%, which might be among the best in your category. Because the system underrates you, your estimated action rate is lower, your effective bid in each auction is lower, and you lose auctions you should win. Clean, well-matched events (high event match quality, EMQ) let Meta see your true performance and deliver more cheaply. How to apply: check Events Manager for event match quality on Purchase, confirm the pixel and Conversions API both fire and deduplicate, and pass customer details such as email and phone where your consent setup allows. Keep it in proportion, though: Blue Sense ranks better first-order economics as a far bigger lever than EMQ improvements.
conditions: Meta purchase campaigns where a meaningful share of conversions may be untracked (iOS, ad blockers, broken setup).
fails_when: Accounts that already track near all conversions; further gains are too small to notice.

true CVR 3% read as 2%

claim: On Meta you still truly control exclusions, minimum age, locations and languages; age bands, gender and interests are only suggestions, and lookalike and interest targeting were deprecated in July 2025.
body: With broad targeting, Meta looks for clusters likely to buy, and one of the most likely clusters is warm, existing customers. Left alone, it will happily push budget there because they convert easily, which flatters ROAS and wastes acquisition money. That is why exclusions are the most important control left: make sure existing customers (and recent purchasers) are excluded from cold campaigns. The other hard controls are minimum age, locations (never just set worldwide) and languages. Meta treats age ranges, gender and interest inputs as hints, not limits, so ads may serve outside them. Blue Sense notes interest and lookalike targeting were deprecated in July 2025, and calls lookalikes long dead. How to apply: build a customer list exclusion (purchasers, ideally synced from Shopify or Klaviyo) on every prospecting ad set, set a minimum age and countries, and stop spending time tuning age bands or interest stacks.
conditions: Meta prospecting campaigns optimised for purchases.
fails_when: Retention or win-back campaigns where existing customers are the intended audience, or legal minimum age and regional restrictions that need stricter setup.

claim: There is no Meta documentation behind the 'never raise budget more than 20%' rule; Blue Sense raises budgets faster routinely, and the dip people see is a purchase lag from newly reached audiences.
body: Many guides warn that raising a budget by more than 20% resets learning. Blue Sense says Meta's documentation contains nothing of the sort and they increase budgets by more than 20% all the time without harm. What people actually see is a business effect, not an algorithm effect: higher spend reaches new people who need time and several exposures before they buy. So if you triple a budget today, revenue does not triple today; it catches up over the following days as those new prospects convert. How to apply: when scaling a winning campaign, make the increase you need, then judge it over a window that matches your normal time to purchase (check the click to purchase lag in your data), not the same day. They list other myths in the same vein: interest and lookalike targeting still being the edge, Lattice being new (it is from 2023), and cookies disappearing (Chrome kept them, decided April 2025).
conditions: Meta campaigns with steady conversion volume being scaled up.
fails_when: Tiny campaigns with very few weekly conversions, where big jumps can swing delivery noticeably; and products with long purchase cycles, where the lag is longer than a few days.

claim: Test a new concept as one ad set holding several ads across awareness stages (for example one unaware, one problem aware, two solution aware for expecting parents), launched together.
body: Blue Sense plans Lovevery's next batch as 15 concepts, each built around a persona. For expecting parents, one concept carries four hooks at different stages: an unaware hook (your baby will not see this nursery the way you do), a problem hook (what to take off the registry) and two solution aware hooks (when to order so it arrives on day one; the registry item guests keep asking about). All go in one ad set and launch on the same day; that ad set is the test of the concept. Other concepts follow the same pattern for newborn parents, gift buyers such as grandparents, and a subscriber retention test. Weighting for the batch moves toward expecting parents and gift buyers, with a few retention ads. How to apply: for each concept, write 3 to 5 hooks across stages, put them in one ad set, and launch together so delivery picks the best entry point. Judge the concept on the ad set's cost per purchase, then scale the winning hooks. Point each concept to the landing page that matches its persona.
conditions: Accounts with budget to give each concept ad set enough spend to reach a read (cost per purchase target times about 10 to 20 purchases).
fails_when: Small budgets that cannot fund several ad sets at once; accounts testing single variables where one ad per ad set is cleaner.

claim: A 2x ROAS on cold prospecting is usually worth more than a 7x on retargeting; most accounts already overspend on middle and bottom funnel, so do not shift 30% of budget down the funnel.
body: Bottom of funnel campaigns (retargeting, existing customers, DPAs) always look best in the platform because they reach people who were already about to buy. Top of funnel cold campaigns look worst because they create the demand that the lower campaigns later harvest. If you read the numbers at face value and move budget from a 2x cold campaign to a 7x retargeting campaign, the business slowly starves: fewer new people enter, so in a few weeks the retargeting pool shrinks and its ROAS falls too. Blue Sense says it rarely sees an account that needs more middle or bottom funnel spend; almost everyone overspends there. Growth comes from more efficient spend at the top: cold Meta with existing customers excluded and cold creative, YouTube, TikTok and other upper funnel channels. How to apply: set targets by funnel stage, not one ROAS for all. Judge cold campaigns on new customer metrics (acquisition MER, CAC) and judge retargeting by frequency and incrementality. When you want growth, ask where you can add cold spend profitably, never which retargeting campaign has the best ROAS.
conditions: Accounts with separate cold and warm campaigns or audiences; brands trying to grow new customer revenue.
fails_when: Brands in a cash crunch harvesting existing demand on purpose, or very small accounts with almost no warm audience yet.

common mistake: moving 30% of spend into middle or bottom funnel

The account was heavily over-segmented, with around 25 campaigns using bid caps and cost caps, because the previous media buyer had too few ads to work with and fell back on structure tricks. Blue Sense's audit named ad count as the bottleneck. Without any in-house production yet, the team pulled past performers that had been switched off, reworked some lightly, and relaunched them, taking the account to about 60 live ads. Results: spend rose by about $40,000 a month, CAC fell about 20 to 30%, and new customer revenue grew about 28%, from memory of the case study. The ending matters too. The founder saw Meta spend as a revenue driver and production as a cost, refused to fund new creative, and backed out of agency deals. As the 60 ads fatigued and had to be switched off, the account slid back to where it started. How to use this: if live ads are very few relative to spend, an archive relaunch is a fast, cheap fix. Treat it as a bridge while you build a steady production pipeline, not as the plan.

claim: About 90% of accounts do not need a website visitor retargeting campaign; the Audience segments breakdown usually shows prospecting already spends enough on engaged visitors at high frequency.
body: Blue Sense splits retargeting into two kinds. Website visitor retargeting reaches warm people who showed intent but did not buy. Existing customer retargeting reaches past buyers to get a second or third order. For most accounts, around 90% of them, a dedicated visitor retargeting campaign is unnecessary, because the testing and scaling campaigns already put a good share of spend on those people. You can check: set up audience segments in Advertiser settings (engaged audience and existing customers), then in Ads Manager use the Breakdown menu, Audience segments, to see spend, ROAS and frequency for new, engaged and existing people. Existing should be near zero in prospecting if excluded; engaged will usually show enough spend at a high enough frequency already. Existing customer retargeting depends on the business: a new store under about $50,000 a month has few customers; a furniture brand with rare repeats needs almost none; a supplement brand with low order value and high repeat or subscription should run some. If repeat buying is expected, keep it low and controlled and use frequency as the measure; if not, skip it.

claim: Above about $250k a month, consider a second Meta ad account on the same pixel with a different bid strategy, to enter other auctions and keep acquisition running if the main account is banned.
body: For the largest spend tier, from about $250,000 to millions a month, Blue Sense gives strategies rather than one template. The first is a second ad account. It uses the same pixel, and the same or a different page, but runs different bid logic: if the main account uses maximize conversions, the second might use maximize conversion value, cost caps or bid caps. The idea is that the second account wins auctions the main one does not enter, getting more volume through the same creative. A possible downside is bidding against yourself and raising CPMs; with the same page and pixel this should be limited, and nobody has proven it either way. The clearer benefit is risk. If the main account is banned or its payment method fails, a brand that depends on Meta for new customers can lose acquisition for a week. A second account holding even 10% of the spend can be scaled up immediately. Blue Sense notes this tactic changes often, so check current practice before relying on it. How to apply: once Meta is a large share of new customer acquisition, set up a second account with its own payment method and run a smaller share through it.
conditions: Brands spending roughly $250,000 a month or more on Meta.
fails_when: Smaller accounts, where splitting conversion data hurts more than the risk saved; tactic details change every few months.

claim: Above about $50,000 a month, the media buyer's job is portfolio management across ads and products; chasing profit alone can leave $2 million of P&L profit beside $3 million of unsold stock, a $1 million cash hole.
body: At this spend, Blue Sense sees three portfolios to manage. Ads: Pareto concentration happens naturally, so decide whether to allow it or add structure so you are not over-exposed to a few creatives. Products: the same 80/20 skew happens across the catalogue. Commercials: is this a profit and loss play or a balance sheet play? Agencies are judged on efficiency and profit contribution, so they optimise for it. But a brand can over-optimise for profit and under-optimise for its balance sheet, ending with slow stock tied up in the warehouse. Blue Sense's illustration: $2 million of profit on paper, $3 million of unsold inventory, so the business is about $1 million short of cash, because the profit it made went into stock. Paid media can fix this. Restructure the account to sell through the slow stock, accept lower efficiency for a period, and make creative for those products, even though it hurts to approve. How to apply it: give your media buyer stock levels by product each week, flag aged or overstocked lines, agree a sell through target, and judge that campaign on cash recovered as well as on ROAS. A media buyer who does not know your inventory is a risk.
conditions: Brands spending around $50,000 a month or more with meaningful inventory across many products.
fails_when: Made to order or very small catalogues with little stock risk; the $2 million and $3 million figures are an illustration.

claim: Aim roughly 70 to 90% of effort at cold buyers, about 20% at the middle and 5 to 10% at the bottom; in consolidated accounts, set this split through the share of ads you make per awareness stage.
body: Blue Sense's rough funnel split puts most budget on reaching new people, around a fifth on engaged audiences, and a small slice on bottom of funnel retargeting (the numbers are directional, not meant to sum exactly). In the past you enforced this with separate cold, warm and hot campaigns, each with its own budget. With today's consolidated broad campaigns, Meta decides who sees what, so the split is now driven by the creative you feed it. How to apply it: tag every ad you produce by the awareness stage it is written for (unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware). Keep about 70 to 90% of new assets aimed at the earlier stages and about 20% at product aware buyers with offers, reviews and objection handling. Keep a separate small retargeting campaign only if you need firm control of bottom of funnel spend, usually for existing customers. Each month, compare the stage mix of new ads and of spend; if spend drifts heavily to bottom funnel ads, brief more cold assets rather than editing budgets. Blue Sense says there is a better way to size the bottom funnel budget, but this split is the starting point.
conditions: Meta accounts using broad or consolidated campaigns where creative steers delivery.
fails_when: Brands with very long buying cycles or high prices that genuinely need heavier mid funnel nurture; tiny accounts with only a few ads.

claim: At about $50k to $250k a month, add one to three cold campaigns only for a clear commercial reason, such as separate persona funnels for one SKU or a high-LTV category given a looser CPA target.
body: In the middle spend tier, the structure grows: more ad sets because there is more creative to test, and perhaps two or three cold campaigns, plus a retargeting campaign that is still mostly existing customers. Each new campaign must have a business reason. For a one-SKU CPG brand, campaigns can be separate funnels for repositioned versions of the product. Blue Sense's fish oil example: one funnel for people aged 65 and over with arthritis, using video sales letters, native statics, testimonials from older people and TV-style ads in UGC format; another for people aged 25 to 35 focused on health or performance at work, with different landing pages, different faces and possibly whitelisting instead of the brand page. They are almost two businesses, so they get two campaigns. For a fashion brand with many SKUs, it might be a new arrivals campaign to lift sell-through, or a campaign for a category that LTV analysis shows brings higher first-order value and better repeat rates (pants, in the example), so it can run a higher CPA target and acquire more of those customers. Adding campaigns because 'one seems weird at $100k a month' breaks the rule that every split must keep data readable. How to apply: write the commercial reason beside each campaign name.

claim: Avoid CBO when order value is high and purchases few (for example $10,000 AOV and about 5 orders a day): Meta then allocates on CTR, CPC and hold rate, which barely correlate with return.
body: Blue Sense works with a brand whose average order is about $10,000, doing around $50,000 a day from only about five orders. With so few purchases attributed each day, a CBO cannot allocate budget between ad sets on purchases or ROAS, because there is not enough signal. Meta moves upstream and leans on pre-click and early signals instead: click-through rate, cost per click, hold rate. Across large data sets, Blue Sense finds CPC has almost no relationship with return on ad spend except at the extremes (a very bad CPC does mean poor returns). So budget ends up following the ads with the best soft metrics rather than the ones that drive sales. How to apply: for high-AOV, low-volume accounts, use ad set budgets so you control spend, consider optimising for a higher-volume event that correlates with purchase if your data supports it, judge ad sets on longer windows, and design a structure specific to the business rather than a default template. The broader point: account design depends on unit economics, audiences, and order value and conversion volume, so no two good accounts look the same.
conditions: Furniture, jewellery and other high-ticket brands with few daily purchases.
fails_when: Accounts with dozens of purchases per ad set per week, where CBO has enough purchase signal.

claim: Avoid Meta's flexible ads (several creatives in one ad): you cannot see which creative worked, Meta may crop or turn them into carousels, and if used at all they should only hold near-identical creatives.
body: Flexible ads (the name changes often) let you load around five creatives into a single ad. It sounds like consolidation, which Meta prefers, but it breaks the feedback loop. When the ad performs well you cannot tell which creative drove it, so you do not know what to make more of, and when it fails you cannot tell what to cut. Blue Sense also dislikes the presentation: you lose control of cropping, so 1:1 images can be stretched into Story placements or Story images cropped into feed, and Meta can stitch several flexible ads into a carousel the client never approved. The only real reason to use them is to get around the page's active ad limit, and there are better ways to do that (see page strategy). If you must, group only very similar creatives so a good result still tells you something about that type of ad. How to apply: turn flexible ads off when launching, check older ads for them, and keep one creative per ad so ad level data stays readable for creative decisions.

fails_when: Accounts hitting the ad limit with no other workaround, using sets of near-identical creatives.

claim: Blue Sense's 2026 Meta settings audit: turn off flexible ads, cost caps and 1-day view in the primary account, disable Advantage+ creative enhancements at ad and advertiser level, and check the Klaviyo audience segment sync.
body: Five settings Blue Sense checks. 1) Flexible ads off, because you cannot read which creative worked, cropping is uncontrolled and Meta may build carousels from them. 2) Cost caps or bid caps off in the primary account unless you spend over about $200,000 a month; bidding is rarely the bottleneck. 3) 1-day view attribution off, or at least excluded from decisions about which ad sets get budget, because it over-credits existing customer purchases. 4) Advantage+ creative optimisations. They must be turned off on each ad you launch, and also in Advertiser settings under the creative section, where automated defaults will otherwise switch enhancements back on over time. Doing only one of the two is not enough. 5) Audience segments. Make sure existing customers and engaged audiences are defined correctly. Blue Sense sees the Klaviyo to Meta customer sync break from time to time; when it does, existing customers start counting as new, the account spends on them believing they are new, and data integrity erodes. How to apply: run this five-point check monthly and after any Meta interface change, and set an alert or reminder to confirm the Klaviyo sync is still populating the customer audience.
conditions: Meta accounts in 2026 using Klaviyo or another customer list source for audience segments.
fails_when: Meta renames and moves these settings often; confirm the current location before acting.

claim: Blue Sense's preferred large-account setup is a CBO with minimum and maximum ad set spend limits controlling about 60% of budget, leaving about 40% for Meta to place freely; it is overkill at around $10k a month.
body: Pure CBO can starve new creative and expensive assets, such as a $20,000 campaign shoot or a $20,000 influencer partnership ad that then gets no spend. Pure ABO gives up Meta's ability to find efficiency. Blue Sense runs most of its accounts these days as a middle path: a CBO campaign where minimum and maximum spend limits on ad sets force about 60% of the budget into places the team chooses (new tests, partnership ads, priority concepts), while the remaining 40% or so flows wherever Meta finds best. Setting min and max limits on every ad set is effectively running an ABO with extra work, so the split is the point. Blue Sense says the approach needs a lot of oversight and management time, which is worth it on large budgets with large revenue, but for an account spending around $10,000 a month it is overkill: just pick ABO or CBO by your risk and efficiency preference. How to apply: when you manage six figures or more a month and creative is being starved, put minimum spend limits on the ad sets that must get tested and leave a free share uncapped.

claim: Budget existing customer ads in dollars, not a percentage: customers times monthly frequency times CPM per 1,000; 300,000 customers at 3 impressions and a $2.50 CPM is about $2,250 a month.
body: Brands, even very large ones, ask what percentage of budget should target existing customers: 20%, 30%, 40%? Blue Sense calls percentage the wrong frame. Meta's Advantage+ existing customer spend cap, set as a percentage, made this habit worse. The share swings with the size of your customer base and your prospecting budget, so it tells you nothing about how often each customer actually sees you. Instead, decide how many times a month you want each existing customer to see an ad and work out the dollars: number of existing customers times desired monthly frequency, divided by 1,000, times the CPM you pay on that audience (find it with the Audience segments breakdown). Example: 300,000 customers, 3 impressions a month, $2.50 CPM gives about $2,250 a month. Real CPMs are usually higher, but the point holds: most brands need far less than they spend. Even brands with millions of customers can usually reach them 3 to 6 times a month for $10,000 to $40,000, while Blue Sense sees small brands spending $40,000 a month here. Then check two things: does the spend return enough to be profitable, and is frequency reasonable.
conditions: Brands with an existing customer list synced to Meta and repeat purchase behaviour.
fails_when: Brands with almost no repeat purchase (furniture), where existing customer spend should be close to zero; very small customer bases where minimum delivery limits apply.

claim: CBO lets Meta spread budget and usually beats a novice, but it gives about 20% of ads 80% of spend, starving new creative; ABO forces spend into tests. Choose by your risk appetite and the buyer's skill.
body: With campaign budget (CBO) Meta moves money between ad sets toward what it predicts is most efficient. In most cases it distributes budget better than a person would, which is good for short-term efficiency. The catch is a strong 80/20 split: about 20% of ads take about 80% of spend. If you make 100 new ads a month, many never get tested; paid influencer partnership ads may get nothing; and spend piles into one creative, so when it fatigues you have no proven backups. With ad set budgets (ABO), you decide where money goes, which can lower risk and force proper testing, but a careless buyer can burn money. Blue Sense's rule for hiring: a first-year in-house media buyer at a $10M brand should run CBO, because Meta will allocate better than they will; an experienced buyer who weighs risk, profit and efficiency can run ABO or a mix to steer spend deliberately. Blue Sense has seen both ABO and CBO run most of the spend on accounts spending a quarter of a million dollars a day, so it is a preference, not a rule. How to apply: decide how much you trust Meta to find winners in your account, then pick the structure that matches that trust and your buyer's experience.

fails_when: High order value, low conversion volume accounts, where CBO optimises on soft signals (see the separate card).

claim: Check any account structure with four questions: does it produce data you can read and act on, does it match how the business makes money, does it fit the spend tier and creative output, and do support layers match retention?
body: Blue Sense's closing test for account structure. 1) Does the structure produce data I can read to make decisions? The whole point of structure is a feedback loop: if naming, consolidation or flexible ads make results unreadable, it fails. 2) Does it match how the business actually makes money? Campaign splits should follow margins, product groups, personas and inventory needs, not habit. 3) Is it right for the spend tier and creative throughput? A $10,000 a month account and a $1M a month account need different complexity, and the number of new ads you produce limits how many concepts and ad sets you can sustain. 4) Are the support layers, DPAs, site visitor and existing customer retargeting, sized to the brand's real retention and repeat purchase? That decides how much spend they deserve. What stays the same at every tier: every added layer must keep data integrity and commercial alignment; breakdowns and ad-level views are no more productive at high spend; the concept framework still applies at $300,000 a day; and KPIs sit at ad set and campaign level. How to apply: answer the four questions for your account; any no means restructure.

claim: Check frequency on existing customers and retargeting: Blue Sense flags overspend when existing customers see ads more than about 8 times a month, and keeps retargeting frequency under 7 on a 30-day window.
body: Platforms like spending on existing customers because those conversions are easy to claim, and they like long attribution windows for the same reason. So retargeting and existing customer spend tends to creep up while its ROAS looks great. Frequency is the simplest live check. Blue Sense's thresholds: if existing customers are being reached more than about 8 times a month, you are almost certainly overspending, because those extra impressions are not incremental; its retargeting KPI is a frequency no higher than 7 on a 30-day window, and for many brands a 3 to 6 frequency on existing customers is enough. It also sees audits where 50% of all spend reaches existing and engaged audiences, which it calls a common and costly mistake. How to apply: in Ads Manager, select the account or campaign, use the Audience segments breakdown to split new, engaged and existing, add the Frequency and Reach columns, and set the date range to the last 30 days. If existing customer frequency is far above your target, cut that budget. Pair frequency with profit: an extra $1,000 there should return enough revenue to pay for itself.

fails_when: Launch or drop periods where a short burst of high frequency to customers is intended.

claim: Consolidate Meta campaigns because conversion data is mostly siloed per campaign: 100 purchases a month split over four campaigns leaves 25 each, and accounts usually improve once a campaign passes about 100 to 200 a month.
body: Every major ad platform uses the same campaign, ad set (or ad group) and ad structure, and data is shared unevenly across those levels. Campaigns share some signal with each other, but not all conversion data. Campaign segmentation exists for business reasons: to move budget through promotions over time, and to separate business units with different buyers (pets versus children) so delivery is not confused. The cost is data. A small account getting 100 purchases a month across four campaigns gives each only 25 to learn from, and small samples make Meta's targeting guesses noisy, so results get worse. Blue Sense often sees efficiency improve, not fall, once a campaign crosses about 100 to 200 conversions a month, because the system finally knows who to target. Ad sets matter less: data from the campaign flows down and ad sets share more, so splitting or merging ad sets moves efficiency by only about 5% to 10%, noticeable at scale but not decisive. Before 2021 the opposite was true: small-sample bias in each new ad set made segmentation and interest testing pay. How to apply: add a campaign only when it serves a clear commercial purpose and can still get enough conversions to learn.
conditions: Meta accounts optimising for purchases; most important for accounts under a few hundred conversions a month.
fails_when: Businesses with genuinely different products, margins or audiences, where some separation is needed despite the data cost.

claim: DPA ROAS mirrors top of funnel investment; Blue Sense audited six fashion brands in two weeks spending about 80% on DPAs, which had cut creative and cold spend and were declining for six months.
body: Dynamic product ads are valuable, especially for fashion and big catalogues, because they show each visitor the products they viewed, if the pixel and catalogue feed work. But they serve right before purchase to people who are already most aware, so they collect far more credit than they earn. Blue Sense's rules: judge DPAs on 7-day click or incremental attribution, never the default; and remember that DPA results reflect top of funnel spend. Push cold spend up and DPA ROAS rises because there is more demand to catch; cut it and DPAs decline. The 'DPA death spiral': in about two weeks Blue Sense audited six fashion brands, each spending about 80% of budget on DPAs and each declining for six months. The agencies kept raising DPA budgets because ROAS looked good. The brands then asked if they needed so much creative, were told no because DPAs were carrying performance, and cut creative production and cold spend. With nothing feeding the bottom of the funnel, the whole business fell away. How to apply: cap DPA spend by frequency, check its share of budget monthly, and never reduce creative production or cold budgets because DPA ROAS looks strong.

claim: Do not run Meta traffic or reach campaigns without a way to measure them; a 3% budget slice launched during Black Friday cannot be read and just wastes 3% of spend.
body: Traffic, reach and other top of funnel objectives show little or no ROAS, so teams run them on the belief that they help overall revenue. Blue Sense says it has never met a brand running them with a real measurement system. A typical story: the campaigns started a year ago, the agency said revenue went up, and the link was assumed. Asked about test design, the answer is that 3% of budget went into a traffic campaign over Black Friday and Black Friday was good. That proves nothing: 3% of budget is too small to move total revenue measurably, and a before and after comparison across peak season is confounded by the season itself. The result is a permanent unmeasured line item. How to apply: if you want to test an awareness objective, give it enough budget to move new customer revenue, run it as a geo split or a lift study, set the success metric in advance, and turn it off if it cannot show an effect. If you cannot measure it, do not run it.
conditions: Meta accounts running traffic, reach, video view or engagement objectives alongside sales campaigns.
fails_when: Large brands with brand lift studies or geo tests already in place to measure awareness spend.

claim: Do not run one campaign with one ad set for everything; segment when products have different unit economics, when audiences differ (check the gender breakdown for men's ads reaching women), or when order value is very high and volume low.
body: A popular online view says consolidate everything into one campaign and one ad set and just add ads. Blue Sense says that fails for about 90% of brands, for three reasons. 1) Different unit economics. Product ranges carry different gross margins, and inventory grades differ: grade C stock gets discounted hard, so its margin shrinks. In one campaign, spend flows to the heavily discounted items, which earn less contribution and push sale messaging at everyone. 2) Different audiences. An activewear brand with men's and women's ranges in one ad set confuses delivery. In audits, open the ad level, use Breakdown by gender, and you will often see women's ads serving to men and the reverse. Men's ads reaching women is less bad, because women often buy for partners, but women's ads reaching men mostly wastes money. Targeting lives at the ad set level, so split there. 3) High order value, low volume, covered in its own card. How to apply: list your product groups by margin and your core buyer groups, and keep separate campaigns or ad sets only where one of these three reasons applies.
conditions: Multi-range, multi-margin or multi-audience brands on Meta.
fails_when: Single-product, single-audience brands with low order value, where full consolidation can work (about 10% of brands, per Blue Sense).

claim: Do not split Meta ad accounts by country unless you need billing in local currency; reporting by region can be solved with campaign naming and filters, while extra accounts multiply management work.
body: At larger spend levels brands often expand internationally, and many split ad accounts by region. Blue Sense has clients with seven ad accounts for seven regions and says it adds a lot of labour and complexity, which also raises agency costs. The only convincing reason it has seen for a separate account per country is being billed in that country's currency: a US site billed in US dollars to a US bank account, a UK presence billed in pounds. Other reasons can be solved without new accounts. Better reporting, for example, comes from filter rules on country or on campaign names in your dashboards. How to apply: when entering a new country, start in the existing account with clearly named campaigns (country code in the name) and only create a separate account if local-currency billing or a separate legal entity requires it. Also plan how pages, catalogues and the Shopify setup (markets or separate stores) will handle the region.

claim: Dynamic product ads look strong on attributed ROAS, but excluding existing customers and switching to incremental attribution can halve them, say from 5 to 2.5; they rarely scale on cold traffic past roughly $1,000 a day.
body: Catalogue retargeting ads mostly reach people who already viewed products, so platform ROAS flatters them. Blue Sense sees this cause a death spiral, especially in fashion: budget moves from cold campaigns with modest ROAS into catalogue ads with high ROAS, fewer new people enter the funnel, the retargeting pool shrinks, and overall return falls. How to check yours: first view results with existing customers excluded. Then in Ads Manager open Columns, choose compare attribution settings, add incremental attribution and apply. Incremental attribution comes from a holdout: Meta keeps a slice of eligible people (around 10%) from seeing your ads and compares purchase rates. If 1% of the unexposed buy and 2% of the exposed buy, the ads caused about 1 point, not 2, so a reported 5 ROAS is really nearer 2.5. Blue Sense has accounts spending about $1,000 a day on catalogue ads to cold audiences, but has never seen one scale to anything like $50,000 a day. Decision rule: cap catalogue ad budget at what its incremental return supports, and protect top of funnel spend even when its attributed ROAS looks worse.
conditions: Meta accounts running catalogue or dynamic product ads with a working pixel and product feed, enough volume for incremental attribution to report.
fails_when: Very new stores with small audiences where incremental columns are too noisy; brands with huge daily site traffic where retargeting pools stay large.

claim: Every ad has a total spend capacity: pushing a winner hard burns it out in weeks, while holding it near $100 a day can keep it alive for months, so set the pace from stock levels and cash cycle.
body: Plot an ad's daily spend over time: it ramps up, hits a ceiling (say $500 or $1,000 a day), holds, then fades as it fatigues until it is switched off. The area under that curve is its total spend capacity, and every ad has one. You can change the shape. Push budget hard and it peaks higher but dies sooner; keep it modest, around $100 a day, and it may last six months instead of six weeks. Which is right depends on the business, not the ad. If you hold a lot of stock that must sell this month to protect profit, squeeze the winner, even at a lower MER. If stock is short, a reorder is pending, or growth is outrunning your cash conversion cycle, squeezing makes no sense; run at higher efficiency and let the ad breathe. Agencies often lack this context and squeeze every winner, because it makes a strong 30 to 90 day case study and looks good on ROAS reports, then the brand stocks out and the account loses its best ad. How to apply it: share stock cover, inbound purchase orders and cash plans with whoever runs your ads, and agree for each winner whether to squeeze or pace it.
conditions: Brands with winning ads and real stock or cash limits; most relevant for physical products.
fails_when: Short promotional windows where the ad's longevity does not matter; stock and cash with no constraints at all.

claim: For small to mid-sized accounts, run a testing campaign with one ad set per concept and at least 3 ads each, an optional scaling campaign using post IDs, and a retargeting campaign for existing customers.
body: Blue Sense's rule is that account complexity should match business complexity: a single product startup doing $10,000 a month needs a very simple account, while a large fashion retailer with dozens of new products a week and several regions needs more. For small and mid-sized brands the default is three campaigns. Testing: ABO or CBO by preference (see the risk card), with each concept in its own ad set. Put at least 3 ads in each ad set; the upper limit depends on budget and can reach 50 to 100. Scaling, optional: copy winning ads by post ID so they keep their likes and comments; use it only if it works in your account, otherwise keep winners in testing. Retargeting: mainly existing customers, so you can exclude them from the other campaigns, keep those purely cold, and control spend on past buyers. If your buying cycle is long and you think engaged people need more frequency, add an ad set for website visitors from the last 90 days. Name ad sets so you can filter by concept, such as concept one shoot two.
conditions: Small to mid-sized brands, roughly up to tens of thousands a month on Meta with a modest catalogue.
fails_when: Large multi-region retailers with many business units, which need structure that mirrors their commercial goals; brands with no repeat customers to retarget.

claim: Grade stock A to D by sell-through and push slow grade C and D stock through paid at break-even or a small loss, in its own funnel or a new country, instead of letting it tie up cash.
body: Blue Sense grades inventory: A sells fast (the only worry is stockouts), B sells at a medium pace, C is slow and D barely moves. Shopify can rank this for you from its inventory data. Product launches are a major growth lever, but many fail: an initial pop from email and organic sells 30% to 40% of the order, then stock stalls. Example: $1M of stock at sell value ordered, about $100k sold, and 400 days of inventory left. Each failed launch adds cash to the balance sheet that limits scaling. An agency judged only on profit will never spend on that stock because its ROAS is poor, so all spend chases grade A and the cash problem worsens. Blue Sense's fixes: push the slow product in its own ad funnel at break-even or slight loss, possibly off the main site and through whitelisted pages; or, as done for one client, send grade D stock to a new country where heavy discounts will not damage brand equity in the main market. Also keep trimming the SKU count as new products arrive. How to apply: share inventory grades and days on hand with the media team weekly, and give them a separate cash-recovery target for C and D stock.
conditions: Multi-SKU brands with product launches and slow-moving stock; fashion especially.
fails_when: Single product or made-to-order brands; stock that is slow because the product is faulty or unwanted at any price.

claim: Ignore bid strategy testing under about $200k a month; above $250k a month a mix of cost caps, bid caps and value bidding becomes worth a dedicated person because 3 to 4% efficiency is material.
body: Blue Sense rarely talks about bidding because 99.9% of advertisers do not spend enough for it to matter. Its test: would the business double if you focused on bid strategies? Usually no, because it is a low-leverage lever compared with creative and offer. You can run cost caps at any spend if you know what you are doing, but testing bid strategies is not the bottleneck below about $200,000 a month, and Blue Sense turns cost caps off in the primary account as part of its standard settings audit. Above about $250,000 a month things change. A 3% to 4% efficiency gain on a million dollars a month is real money, so a dedicated person working on bidding pays for itself. At that level Blue Sense mixes strategies: maximize conversions alongside bid caps, cost caps, and maximize conversion value or target ROAS. Each strategy enters auctions differently, so a mix tends to win more auctions overall. About 60% of Blue Sense's client portfolio spends over $250,000 a month, which is why it matters to them internally. How to apply: below the threshold, leave bidding on the default and work on creative; above it, introduce one alternative bid strategy at a time alongside the default and compare blended efficiency.
conditions: Meta accounts above roughly $250,000 a month for the bidding mix; below $200,000 a month for leaving it alone.
fails_when: Specific cases such as tight unit economics, where an expert may use cost caps at smaller spend.

claim: In a $20M to $30M furniture brand's audit, 57% of Meta budget went to a DPA ad set showing 7x ROAS that was only 1.9x on 7-day click or incremental attribution, below every other ad set.
body: A tactical audit example from Blue Sense. The furniture brand ran one consolidated cold campaign as a CBO with several ad sets. Meta had pushed 57% of the whole Meta budget into the top ad set, which was a dynamic product ad. On the default attribution it looked excellent at about 7x ROAS. Broken down to 7-day click, or to incremental attribution, both gave the same answer: about 1.9x. Every other ad set in the campaign performed better than that on an incremental or 7-day click read. Two lessons. First, DPAs inside a consolidated cold campaign will soak up budget, because they find the warmest people and claim their purchases; in high-ticket categories that ad type does not perform well on genuinely cold audiences. Second, the problem was invisible until attribution was changed. How to apply: in any CBO containing a DPA or catalogue ad set, compare spend share against 7-day click and incremental ROAS by ad set. If the DPA takes a large share while its click-only or incremental return trails the others, move it into its own capped campaign aimed at retargeting.

fails_when: Accounts where DPAs are already separated and capped, or broad catalogue prospecting that tests well on incremental reads.

claim: Maximize conversions pushes spend to the cheapest CPA product, not the most profitable: a $45 CAC hoodie making $24 contribution beat a $15 CAC tee making $12, so segment campaigns by product economics.
body: Blue Sense's example: a hoodie sells for $90 with $21 COGS, so $69 gross margin; its CAC through the Advantage+ campaign is $45, leaving $24 contribution per sale. A t-shirt has about the same COGS but a lower price, $27 gross margin and a $15 CAC, leaving $12. The hoodie makes twice as much per sale. Yet maximize conversions, the default bid strategy on Meta, Google and TikTok, optimises for the lowest cost per purchase, so it will pour budget into the t-shirt. Switching to maximize conversion value does not fix it here either, because the t-shirt may also show the better ROAS. The fix is structural: split campaigns or ad sets by product group based on product-level unit economics so you can set budgets and targets per group. A second check: when a product's CAC is suspiciously low, ask whether it would sell anyway through organic demand or retail. If so, reduce paid support for it (raising its contribution from $12 toward $27 per sale) and move that money to the product that needs paid spend to sell through. How to apply: build a product economics sheet (price, COGS, gross margin, CAC, contribution) and review spend share per product against it monthly.
conditions: Multi-product stores where products differ in margin or CAC; fashion and omnichannel brands especially.
fails_when: Single hero product stores, or accounts too small to support more than one campaign without splitting conversion data.

claim: Name ad sets by persona, angle, offer, content type and launch date, not batch names like 'March 7 creatives', so concepts can be filtered and judged across the account.
body: Most accounts name ad sets by batch, for example 'March 7 creatives'. That says nothing about what is being tested, implies concepts were mixed together instead of structured, and makes it hard to filter results. When Blue Sense takes over such accounts, it often renames historic ad sets just to rebuild a usable record of what worked. A naming convention makes concept-level reporting possible: you can filter or pivot spend and results by persona, by angle or by offer across all campaigns and see which ideas carry the account. Recommended order: persona, angle, offer, content type (if the ad set groups one type), and launch date. How to apply: agree a fixed format with separators that are easy to split in a spreadsheet, apply it to all new ad sets, rename the last few months of ad sets that still spend, then build a simple report that sums spend and results by each name field so the creative team gets feedback on concepts, not just ads.

claim: Never add ads to an ad set that is hitting target, since it disrupts Meta's learned sequencing; put new ads for that concept in a new ad set, and scale winners by raising budget, never by pausing them.
body: Within an ad set, Meta learns an order in which to show the ads to people. Adding ads resets part of that learning while it redistributes spend. If the ad set is doing well, that disruption can break it; Blue Sense learned this the hard way. Decision rule: if an ad set is beating its target, leave its ads alone. When you make more ads for that winning concept, launch them in a new ad set named so you can tell it apart yet filter it with the original (for example concept one, shoot two). If an ad set is below target, change anything: add ads, turn ads off, since the current order is not working anyway. To scale a winner, increase its budget. Never turn it off to relaunch it in a scaling campaign, which throws away what it learned. You may also copy its post ID into a scaling campaign while leaving the original running, if that works in your account. The same idea applies in reverse: do not tinker with a working setup just to look busy.
conditions: Meta campaigns with ad sets holding several ads, judged against a clear CPA or ROAS target.
fails_when: Ad sets far below target, where disruption costs nothing; ads breaking policy or showing wrong prices, which must change at once.

claim: Only move a winner into a scaling campaign once it holds about $400 a day; the move adds about 20% spend at best, so a $60 a day ad gains only about $10.
body: A scaling campaign takes creatives that have hit their spending ceiling and relaunches them, usually by post ID so likes and comments carry over, in another campaign, while the original keeps running. For some reason Meta can often push a bit more spend through the same asset this way: an ad holding $300 a day in testing might reach $400 a day total. Blue Sense's rule of thumb is that this move gets, on a good day, about 20% more daily spend through the ad. That makes the threshold obvious. An ad at $60 a day gains about $10, not worth the added complexity; the real problem there is the landing page, the offer or that you have not yet found a concept that works, so make better ads. An ad at $400 a day gains about $80, and doing it for your top ten ads at once may unlock about $1,000 a day, which is worth having. There is no reason to build a scaling campaign at all until you have creatives that have been pushed to their limit. How to apply: list ads by daily spend, pick those near $400 a day or more that have plateaued, and move their post IDs into a scaling campaign every one to two weeks.
conditions: Meta accounts with proven winning ads at meaningful daily spend.
fails_when: Accounts whose best ads spend well under a few hundred dollars a day; there the effort belongs in creative and the offer.

claim: Put 3 to 15 ads in each ad set so Meta can sequence them, and keep top, middle and bottom of funnel creative for one concept together instead of splitting by awareness stage.
body: Whether you run ABO or CBO, ad set make-up is the same. Minimum three ads, because people usually need to see two to six ads before buying and an ad set with one ad can only show that one ad again and again. Maximum is set by spend: Blue Sense runs ad sets with up to 200 creatives in some accounts, but most brands lack the volume, and 200 ads usually contain several concepts that should be separated, so the rule of thumb is three to 15. All ads in an ad set should speak to the same audience. A common question is whether a five-minute story video and a blunt '50% off rain jacket' static for the same persona belong together. Blue Sense leans toward one ad set holding all stages, because Meta can sequence people through the journey. Splitting by stage can also work, but it creates a human bias problem: the top of funnel ad set might show 2x and the bottom 6x, and people (especially clients) then refuse to fund the 2x even though it feeds the 6x. Blended, the concept was 4x. How to apply: brief each concept with top, middle and bottom creatives and launch them together in one ad set.

fails_when: Teams disciplined enough to read split stage ad sets as one blended concept; very high ad volumes better grouped by concept.
