claim: Rank creative metrics by reliability: amount spent first, then ROAS or CPA on 7 day click or incremental attribution, then CPC and CTR as early signals, with hook and hold rates only for diagnosis.
body: Spend is the best long run signal because Meta credits a purchase to the last ad seen, yet its delivery reflects which ads move people across the account. If one ad has a 1.7 ROAS but twice the spend of an ad on 2.2, Meta is probably giving it budget because it starts journeys that finish on other ads; it is likely a low frequency top of funnel ad reaching new people, and Blue Sense would call it the best of the set. A high ROAS ad that could scale would already have more spend. Second, ROAS or CPA, read on 7 day click or incremental attribution. Third, CPC and CTR as leading signals, most useful at the extremes: if ads above a certain cost per click (say $3) have never been profitable in your account, you can cut such ads early. Good click metrics with poor conversion still mean a poor ad. Fourth, hook rate (share past 3 seconds) and hold rate (Blue Sense's usual definition: past 15 seconds). They do not predict conversions but show what to fix: a low hook rate means swap the opening; a hold drop at the bridge means re-edit that part.
conditions: Meta accounts with consolidated campaigns where Meta distributes budget across several ads.
fails_when: Manual ad level budgets, where spend reflects your choices, not Meta's; very new ads with too little time for spend patterns to form.

claim: Rotate into CBO for Q4 peaks, when the goal is to spend as much as possible efficiently, and back to ABO in Q1, when lower risk and structured creative testing matter more.
body: Blue Sense frames CBO and ABO as risk profiles rather than right and wrong. CBO is higher risk with slightly higher return: it concentrates spend on whatever Meta rates best. ABO is lower risk with a slightly lower return, perhaps around 10% less, but forces spend across tests. That suggests switching by season. In Black Friday, November, December and other peak windows, the job is to spend as much as possible in a short time at the best efficiency, and it does not matter which creatives get the money, so CBO fits. In January, February and the rest of Q1, the job is to set up the year with lots of creative testing; it is a good testing environment because peak season is no longer inflating conversion rates and making weak ads look good, and the brand wants a lower risk profile. So Blue Sense often moves some accounts into CBO for Q4 and back to ABO in Q1. How to apply: plan the structure change in your Q4 and Q1 calendars, carry winning post IDs across so social proof is kept, and set testing targets for Q1.
conditions: Seasonal DTC brands with a clear Q4 peak and a creative pipeline.
fails_when: Brands with flat year-round demand or very high order value and low volume, where CBO is not advised.

claim: Run a creative test for about one week to cover weekday swings and the 3 to 4 days buyers take; large stable accounts can read in 3 to 4 days, small slow ones need 10 to 14.
body: Two forces set the length of a test. Speed: growth depends on how fast you get feedback, learn and iterate, so shorter is better. Accuracy: the test must cover daily seasonality (weekday swings) and the time people take to buy. Many buyers see an ad several times, maybe click once or twice, and decide over three or four days. If you kill a top of funnel test after one day, the people it warmed up may convert later through other ads, and you will have switched off the ad that started their journey. Blue Sense's default: about one week. A large business with stable volume and short time to purchase can cut it to three or four days. A small business with a tiny budget, a long time to purchase and big daily swings may need 10 to 14 days. The same applies on Google and other platforms. How to apply: check your typical click to purchase lag (in Meta, compare 1-day and 7-day click results; in Shopify, look at time from first visit to order), then set test length to cover at least one full week plus that lag for slow categories.
conditions: Prospecting creative and concept tests on Meta, Google and similar platforms.
fails_when: Promotions or launches with short fixed windows, where you read what you can in the time available.

claim: Run partnership ads through relevant creators: Meta uses the audience data of both handles to find new buyers, and some Blue Sense accounts put up to 40% of total spend through them.
body: A partnership ad shows the brand and the creator together at the top of the post, and a newer setting lets Meta test showing the brand, the creator or both. Blue Sense calls it one of the most underused formats of 2026, with the caution that the advantage may be fading as more brands catch on. Two reasons it works. Targeting: Meta draws on the audience signals of both handles, so a creator whose followers match your buyers helps the ad find new cold prospects, not just warm ones. Feel: a post from a creator's profile reads like content rather than an ad, so it lands better. How to apply it: pick creators whose audience genuinely matches your buyer, agree partnership ad access in their content agreement, run their posts as partnership ads alongside your own handle ads, and track spend share and new customer results. In some accounts Blue Sense manages, these collaborator ads carry up to 40% of total spend. If you run none, you are likely behind competitors. Relevance matters more than follower count, because the creator's audience data is part of the targeting.

fails_when: Creators with irrelevant or fake audiences, whose data steers delivery to the wrong people; the advantage may shrink as adoption grows.

claim: Set each test's daily budget as target conversions times expected CPA divided by test days: 20 conversions at $100 over 14 days is about $143 a day, while Meta's 50 a week rule would need $714 a day per test.
body: Before launching a test, answer two questions. What conversion count will you treat as enough to call it (5, 10, 20)? And how fast do you want the answer (3, 7, 14 or 30 days)? Then daily test budget equals target conversions multiplied by expected cost per acquisition, divided by the number of days. Example: a threshold of 20 conversions, a $100 expected CPA and a 14-day test gives about $143 a day for that test. Blue Sense says Meta's common guidance, about 50 conversions per week to leave the learning phase, is wrong for most advertisers when turned into budgets. With the same $100 CPA, 50 conversions in seven days needs about $714 a day for a single concept ad set, so five or ten tests would cost about $3,500 to $7,000 a day in testing alone, impossible for 99% of advertisers. How to apply: pick a conversion threshold and duration that your budget can afford across the number of concepts you want to test at once; if a cell cannot reach its threshold, test fewer concepts, extend the window, or judge on an earlier metric and say so.
conditions: Any account running structured creative or concept tests.
fails_when: Very low CPA accounts where Meta's 50 a week is cheap enough to reach; or tests judged on earlier metrics by design.

20 x $100 / 14 = about $143 a day
50 x $100 / 7 = about $714 a day
10 tests at that rate = about $7,000 a day

claim: Stop daily bid tweaks, daily budget pacing, interest targeting and lookalikes; put that time into account structure, concept-level ad set testing, existing customer allocation, landing page tests and better creative.
body: Blue Sense's list of what no longer pays in Meta buying for 99% of advertisers. Daily bid changes with cost caps or bid caps: maybe 5% more efficiency for an hour a day, when the same hour spent on creative could double or triple the account. Daily budget pacing on smaller accounts, adjusting budgets to expected daily conversion swings: it disrupts campaigns and is decided on tiny samples. Interest targeting: Blue Sense says it should not be in your account at all, and it has not used it in most accounts for about two years. Lookalike audiences: broad targeting does the job better. What still matters: account architecture aligned with commercial goals; concept-level segmentation at the ad set level; controlling spend going to existing customers; and testing landing pages and site conversion rate, which Blue Sense calls a far better use of a test than interest testing because it can shift conversion rate across all traffic. How to apply: audit how your media buyer's week is spent. Move time from bid and budget fiddling and audience testing into creative briefing, concept analysis and landing page split tests.

fails_when: Very large accounts where a few percent efficiency is a lot of money and a specialist can manage bid strategy.

claim: To grow at $50k to $250k a month spend, launch about 100 to 300 new ads a month; with two campaigns of 10 ad sets that is 5 to 15 ads per ad set, a manageable load.
body: Blue Sense ties creative volume to the account structure. In the $50,000 to $250,000 a month tier, if the goal is growth, it recommends launching roughly 100 to 300 new ads every month; if you are not trying to grow, you do not need that many. The structure has to be able to absorb them so data stays readable. Two cold campaigns with 10 concept ad sets each gives 20 ad sets, which works out at about 5 ads per ad set at the low end and about 15 at the high end. That matches its ad set rule of three to 15 ads each, and you could even run fewer campaigns or ad sets and still be fine. The main skill at this tier is continuous concept testing to find the roughly 20% of concepts that can hold hundreds of thousands a month. How to apply: set a monthly ad launch target for your tier, map how many concepts and ad sets will hold them, and plan briefs so each ad set is filled with three or more ads under one concept rather than one-off ads scattered across the account.
conditions: Brands at $50k to $250k a month Meta spend that want to grow.
fails_when: Accounts that pump out volume without a concept strategy; volume without strategy does not scale (see the 2,000 ads card).

claim: Treat retargeting as a capped support layer: aim to spend as little as possible on it, merge cart, checkout and visitor audiences into one ad set, and manage it by frequency.
body: Three Blue Sense principles for retargeting, DPAs and existing customers. 1) It is capped support, not a growth driver. A very common audit finding: run the Audience segments breakdown and see about 50% of spend going to existing customers and engaged audiences, which supports sales that would mostly happen anyway. With cold spend, ask where you can spend more profitably; with retargeting, ask where you can spend less. Be generous at the top of the funnel and stingy at the bottom, across Meta, TikTok and Pinterest. 2) Consolidate retargeting audiences. Separate ad sets for viewers of each product category, add to cart, initiate checkout and site visitors is a 2019 approach. Splitting tiny warm pools raises CPMs, and Blue Sense has never seen the conversion rate gain outweigh that cost. 3) Use frequency as the main KPI after incremental revenue: how many times a week and month are existing customers and engaged visitors seeing ads, and is that reasonable? Thirty times a month is almost certainly too much. How to apply: collapse warm ad sets into one, set a monthly frequency target, and cut budget until frequency sits there.
conditions: Meta, TikTok and Pinterest accounts with retargeting or DPA spend.
fails_when: Brands with long purchase cycles and high order values, where a structured sequence for warm prospects may justify some segmentation.

claim: Under CBO, the 80/20 rule compounds so that about 4% of ads end up holding about 64% of spend and revenue: often higher return, but high fatigue risk, so ABO is the safer steady state.
body: Blue Sense frames the choice between ad set budgets (ABO) and campaign budgets (CBO) as a choice about risk. Pareto's pattern shows up in every account they analyse: 20% of ads drive 80% of revenue, and it nests, so 20% of that 20% (4% of ads) holds about 80% of the 80% (64% of spend and revenue). Left to itself, CBO pushes budget into that tiny group. That usually gives the best short term efficiency, but if those few ads fatigue there is no backup, which is the opposite of portfolio thinking. It also skews products: if many products share one CBO, spend piles onto a few, hurting sell through on the rest. Decision rule: use CBO when you need a quick lift in efficiency and are not worried about testing or spreading risk, such as a weak month. Run ABO as the normal state, so spend is spread across more ads and products and one fatigued ad does not sink the account. How to check: export ad level spend for 90 days, sort it, and see what share the top 4% of ads hold. If it is far above two thirds, you are over-exposed.
conditions: Meta accounts with many live ads or products where concentration risk matters.
fails_when: Accounts with only a few ads or one product, where concentration is unavoidable; short promotional bursts where efficiency is all that counts.

about 4% of ads hold about 64% of spend and revenue
20% of products drive about 80% of revenue

claim: Under about $50k a month, run a consolidated ABO testing campaign, a scaling campaign and optional existing customer retargeting; read tests over no less than 5 days and raise budgets 20% a day when they hit KPI.
body: Blue Sense's starting structure for the lowest spend tier. Testing campaign as ABO, so you can force spend into each new concept ad set and learn, because at this level you probably have no big winner yet. A scaling campaign for winners once they hold real daily spend. An optional retargeting campaign, usually existing customers only. Why it suits this tier: conversion volume is low, so data should stay consolidated rather than split; you need structured creative testing; and the product range and business are usually simple. KPIs: judge the testing campaign at the ad set level, asking whether each ad set hit the target CPA or ROAS over a sensible rolling window. The window depends on volume: you cannot read three days if you get three purchases in three days, but you can read two days at 1,000 a day. At this scale Blue Sense would not judge on less than five days. If an ad set hits KPI, increase its budget in 20% steps per day. If not, work out what was wrong with the creative, make new ads or concepts, and wind it down or switch it off. Judge the scaling campaign at the campaign level. Judge retargeting on incremental ROAS from an attribution breakdown, with frequency no higher than 7 over 30 days.
conditions: Meta accounts spending up to roughly $50,000 a month.
fails_when: Very low budgets that cannot fund several concept ad sets to a readable result; accounts with many product lines needing separation early.

claim: When a winning ad fatigues, use four moves: new hooks, a cost cap campaign for a short squeeze, its post ID in a scaling campaign, or rebuilding it in another format; duplicating ad sets is not worth it.
body: Once an ad truly fatigues there is little you can do, which is why the portfolio approach matters, but these moves can squeeze more from its tail. One: iterate, rotating fresh hooks onto the proven body (the cheapest and most reliable). Two: move it into a cost cap campaign to push more spend at your target cost; it works, but burns the ad out faster and is a short term buying tactic, not a business fix. Three: take the post ID, which keeps its likes and comments, into another campaign such as a scaling campaign; sometimes it works, but it will not save the account. Four: rotate format, rebuilding the idea in a new form: a winning video as an image, a winning video sales letter as UGC, a winning image as a long copy static for unaware buyers, which is a very different strategy. Blue Sense does not recommend duplicating ad sets; it says this worked years ago and now looks like a crude tactic. How to apply it: when a hero ad's spend and return slide for a week or more, brief hook swaps and one format rebuild at once, and test cost cap only as a temporary measure while new concepts come through.
conditions: Meta accounts with a proven ad that is starting to fatigue.
fails_when: The fall is caused by offer, stock, tracking or seasonality rather than the ad; accounts with no pipeline of new concepts, where tail tactics only delay decline.

duplicating ad sets not recommended

claim: The first frame, voiceover, on-screen text, primary text, headline and landing page top are all hooks seen together; make them one claim, not luxury in one and sale or science in another.
body: A common mismatch: the first frame signals luxury, the spoken words sound cheap, the overlay or primary text pushes a sale, and the headline talks science. Some call that a curiosity gap, but conflicting signals just confuse. Every element should push the same opening claim. Example: introducing Nourish Plus is a weak headline, hook or advertorial opening; why hair thins at the part line first is stronger and pulls in the exact persona. How to apply it: before launch, put the first frame, the first spoken line, the overlay, primary text, headline and the landing page or advertorial headline side by side and check they make one claim to one awareness stage.

claim: Even a brand doing $200,000 a month needs a simple Meta structure: Caden's team loads up to 50 ads into one ad set and reads winners from first click new customer data in back end tools.
body: Caden said his team no longer builds many campaigns for a business doing around $200,000 a month. They fill one ad set with as many as 50 ads, the most Meta allows in one ad set, and let the system spread delivery. To tell which ads matter, they do not trust Ads Manager ROAS. They use back end or server side tracking (he named Blotout as one tool) and look at first click data for new customers: which ad first brought in a person who then bought for the first time. That links creative to real new customer sales and shows cause and effect as budgets move. He said it brings the job back to building marketing rather than running endless settings tests. This adds a higher ad count to other Blue Sense cards, which test one concept per ad set with 10 or more ads. How to apply: consolidate prospecting into a small number of ad sets, load many distinct ads, and set up a way to join orders to ad IDs, through server side tracking or UTM parameters read in Shopify, filtered to first time buyers. claim: A $20M to $30M furniture brand had 57% of cold Meta budget in a DPA ad set showing 7x ROAS; on 7-day click and incremental attribution it was 1.9x, below every other ad set.
body: Catalog ads (DPAs) tend to serve right before the moment of purchase, so they collect last-touch credit for sales other ads created. Put them inside a consolidated cold CBO and Meta keeps feeding them, because their reported ROAS looks best. In this audit the brand's only cold campaign was a CBO with several ad sets, and the DPA ad set took 57% of spend at a 7x platform ROAS. Switching the read to 7-day click, or to incremental attribution, gave the same answer: about 1.9x, worse than every other ad set. How to apply: in Ads Manager use Columns, Compare attribution settings, and check 7-day click and incremental for any DPA ad set. If DPAs sit inside a cold campaign and hold a large share of spend, move them to a separate, capped retargeting or catalog campaign, and judge them only on 7-day click or incremental numbers.

claim: A Blue Sense account spending about $25k a day runs ABO testing, a CBO cost-cap scaling campaign fed winners every one to two weeks, plus separate promo, advertorial and low-spend DPA campaigns.
body: The worked example spends around $25k a day, roughly $750k a month. Testing is an ABO with concept ad sets, and some of those ad sets are themselves scaled to thousands of dollars a day. Scaling is a CBO with one ad set on cost caps. Every one to two weeks the top post IDs from testing are added to it, while the originals stay on in testing. Promos run every three to four weeks, so they get their own campaign: launching and pausing promo ads inside testing or scaling would keep disrupting learning, and promos attract more price-sensitive buyers who should be optimized separately. Advertorials began as a test, grew to about 30% of total spend, and were pulled into a dedicated campaign so that funnel could be judged on its own. Last is a DPA campaign mainly for existing customers and some visitors, judged on incremental attribution and kept low in line with frequency.

claim: A one-SKU, one-persona CPG brand at about $5M a year needs only one Advantage+ cold campaign per country with existing customers excluded, plus a tiny existing-customer campaign held under 7 frequency a month.
body: Blue Sense's worked example: a consumables brand with one SKU, about $5M a year, 70% gross margin, one persona (busy mums), selling in Australia and the US. Structure: one Advantage+ cold campaign for each country, with creative tests as ad sets built around concepts, and most spend behind the one concept and persona that works now. Exclude existing customers from both cold campaigns. In CPG, repeat buyers drive lots of revenue and would otherwise soak up cold spend, inflate cold results and push frequency up. Add a small existing-customer retargeting campaign, sized only to keep frequency below 7 over a rolling 30 days. At this size that is about $20 a day. claim: ABO versus CBO is a risk choice; at scale Blue Sense mostly runs CBO with ad set minimum and maximum spend limits controlling about 60% of budget and 40% left free.
body: A CBO lets Meta move budget to the best ad sets, so it usually gets the most short-term efficiency. It also follows a Pareto pattern: about 20% of ads take 80% of spend, and new tests, a $20,000 campaign shoot or a paid influencer partnership can sit unspent. An ABO forces spend where you choose, which helps testing and lowers the risk of one fatiguing winner carrying the account, but it burns money in unskilled hands. Blue Sense has seen both run accounts spending a quarter of a million dollars a day, so neither is right for everyone. How to apply: pick by who is buying. A first-year in-house buyer should run a simple consolidated CBO and let Meta allocate. An experienced buyer can run ABO, or the hybrid: CBO with min and max limits on key ad sets so roughly 60% is directed and 40% flows freely. Below about $10k a month the hybrid is too much work; pick one and run it.
conditions: Accounts big enough that budget control and creative testing both matter, roughly $50k a month and up for the hybrid.
fails_when: Very high order value with few daily purchases, where CBO allocates on clicks rather than sales; or small accounts where min and max limits are more management than they are worth.

claim: About 90% of accounts do not need a website visitor retargeting campaign; check the audience segment breakdown, because cold campaigns already spend on engaged visitors at high frequency.
body: There are two kinds of retargeting: people who visited or engaged but did not buy, and existing customers. Broad cold campaigns already find recent visitors, because those people are likely to buy, so a separate visitor campaign mostly double counts. How to check: in Advertiser settings, set up audience segments (engaged audience and existing customers, usually from your pixel, site and Klaviyo lists). Then in Ads Manager use Breakdown, Audience segments to see spend, ROAS and frequency for new, engaged and existing people. Existing should be near zero if you exclude customers. Engaged will usually show enough spend at high enough frequency that no extra campaign is needed. Existing-customer spend is a separate call that depends on repeat behavior: low for furniture where people rarely rebuy, higher for low-price subscription supplements. Keep it low and controlled, using frequency as the gauge.
conditions: Accounts running broad cold campaigns with audience segments configured.
fails_when: Very long consideration products where visitors need a different message, or accounts where the breakdown shows almost no spend reaching engaged people.

claim: Above $250k a month, consider a second Meta ad account on the same pixel with different bid logic; it can win other auctions and keeps acquisition alive if the main account is banned.
body: At large spend, Blue Sense adds a second ad account that uses the same pixel (and often the same page) but a different bidding approach. If the main account runs highest volume (maximize conversions), the second might run maximize conversion value, cost caps or bid caps. Different bid logic enters different auctions, so the same creative can find more volume. Critics say you may bid against yourself and raise CPMs; with the same page and pixel Blue Sense thinks overlap is small, but admits nobody has proven it either way. The clearer benefit is risk. If the main account is banned or its payment method fails, a brand that depends on Meta for new customers can lose a week of revenue. A second account that normally holds even 10% of the main one's spend can be turned up at once. Blue Sense warns this tactic changes often, so recheck it every few months.

claim: Audit any Meta structure with four questions: does it produce readable data, does it match how the business makes money, does it fit the spend tier and creative throughput, and are support layers sized to retention?
body: Blue Sense closes its structure guide with four checks. If any answer is no, restructure. One: does the structure give data you can read and act on? Flexible ads, batch-named ad sets and lumped concepts fail this. Two: does it match how the business earns profit, with margin bands, categories that need sell-through, and regional stock all visible? Three: is it right for the spend tier and the number of new ads each month? Twenty campaigns on $50k a month fails; one campaign on $1M a month with five business units also fails. Four: are the support layers (DPA, visitor retargeting, existing customers) sized to real retention and judged against new-customer revenue? A brand with low repeat rates should spend little there; a fashion brand with weekly drops may justify more. How to apply: score your account against the four questions every quarter, or after any big change in range, markets or spend, and write down which campaign fails which question.

claim: Check the Klaviyo to Meta customer sync regularly; Blue Sense sees it break from time to time, and then existing customers are treated as new in cold campaigns and segment reports.
body: Exclusions and audience segment reports depend on your customer list reaching Meta. Many brands feed it from Klaviyo. Blue Sense watches this sync because it breaks periodically. When it does, existing customers stop being recognized, cold campaigns start spending on them as if they were new, new-customer results look better than they are, and the audience segment breakdown stops being accurate. How to apply: in Meta, open the custom audience or customer list that feeds your existing customer segment and check its last update date and size; it should refresh on schedule and grow in line with your customer count. Add a monthly reminder to check it, and check it right away if the existing share in your segment breakdown suddenly drops to near zero, or new-customer CPA suddenly improves with no change in creative.

claim: Copying winning post IDs into a scaling campaign adds at best about 20% more daily spend per ad, so only do it once winners reach around $300 to $400 a day.
body: A winning ad set can be pushed until ROAS breaks, then pulled back to the level it can hold, say $300 a day. A scaling campaign is a second home for those maxed-out creatives: you launch the same posts there and keep the originals running, hoping the new campaign finds extra spend. On a good day this adds about 20% to the creative's daily spend. At $60 a day that is about $10 more, not worth the extra complexity. Fix the offer, landing page or concept instead. At $400 a day it is about $80 more for little effort, and moving 10 such ads at once can unlock roughly $1,000 a day. How to apply: keep a list of ads that have held target for at least a couple of weeks and their daily ceiling. When several sit at a few hundred dollars a day, launch their post IDs into one CBO scaling campaign with existing customers excluded, and judge it at campaign level. Never run tests inside the scaling campaign.

fails_when: Winners spend under about $100 a day, or the scaling campaign has no exclusions and simply retargets warm people.

claim: DPA results mirror top-of-funnel spend; Blue Sense saw six fashion brands in two weeks putting about 80% of spend into DPAs, cutting new creative, and declining for six months.
body: Catalog ads mostly serve right before purchase, so they collect last-touch credit and their ROAS looks better than it is. Rule one: judge DPAs on 7-day click or incremental attribution only. Rule two: DPA results depend on how much you spend on cold ads. Push top of funnel and DPA ROAS rises, because more people reach the bottom. Cut it and DPAs fall too. The death spiral: an agency sees DPAs doing well and keeps raising their budget. The brand asks if it still needs as much new creative, is told DPAs are carrying results, and cuts production and cold spend. With nobody new entering the funnel, the whole account declines. Blue Sense saw this in six fashion audits in about two weeks, each with around 80% of spend in DPAs and six months of decline. How to apply: cap DPA spend by frequency, report it separately from prospecting, and never reduce creative production or cold budget because DPAs look strong.
conditions: Catalog-heavy brands, especially fashion and large-SKU stores.
fails_when: DPAs are run as broad prospecting with customers and visitors excluded, and hold up on incremental attribution.

claim: Daily bid and budget tweaks squeeze at most about 5% more from a Meta account; the same hour spent on creative can double it, so skip them below roughly $200k a month.
body: Hand-tuning bids and budgets was a real edge around 2019 and 2020. Today the delivery system does most of that work, so the payoff is small. Blue Sense puts the gain from an hour a day of bid or cost cap changes at around 5%. That same hour spent making and launching better creative can grow the account two or three times over. How to apply: write down where your media buyer spends their week. If daily bid edits, daily budget pacing by day of week, or interest tests take more than a small slice, move that time to new concepts, landing page tests and offers. Daily budget changes on a small account are also judged on tiny samples, so they add noise more than signal. Media buying still pays at scale: at $100k to $300k a month in spend, good structure and buying can add 10% to 20% efficiency. Above about $250k a month, even 3% to 4% gains are big money and worth a dedicated person.
conditions: Accounts spending under roughly $200k to $250k a month on Meta, where creative and pages are the main constraint.
fails_when: Spend is well above $250k a month, where a few percent of efficiency is a large profit sum and bidding mixes become worth managing; or the creative pipeline is already strong and structure is the bottleneck.

10% to 20% efficiency lift from good media buying at $100k to $300k a month
bidding focus worth it above about $200k to $250k a month

claim: Design Meta structure from five questions: how many distinct categories, how wide the margin spread, how many non-overlapping personas, how many regions, and how many new ads a month.
body: Blue Sense says there is no single correct structure, only two rules every structure must pass. Data integrity: the setup must produce numbers you can read and act on in a loop of look, decide, wait, decide. Commercial alignment: the setup must mirror how the business makes money, so a category that needs sell-through, a low-margin range that cannot fund paid acquisition, or a goal with its own KPI must be visible in the account. The five questions then tell you where to segment. More categories with different goals mean more splits. A wide margin spread needs separate targets. Personas that truly do not overlap need their own campaigns or ad sets. Each region with its own stock or revenue target needs its own control. Creative throughput sets the ceiling: 10 new ads a month supports almost no segmentation, 2,000 a month needs a planned path from test to scale. How to apply: answer the five in writing before building or rebuilding, and justify every campaign by one of them.
conditions: Setting up or restructuring any Meta account beyond a single-product starter setup.
fails_when: Spend and conversion volume are too low to support the splits the answers suggest; then fold splits down to ad set level or wait.
numbers: 10 new ads a month supports little segmentation vs 2,000 a month needing a planned path

claim: Do not split countries into separate Meta ad accounts unless you need billing in local currency; filter reports by campaign name instead, since each extra account adds a lot of labor.
body: Brands expanding abroad often open one ad account per region. Blue Sense has clients with seven ad accounts for seven regions and finds it multiplies management work, and agency fees with it. The one convincing reason is billing: if you have a US entity and bank, you may want Meta to bill in USD, and a UK entity in GBP, which needs separate accounts. Better reporting is not a good reason. You can tag campaigns by country in their names and filter dashboards on that, or segment reports by country. How to apply: keep one ad account with country campaigns (or country ad sets) unless finance has a real need for local-currency invoices. If you do split for currency, keep the naming convention identical across accounts so reporting stays simple.
conditions: Brands selling in several countries from one or more Meta ad accounts.
fails_when: Separate legal entities, tax or banking rules require local-currency invoices per region, or a region's team runs its own marketing.

claim: Do not split out a placement, age band or region just because its breakdown ROAS looks higher; Meta spends on marginal return, so the high-ROAS slice usually has no room left.
body: Meta publishes this as the breakdown effect. In a breakdown you might see Stories at 4x ROAS and Feed at 3x, yet Feed takes 80% of the spend. The tempting fix is a Stories-only campaign. But the breakdown shows average return, not the return on the next dollar. Meta has usually already tried to push more into Stories, found the extra spend returned almost nothing, and moved it to Feed where the next dollar still earns something. The same logic explains why a lower-ROAS ad keeps getting budget inside an ad set. How to apply: treat breakdowns as a health check, not a list of campaigns to build. Act on a breakdown only when something is clearly broken, such as women's products serving mostly to men, or a country you do not ship to. If you do test a split, run it as a proper test with a holdout or a matched period, and judge total account profit, not the slice's own ROAS. Blue Sense's view is that only very experienced buyers should restructure from breakdown data.
conditions: Meta campaigns using automatic placements and broad targeting, judged on blended results.
fails_when: The breakdown exposes a real error (wrong country, wrong gender for a gendered range, a placement that crops the creative badly), where Meta's spread reflects a setup problem rather than marginal returns.
numbers: example: Stories 4x ROAS vs Feed 3x with Feed holding about 80% of spend

claim: Every extra Meta campaign splits conversion data; 100 purchases a month across four campaigns leaves 25 each, and accounts often improve once one campaign clears 100 to 200 a month.
body: Campaigns, ad sets and ads exist on every ad platform for a reason: campaigns let a business run separate budgets, KPIs and reports. The cost is that learning is mostly kept inside each campaign. Some signal is shared across campaigns, but much less than within one. If a small account gets 100 purchases a month and runs four campaigns, each learns from about 25, and small samples make Meta guess who to target. Blue Sense often sees efficiency improve, not fall, once an account pushes past 100 to 200 conversions a month in a campaign. Ad sets matter far less: data shared at campaign level flows down, and hyper-splitting versus merging ad sets moves results by about 5% to 10%. How to apply: count monthly purchases per campaign. If several campaigns sit well under 100 a month and have no separate business reason (different margin, market, persona or stock goal), merge them and use ad sets for the splits you need to read.
conditions: Accounts under roughly $50k to $100k a month or with fewer than a few hundred purchases a month.
fails_when: The split serves a real commercial need such as a different margin band, a country with its own stock and targets, a separate funnel, or very high order value with tiny volume.

claim: For a $6M fashion brand with three categories selling in AU, NZ and UK, run one AU plus NZ campaign and one UK campaign, with category ad sets on ABO inside each.
body: The second worked example: fashion, about 50 SKUs in three categories (pants, tops, dresses), $6M a year, 50% gross margin (low for fashion, a sign of constant discounting), four personas, selling in Australia, New Zealand and the UK. Each category has its own purchase orders and sell-through goals, so categories need budget control. But three categories times two regions makes six campaigns, too many for this size. So segment by region at campaign level and by category at ad set level, using ABO so each category's budget is set by hand. The UK gets its own campaign because it sits on a separate subdomain with its own URLs, and the seasons are opposite, so the UK range is bought and sold on its own timetable. Australia and New Zealand share a campaign: New Zealand ships from the Australian warehouse and naturally takes only about 7% to 10% of spend. Add a DPA retargeting campaign on 90-day visitors and an existing-customer campaign.
conditions: Multi-category fashion or apparel brands in roughly the $3M to $15M range selling in two or three markets.
fails_when: All markets ship from one warehouse with no regional targets and the same season, where category campaigns with all regions combined work better.

claim: From $50k to $250k a month, add a Meta campaign only for a distinct funnel or business reason, such as a 65 plus persona with its own ads and landing page, or a high-LTV category given a higher CPA target.
body: As spend grows past $50k a month, structure grows mostly by adding ad sets for more concept tests, and perhaps a second or third campaign. Each extra campaign needs a reason tied to how the business makes money. For a one-SKU supplement, say fish oil, the reason is a different funnel: one aimed at people over 65 with joint pain, using long video sales letters, native-style statics and older testimonials, with its own landing page and photos; and another aimed at 25 to 35 year olds framed around brain health or work performance. Those are nearly two businesses, so two campaigns. For a fashion brand it may be a new arrivals campaign to drive sell-through, or a category campaign. If an LTV analysis shows one category, say pants, brings buyers with higher first order value and better repeat rates, give it its own campaign with a higher CPA target so you can acquire those customers harder. Adding campaigns just because one feels too few at $100k a month breaks data integrity.
conditions: Accounts at roughly $50k to $250k a month with LTV data by category or clearly separate funnels.
fails_when: There is no measurable difference in margin, LTV, landing page or persona between the proposed campaigns.

claim: Give a country its own Meta campaign only when you hold stock or revenue targets there, it uses its own site or URLs, or its season differs; otherwise sell all regions from one campaign.
body: Splitting by country costs conversion data, so it needs a business reason. The strongest reason is stock. If you hold inventory in a market and that market has its own sales target, you need to steer spend there to sell it through, and only a separate campaign lets you do that. If every order ships from one warehouse, it does not much matter which country buys; you just need to clear stock, so regions can share a campaign. Two other reasons force a split even then: a separate regional site or subdomain, so ads must point to different URLs, and opposite seasons, such as Australia and the UK in fashion, where what sells in one market flops in the other unless the product is trans-seasonal. How to apply: for each market, list where its stock sits, whether it has its own target, its URL, and its season. Split only where at least one answer differs, and push other splits (like category) down to ad sets.
conditions: Brands selling in two or more countries from one Meta account.
fails_when: Spend in a market is too small to run its own campaign well, or currency billing needs force a separate ad account anyway.

claim: If you sell separate men's and women's ranges, check the gender breakdown per ad set; mixed ad sets routinely serve women's products to men, so split ad sets by range.
body: Targeting mostly lives at the ad set level, so an ad set holding both men's and women's ads cannot tell who each ad is for and serves them to everyone. This is one of Blue Sense's quickest audit findings for activewear and apparel brands. Men's ads reaching women is less of a waste, because many women buy for partners; women's ads reaching men rarely pays. Sales still come in, but it is not the best use of the budget. How to apply: in Ads Manager open each ad set, use Breakdown, then By delivery, then Gender, and compare where each gendered ad is going. If women's product ads show a large share of male delivery, move men's and women's creative into separate ad sets (or campaigns, if each range has its own targets). Keep targeting broad within each, and let the creative define the audience.
conditions: Brands with distinct men's and women's product ranges in one account.
fails_when: Products are unisex, or a large share of sales are gifts bought by the other gender, which the breakdown will show as profitable.

claim: Judge Meta results at ad set and campaign level, not ad level: delivery optimizes the ad set's CPA across a chain of ads, while Ads Manager shows last-click credit per ad.
body: Ads Manager credits a sale to the last ad a person touched. Meta's delivery works differently: it optimizes toward the ad set's cost per result and learns from the whole chain of impressions and clicks that led to the sale. So three ads in one ad set might each spend $5,000 at very different ROAS, and the low-ROAS ones may be doing the early work that the top ad gets paid for. Kill them and the winner often drops too. How to apply: set your keep or kill rule on the ad set (did it hit target CPA or ROAS over a fair window?), and only pause single ads when they get spend but clearly fail on soft metrics too. Put any cost cap or bid cap on the ad set, never think of bidding as an ad level lever, because bidding is inherited from the ad set. Ad level data is still useful for creative learning: which hooks, formats and angles to make more of.
conditions: Ad sets with several ads where Meta spreads spend across them.
fails_when: An ad gets meaningful spend and is weak on every signal (hook rate, click rate, add to carts) as well as ROAS; then pausing it is fine.
numbers: example: three ads each spending about $5,000 at different returns in one ad set

claim: Meta caps live ads per page at roughly 300 to 500; heavy creative launchers should spin up duplicate brand pages and per-country pages so each gets its own cap.
body: Brands launching lots of creative every week run into the live ad limit per Facebook page, and the usual response, turning off ads or bundling them into flexible ads, costs data or reach. Blue Sense hits this with nearly every client. Two of its fixes use extra pages. First, duplicate pages: Grüns runs around 15 brand pages where only the logo color changes, and spreads ads across them. Second, regional pages: if you run separate campaigns for the UK, Australia and the US, 100 ads in each counts against one page even when the ads are the same. A Brand UK, Brand Australia and Brand USA page each get a fresh cap. How to apply: count live ads per page in the ad library. If you are within about 100 of the cap, set up the extra pages before the next big launch, and assign each country campaign to its own page. Spread new tests across pages rather than pausing working ads to make room.
conditions: Brands with high creative throughput, roughly 100 plus new ads a month or several country campaigns.
fails_when: A small account with tens of live ads, or a brand whose legal or brand team will not approve extra pages.

Grüns: about 15 duplicate pages differing by logo color
example: 3 country campaigns x 100 ads each hit one page's cap

claim: Name each ad set by persona, angle, offer, content type and launch date, not by batch like March 7 creatives, so you can filter and judge results by concept.
body: Most accounts Blue Sense picks up name ad sets by creative batch, such as a date or a drop name. That hides what is being tested and suggests several concepts were lumped together. You then cannot filter Ads Manager to see how all bride-angle ad sets or all founder-video ad sets have done over time. Blue Sense often goes back and renames old ad sets so the history becomes usable. How to apply: agree a naming pattern before the next launch, for example persona, angle, offer, content type (if the ad set is grouped by type), and launch date, separated by a fixed symbol. Keep one concept per ad set so the name is true. Then build saved filters or a sheet that rolls results up by persona and by angle each month, and use it to brief the creative team. When you inherit an account, rename past ad sets in the same pattern before drawing conclusions.

claim: Put at least 3 ads in every ad set so Meta can sequence them, and mix top, middle and bottom of funnel ads in one ad set rather than splitting by awareness stage.
body: Most buyers see an ad several times before purchasing. An ad set with one ad can only show that one ad over and over, so it cannot walk people from a story-led video to a direct offer. Blue Sense's rule of thumb is 3 to 15 ads per ad set, with no hard upper limit for accounts with huge creative volume; some of their ad sets hold 200 creatives. On awareness stage, both splitting and mixing can work, and Meta's learning slightly favors mixing so ads can sequence. The bigger reason is human. Split them and the top-of-funnel ad set might show 2x ROAS and the bottom-of-funnel one 6x, while together they make a 4x concept. People, and especially clients, then cut the 2x ad set, even though it feeds the 6x one. In one mixed ad set you simply see a 4x concept and scale it. How to apply: keep each ad set to one persona and concept, and include ads for every awareness stage inside it.
conditions: Any Meta ad set built around one concept or persona.
fails_when: You deliberately need to measure a stage on its own for a specific test question, and the team will read blended results correctly.

claim: Replace interest and lookalike tests with landing page split tests: a reported 30% of people in interest groups are wrongly assigned, and Meta now finds buyers from the creative.
body: Interest targeting tags people by what they interact with, not why. Someone who comments that they hate dogs can land in a dog interest group. A report Blue Sense cites put about 30% of interest group members in the wrong group. Signal loss after iOS 14 made labels weaker still, and Meta's newer retrieval system reads the creative and finds people who match it from a much richer picture of behavior. Broad targeting with strong creative now beats labels, and lookalikes add little. How to apply: stop spending test budget on interest stacks and lookalike percentages. Run broad with existing customers excluded, and let the concept in each ad set define who it reaches. Move the saved test budget into website tests: split test landing pages and product page changes, because a lift in conversion rate improves every campaign at once. When a broad campaign stalls as it scales, read it as the creative not convincing colder people, and fix the creative, not the targeting.
conditions: E-commerce accounts with enough conversion volume for broad delivery to learn, roughly the 100 plus purchases a month range.
fails_when: A very new pixel with almost no purchase history, a tiny niche where broad cannot find buyers quickly, or legal limits that require specific targeting.

claim: Rotate some accounts into CBO for November and December to spend as much as possible efficiently, then back to ABO in Q1 to force spend through new creative tests.
body: Think of CBO as higher risk with slightly higher return, and ABO as lower risk with return maybe 10% lower. In the peak sale period the goal is to push as much profitable spend as possible in a short window, and nobody cares which creative carries it, so CBO fits. Q4 is also a poor time to judge tests: sale demand lifts conversion rates and makes weak ads look good. January and February are the reverse. Demand is calmer, the team wants to set up the year's creative pipeline, and forced spend through new concepts gives cleaner reads. How to apply: before Black Friday, move proven ads into a CBO and pause most new concept tests. In early January, return to ABO testing with fresh concepts and fair budgets per ad set. Keep a note of which ads won in Q4 so you can retest them in Q1 at normal conversion rates before trusting them.
conditions: Brands with a strong Q4 peak and a steady creative pipeline.
fails_when: The brand's peak is elsewhere in the year, or the account is too small to run separate testing and scaling setups.
numbers: ABO return roughly 10% lower than CBO in this framing

claim: Set existing-customer Meta budget in dollars from customer count times CPM divided by 1,000 times target monthly frequency, not as a percentage cap of spend.
body: When Advantage+ shopping campaigns launched, the first setting was an existing customer budget cap as a percentage. That framed everyone around picking a share. The share tells you little: it moves whenever your customer list grows or your cold budget changes. Twenty percent can mean a customer sees you 50 times a month, or once. Blue Sense cares about two things instead. Is the extra spend profitable, meaning does another $10 or $1,000 a day on customers bring back enough repeat revenue? And what is the frequency, which gives a quicker read? How to apply: take the number of reachable existing customers, multiply by your CPM on that audience divided by 1,000, then by the frequency you want per month. That is your monthly existing-customer budget. Check the result against repeat revenue and adjust frequency up or down. In Blue Sense's fashion guidance the sensible band is about 3 to 7 per 30 days.
conditions: Brands with a meaningful customer list and some repeat purchase behavior.
fails_when: Products are rarely rebought (furniture, one-off purchases), where the right budget may be near zero.

claim: Split Meta campaigns when product ranges carry different margins after discounts; in one shared campaign, spend drifts to heavily discounted slow stock where contribution margin is thinnest.
body: Full consolidation is wrong for most brands, and margin is the first reason. A brand with many SKUs often has ranges at 70% gross margin and others at 60%, plus slow stock that only sells when marked down hard. Put the full-price and the deep-discount ads in one campaign and Meta will often pour budget into the sale items, because a discount converts easily. Your platform ROAS looks fine while contribution margin falls, and pushing sale messages to every new buyer weakens the brand. How to apply: list your ranges with gross margin after typical discounts. Where the post-discount margin differs a lot, give those ranges their own campaign with their own CPA or ROAS target, set from what each can afford. Keep promo and clearance spend in its own campaign so it cannot crowd out full-price acquisition.
conditions: Multi-SKU brands with clearly different margin bands or a regular clearance range.
fails_when: Margins are similar across the range and stock sells evenly, or spend is so low that splitting starves each campaign of conversions.
numbers: example margins: 70% vs 60% gross margin across ranges

claim: Treat retargeting as a capped support layer: audits often find about 50% of spend on existing and engaged people; merge retargeting audiences and steer by frequency, not ROAS.
body: Blue Sense often opens the audience segment breakdown in an audit and finds around half of spend going to existing customers and engaged visitors. That spend supports sales that would mostly happen anyway; it does not grow new customers. Their rule is opposite mindsets. On cold acquisition, keep asking where you can spend more while it stays profitable. On retargeting, keep asking where you can take money out, on Meta, TikTok and Pinterest alike, because the top end of retargeting spend is usually not incremental. Second, do not split retargeting into separate ad sets for add to cart, checkout started, page viewed or category; that 2019 setup raises CPMs and the conversion rate gain never covers it. Third, after incremental revenue, the main gauge is frequency. If existing customers see your ads 30 times a month, you are overspending. How to apply: run the breakdown, merge retargeting audiences into one or two ad sets, and cut budget until frequency sits in a sane band.
conditions: Accounts with established customer lists and site traffic.
fails_when: Fashion and other frequent-drop categories where holdout tests show existing-customer spend is incremental; still steer by frequency.

claim: Turn off Advantage+ creative enhancements in the advertiser settings as well as on every ad, because automated rules there quietly switch them back on; and ignore 1-day view in budget decisions.
body: Blue Sense's settings audit has a few quick checks. First, Advantage+ creative optimizations: unticking them on each ad is not enough. In Advertiser settings, under the creative section, there are automated defaults that turn these enhancements back on over time unless you switch them off at account level too. Do both. Second, attribution: do not use 1-day view to decide which ad sets get budget. View-through credit over-counts sales from existing customers who would have bought anyway. Read on 7-day click, and use incremental attribution where you can. Third, bidding: under about $200k a month, cost caps and bid caps are rarely the bottleneck; ask whether the business would double from bidding work, and the answer is usually no. Fourth, flexible ads off unless the page ad cap forces them. How to apply: run these checks when you take over an account and again every quarter, since Meta changes defaults often.
conditions: Any Meta account, especially ones set up with default settings.
fails_when: A brand deliberately tests Advantage+ enhancements in a controlled split and finds they help.
numbers: bidding strategy work not a priority under about $200k a month

claim: Turn off Meta flexible ads and dynamic creative unless you have hit the page ad limit; you cannot tell which asset drove results, and Meta crops and stitches assets into carousels.
body: Flexible ads (the current name for loading several creatives into one ad) look like neat consolidation. The problem is data. When that ad does well you cannot see whether asset one or asset four did the work, so you cannot make more of it. That breaks the basic loop of read the data, decide, make the next batch. Blue Sense also dislikes the presentation: Meta crops square assets into Story slots and Story assets into Feed, and can join several images into a carousel the brand never approved. How to apply: in each new ad, and in the advertiser settings, keep single creative ads as your default. The only good reason to use flexible ads is the live ad cap per page. Fix that first with extra pages, whitelisting or partnership ads. If you still must use them, group only near-identical assets in each flexible ad so any win still teaches you something. In ad library audits, heavy dynamic creative use far below the page limit is a red flag for weak creative feedback.
conditions: Brands that rely on creative testing to learn what to make next.
fails_when: The page is at its live ad cap and other fixes are not possible yet, or the assets in the flexible ad are near-identical variants.

Why can't I tell which creative is working?

claim: Under $50k a month, run a testing campaign with one concept per ad set and 3 to 5 creatives each; when a concept wins, launch its new creative in a new ad set rather than touching the working one.
body: Blue Sense's generic setup for accounts under $50k a month is a testing campaign (ABO or CBO), an optional scaling campaign, and an optional existing-customer campaign. In the testing campaign each ad set holds one concept: a persona, an angle and an offer combined, with 3 to 5 creatives built for it. When you make more creative for a concept, where it goes depends on how the ad set is doing. If the ad set is not hitting target, add the new ads to it and try to revive it. If it is hitting target, leave it alone and launch the new ads as a fresh ad set next to it. You can end up with 10 ad sets, six of them the same winning concept, and that is fine because one concept usually outshines the rest. Exclude existing customers so repeat buyers do not make a test look better than it is, and read results on 7-day click.
conditions: Accounts under roughly $50k a month in Meta spend with a steady flow of new creative.
fails_when: Creative volume is too low to fill concept ad sets, or the product has very long buying cycles where tests need much longer windows.

3 to 5 creatives per ad set

claim: Whitelisting runs ads through a third-party page you create (for example a health magazine style page), while partnership ads run through a real creator's handle; both feel less like a sales pitch and lift the ad cap.
body: The two are often mixed up. Partnership ads use a real creator or influencer who exists outside your brand, and you run ads through their handle, often paying them for the right if they have a following. Whitelisting in Blue Sense's sense means building your own third-party page, say a page named like a fiber health magazine for a gut health brand, and running ads through it. The upside of both is that the ad appears to come from someone other than the seller, and each new handle adds room under the per-page live ad cap. How to apply: for a whitelisting page, rework the creative to fit the third-party frame, more advertorial and editorial than brand ad. For partnership ads, line up as many creator handles as you can afford. Use both alongside duplicate and regional brand pages. Partnership ads earn their cost on cold audiences, so do not pay creators to front hard-sell retargeting ads.
conditions: Brands that have outgrown one page's ad cap or want cold creative that reads as third-party content.
fails_when: The third-party page misleads people in a regulated category or breaks Meta's rules on authentic identity; disclose the brand link where required.

How do I make ads look less like ads?

claim: With very high order value and only a handful of purchases a day, avoid CBO: Meta allocates on clicks and CPC, which barely correlate with return, so force budgets with ABO.
body: A CBO decides which ad set gets money from the signals it has. When a store sells a $10,000 item and gets about five orders a day, there are far too few purchases for that. Meta falls back on earlier signals like click rate, cost per click and hold rate. Across large data sets Blue Sense finds cost per click has almost no link to return except at the extremes, so budget ends up following the ads that win clicks rather than sales. How to apply: if your account gets only a few purchases a day, run ad set budgets so you decide where money goes, and judge ad sets on purchases over longer windows. Consider optimizing for a deeper event only if it truly predicts sales. Expect your structure to look unlike the standard playbooks, and avoid copying a CBO setup from a low-price brand.
conditions: Order values in the thousands and purchase volume of roughly single digits per day.
fails_when: Purchase volume is high enough (dozens a day or more) that CBO can learn from sales directly.
numbers: example: about $10,000 average order value, about 5 orders a day

claim: Scale Meta before YouTube: a brand spending $50,000 a month on Meta can likely reach $200,000 there first, because YouTube needs more spend to learn, attributes poorly and needs its own creative.
body: Nathan's reasons for holding most e-commerce clients back from YouTube: it is worse than Meta at learning where to show ads, so it needs more budget to get going; few viewers click a YouTube ad and buy, so most of its effect is a halo you can only see with marketing mix models or incrementality tests, which smaller brands cannot run well; and a Meta ad dropped into YouTube usually fails, so creative has to be reworked for the platform. Austin agrees and sends clients to Meta first. The brands he sees winning on YouTube fall into two groups: very large budgets, for example $50,000 a month on YouTube next to $250,000 on Meta plus Search and Shopping, or brands with a big YouTube channel of their own, who remarket to their viewers. He finds it easier for high ticket info products with video sales letters than for stores. He does think a properly built Demand Gen campaign does not waste much money, and a small remarketing budget can be reasonable if you accept weak attribution. Decision rule: add YouTube when Meta growth has truly capped out, when you have an engaged channel audience to remarket to, or when you can measure lift with a holdout test. Start with viewer remarketing or Demand Gen, judge it on total business results over time, and make video for YouTube rather than reusing Meta cuts.
conditions: E-commerce brands spending well under about $250,000 a month on Meta, without a large YouTube channel or the tools to measure lift.
fails_when: Brands with a big YouTube audience; brands that can run geo holdout tests or a marketing mix model; categories where Meta is restricted or already saturated.

Example big spender: $50,000 a month on YouTube beside $250,000 on Meta

claim: Assume Meta CPMs rise every year; since CAC equals CPC divided by conversion rate and CPC rises with CPM and falls with click rate, you must lift click rate or conversion rate yearly to stand still.
body: Blue Sense's stance is that the long story of iOS 14, Andromeda and other platform changes matters less than one fact: Meta must make more money each year, either by showing more ads or by charging more per impression, and ad load has a ceiling while price does not. So plan for higher CPMs every year. Then trace the effect through the maths. CAC is cost per click divided by conversion rate. Cost per click is CPM divided by 1,000 impressions, divided by click-through rate, so it rises with CPM and falls as click rate improves. The only offsets you control are click rate (better creative and hooks) and conversion rate (better page and offer). Meta's own targeting upgrades such as GEM, Lattice and Andromeda help both, but Meta keeps most of that gain through pricing. If you improve a little every week, you outpace the CPM rise while most competitors feel the squeeze and pull back, which is when you can push harder. How to apply: track CPM, click rate and conversion rate monthly against the same month last year, and plan creative and CRO work to beat the CPM increase.
conditions: Brands buying traffic on Meta and similar auction platforms.
fails_when: Short periods where CPMs fall (for example after a sharp drop in competition), though Blue Sense expects the yearly trend to keep rising.
numbers: CAC = CPC / conversion rate
CPC = CPM / (1,000 x CTR)

claim: Check budget across new, engaged and existing audiences by 30-day frequency, not percentage split: existing around 30 means overspending on customers, engaged around 14 means too much middle-of-funnel creative.
body: After counting campaigns, look at how delivery spreads across the three audience segments Meta reports: new, engaged and existing customers. Blue Sense ignores the percentage split and reads the 30-day frequency in each. If existing customers are seeing ads around 30 times in a month, the account is spending too much on people who already buy and you need a dedicated, capped campaign for them with exclusions everywhere else. If engaged audiences sit around 14, the creative mix leans too far toward middle-of-funnel assets that only work on people who already know you, so cut some of that content and brief more top-of-funnel ads. They call this one of the most common mistakes they find: content that is not broad enough to reach cold people, and existing customer spend that is not controlled in its own campaign so it bleeds into every campaign. How to check: in Ads Manager, break down results by audience segment over the last 30 days and read frequency and spend for each.
conditions: Meta accounts with audience segments defined (new, engaged, existing) so the breakdown is available; mid to large spend where frequency is meaningful.
fails_when: Brands with a deliberate retention or launch push to existing customers, or very small accounts where frequency numbers are low across the board.
numbers: existing customer 30-day frequency around 30 = overspend
engaged audience 30-day frequency around 14 = too much MOF creative

claim: Do not let dynamic product ads take most of the budget (70% is a red flag, as they are bottom of funnel and not incremental), and break every winner down by variable before replicating it.
body: Three creative-side checks from the audit. First, dynamic product ads (catalogue ads) can spend and do acceptably on cold audiences, but they mainly catch people already close to buying, so an account with 70% of spend in DPAs is mostly harvesting demand rather than creating it. Shift budget back to concept-led creative. Second, many brands find a winner and then never build on it, jumping straight to new ideas. Before moving on, work out why it won: the persona, the angle, the format, the script, the creator or talent. Then make new ads that keep the winning variable and change the rest. Third, ask whether there is a creative roadmap at all. Shooting ads only when the account runs dry is a sign of trouble; you want a steady production system that pushes high volume into the account and a feedback loop where results from the account shape the next briefs.
conditions: Meta accounts with catalogue campaigns and an ongoing creative pipeline.
fails_when: Large-catalogue retailers whose shoppers browse widely, where catalogue ads may justify a bigger share if holdout tests show they are incremental.
numbers: 70% of spend in DPAs flagged as a mistake

claim: Every paid media bottleneck sits in one of three pillars (account structure and testing, creative velocity and diversity, or data integrity), and Blue Sense audits each one in turn.
body: Blue Sense frames paid growth for e-commerce as three schools of thought. First, technical account structure: how the Meta and Google accounts are built and how new tests enter them. Second, creative velocity and diversity: how many new ads go in each month and how different they truly are. Third, data integrity and assurance: whether the number you optimise in the platform (usually ROAS) actually moves with the business number that matters (acquisition MER, new customer revenue over ad spend). Their view is that getting these three right covers almost all of what is needed to grow a retail brand profitably. Each pillar looks different by size and model: a seven figure store, a nine figure retailer and a brand with wholesale or physical retail need different structures and measurement, and a fashion brand needs different creative volume and mix than a CPG brand. How to apply: score your business on each pillar separately, decide which single one is the current constraint, and fix that before spreading effort across all three.
conditions: Shopify-style DTC brands spending meaningfully on Meta and Google; the framework is Blue Sense's current thesis and they expect it to evolve.
fails_when: The real constraint is outside paid media, such as stock, product quality, pricing or fulfilment, which none of the three pillars will reveal on its own.

claim: Set Meta campaigns to 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view, because Meta moved engaged actions (likes, comments, shares or 5+ seconds watched) out of click attribution around mid 2026.
body: Blue Sense used to recommend 7-day click alone as the setting that best matched the P&L. Meta then redefined attribution: an engaged view covers someone who liked, commented, shared or watched at least five seconds of the ad before converting, and those people used to be counted inside 7-day click. Since that change (about three months before this September 2026 video), 7-day click plus 1-day engaged view is the equivalent of the old 7-day click, so it is their default now. It is not the same as plain 1-day view, which credits people who merely scrolled past. In an audit, also check that settings are consistent across campaigns, because mixed windows make ROAS across campaigns impossible to compare. How to apply: in each ad set's conversion settings, choose 7-day click and 1-day engaged view; then confirm with an attribution comparison that ROAS on this setting tracks acquisition MER from your first-time P&L.
conditions: Meta purchase-optimised campaigns after Meta's 2026 change to engaged-view definitions.
fails_when: Brands whose tests show a different window tracks their business better; Meta's definitions can change again, so recheck against acquisition MER.

definition changed about 3 months before Sept 2026

claim: Start any Meta or Google account from one cold campaign and require a written, defensible purpose for each extra one; accounts spending $1M to $5M a month often run only four or five campaigns.
body: The premise is that every element of the account must have a reason to exist and the goal is a single campaign. In an audit they list every live campaign and write down what each one is for. Two cold campaigns both doing creative testing, or a separate add-to-cart optimised campaign, usually cannot be defended, and roughly half of campaigns in typical accounts get cut or merged, which tends to improve results. Do it yourself: put every campaign in a sheet, add a column for its purpose, and argue why it cannot be rolled into another. If you or your agency cannot defend it, consolidate it. More spend does not justify more campaigns; more business complexity does. Retailers selling in seven countries, with three sub-brands, a fast-turning range and different priorities by category need separate campaigns so they can push budget into, say, dresses or New Zealand and read the return quickly. A smaller Australian brand would normally run Australia and New Zealand together in one campaign.
conditions: Meta and Google accounts at any spend; the separate-campaign exceptions apply to multi-country, multi-brand or multi-category retailers.
fails_when: The business genuinely has separate targets by country, sub-brand or category that need their own budget lever; consolidating those hides which part is underperforming.

claim: The errors Blue Sense finds most in Meta audits: undefined new, engaged and existing audiences, local campaigns leaking into Audience Network app rewards, interest or lookalike targeting on purchase campaigns, missing customer exclusions, and names that do not match settings.
body: Settings errors come last in their audit, but these are the common ones. One: audience segment definitions for new, engaged and existing customers are not set, so reporting and frequency checks are meaningless. Two: campaigns built to drive people into a physical store with local targeting often spill into Audience Network and specifically the app rewards placement; Nathan says he has never seen it produce a purchase, so remove it. Three: old targeting methods such as lookalikes or interests on purchase objectives, which they would not use in almost any e-commerce account. Four: existing customers not properly excluded from cold campaigns. Five, the most frequent: naming that does not match reality. A campaign labelled cold top of funnel turns out to target existing customers with bottom-of-funnel creative, so its ROAS looks great and someone tries to scale it. Or an ad set labelled problem aware is full of solution aware ads. Open each campaign, ad set and its ads and check that targeting, settings and creative all do what the name says.
conditions: Meta accounts of any size, especially ones that have passed through several managers or agencies.
fails_when: Brands with deliberate store-traffic or lead objectives where some of these settings are intended; check purpose before removing.

claim: Do not plan BFCM 2026 from 2025: in Q4 2025 Meta's impressions rose 18% while price per ad rose only 6%, and in 2026 impression growth has slowed while CPMs climb.
body: Meta reports total ad impressions and average price per ad every quarter. In Q4 2025 it opened up much more ad inventory, so people saw more ads and fewer organic posts: impressions grew 18% year on year while price per ad grew 6%, and Triple Whale data showed CPM inflation of about 7.8%. That extra supply kept Black Friday CPMs from spiking. By Q1 and Q2 2026, impression growth had started to compress and year-on-year CPM growth was already worse than during last Black Friday. Blue Sense expects higher CPMs and less extra inventory this time, sold to weaker consumers. In Australia the cash rate was 3.60% after three cuts before BFCM 2025 and 4.35% after three hikes before BFCM 2026, with sticky inflation, and they see similar pressure in the US. How to apply: forecast BFCM with higher CPMs than last year, stress test the plan at your current year-on-year CPM growth, and do not assume that a 20% discount plus a bit more spend will repeat last year's result.
conditions: Planning Q4 2026 paid social budgets; the cash rate figures apply to Australian brands, the platform trend to all Meta advertisers.
fails_when: If Meta again expands inventory sharply in Q4, CPMs may hold; markets or categories whose seasonal demand differs.

Triple Whale: about 7.8% CPM inflation

claim: From about 16 December the auction gets as cheap as it gets all quarter, so plan a post-Christmas (Q5) offer to buy cheap media after the BFCM peak.
body: CPMs peak around Black Friday and stay high in early December while gift buying runs. Blue Sense's portfolio data shows November has the best conversion but the most expensive reach, and the cheapest media of the quarter comes after Christmas, from around 16 December. Saturation during the peak is real but smaller than many fear. How to apply: plan a Q5 offer (Boxing Day, new year, clearance or a fresh launch) and have budget ready to scale as CPMs fall. Across the whole period, roll through several offers (early access, main sale, Cyber Monday, Q5) rather than one long discount, which helps prevent offer fatigue. Build an offer ladder in advance, a ranked set of stronger and weaker offers, so you can switch quickly if trade is weak on the day.
conditions: Brands whose buyers shop for themselves after Christmas; markets such as Australia and the US where Boxing Day and new year sales are normal.
fails_when: Gift-led categories whose demand ends at Christmas; brands that discounted deeply in November and risk teaching buyers to always wait.
numbers: cheapest auction of the quarter from about 16 December

claim: Put 31% to 43% of the September to December paid budget into September and October, because underspending before the sale shrinks the audience the sale converts.
body: Conversion rates dip in the weeks before Black Friday because shoppers know a sale is coming, and many brands respond by cutting spend. That starves the awareness and site traffic the sale depends on, so the sale peak comes out smaller. Blue Sense's portfolio data puts 31% to 43% of the four-month budget in September and October. Every sale is followed by a slump, because it pulled future buyers forward; that is normal and not a reason to underfund the build-up next time. How to apply: take your planned September to December spend and set a pre-season floor in that range. Do not judge pre-season on real-time ROAS; apply the attribution multiplier you measured from last year. Use the pre-season to prepare Google, get sale creative live early enough to collect delivery data, and lock offers. Then ramp budgets on a written schedule into mid November instead of pulling back when early November reads badly.
conditions: Brands doing roughly $1M to $50M a year with a major BFCM sale and an audience to build; the range comes from Blue Sense's own client portfolio.
fails_when: Brands that do not run a sale, or whose cash is too tight to fund spend that pays back weeks later; brand-new stores with no audience yet.
numbers: 31 to 43% of September to December budget in September and October
asks: How much of my Q4 budget should I spend before Black Friday?

claim: Write BFCM scaling rules on a 3-day rolling read of marginal CM3: raise budget when it is improving, hold when it is not, and cut after two poor reads in a row.
body: Daily results in a sale swing with time zones, email sends and attribution lag, so changing budgets day to day mostly chases noise. Blue Sense writes the rules down before the period starts. Each read uses a 3-day rolling average of the marginal change in contribution margin after ad spend (CM3). If marginal CM3 is improving, budget goes up. If it is flat or worse, budget stays where it is. Two poor reads in a row and budget comes down. On the busiest days they may switch to daily reads, depending on total spend and how quickly it is moving against the pacing sheet. Build that pacing sheet from last year's hourly revenue and spend curves so you know what a normal hour looks like on each sale day. Do not grade a sale day against a fixed early morning target, since sale days book late. Agreeing the rules in advance stops panic cuts and blind scaling in the middle of the night.
conditions: Accounts with daily contribution margin data (revenue, COGS, shipping, discounts, ad spend) available quickly; mid to large spend during BFCM.
fails_when: No reliable daily margin data; very small budgets where even three days of data are noise.

pacing sheet built from last year's hourly revenue and spend
