claim: Choose CBO or ABO as a risk decision: CBO puts about 80% of spend on 20% of ads for best efficiency but fragile results; Blue Sense often runs CBO with ad set minimum spends.
body: Blue Sense reframes the ABO versus CBO argument. With campaign budget optimisation, the Pareto pattern will show up: about 20% of ads take about 80% of spend. That gives the best efficiency now but the weakest portfolio, because when those few winners fatigue, spend shifts to unproven ads and results swing. With ad set budgets you force spend into more ad sets, including weaker ones, which lowers return a little but cuts risk materially; you usually end up with more offers, angles and concepts working at the same time, which is the position Blue Sense prefers. Their common middle ground is a CBO campaign with minimum spend set on each ad set, so the algorithm still allocates but every concept gets enough budget to be read. How to apply: check how concentrated your spend is. If one or two ads hold most of a CBO's spend, add ad set minimums to protect testing of the others, or move tests into ABO, and track how many concepts are profitable at once, not just overall ROAS.
conditions: Meta accounts with several concepts or ad sets live, at a spend level where one fatiguing ad can swing the month.
fails_when: Very small budgets where forcing spend into weak ad sets wastes money that one strong ad could use, or accounts in a short sale window where efficiency now matters more than future stability.

claim: Do not scale the 6x ROAS bottom-funnel ad; Meta sequences your ads but credits the last one, so the 1.4x unaware ad is often what made that purchase possible.
body: Picture one ad set with three ads: an unaware ad, a problem-aware ad, and a product-aware ad as simple as a product image with a discount. Meta tends to show them in sequence: the unaware ad reaches a new person first, the problem-aware ad follows, then the product ad works like retargeting and gets the click. The purchase is credited to the last ad, so it shows something like 6x ROAS while the unaware ad shows 1.4x. Most buyers then make more ads like the product ad and try to scale it, which fails because it was never reaching new people. Take away the first two ads and the third barely works. Blue Sense's four consequences: run one concept per ad set; keep a variety of formats because users prefer different content types; keep producing volume because each ad has a spend limit; and separate top and bottom of funnel with different efficiency targets, since bottom-funnel ads over-attribute. How to apply: set a lower ROAS or higher CPA target for cold, high-awareness-stage ads, and judge them on spend held, new reach and blended new-customer results.
conditions: Meta accounts mixing awareness stages in the same campaigns or ad sets and judging ads on in-platform ROAS.
fails_when: The bottom-funnel ad truly reaches new buyers on its own (for example a well-known product with strong search demand), which a holdout or ad set split can confirm.

claim: Keep ad-level frequency on cold campaigns below 2 over the last 30 days; above 2 means your ads are too similar and are being served to the same people.
body: Meta no longer matches your ad to an audience you picked; it reads the ad and finds people for it. So several similar ads land in the same audience pool: frequency rises, reach falls and returns decline. Blue Sense adds that the chance of a purchase drops after about two views of the same ad; by the third to fifth view the viewer knows the message and has already passed, so showing a fresh ad works better than repeating. Their 30-day check: in Ads Manager, set the date range to the last 30 days, open cold (prospecting) campaigns at ad level, sort by amount spent, and read the frequency column. Ad-level frequency above 2 on cold campaigns signals a creative diversity problem, not an editing one. Do not blame the editor; the cause sits upstream in the idea, the concept and the format. Ignore warm and existing-customer campaigns, where higher frequency is normal. One exception they name: in a small market such as Australia at around $300,000 a month, high frequency may simply mean you have hit the market's ceiling.
conditions: Cold prospecting campaigns on Meta in large markets such as the US, read at ad level over 30 days.
fails_when: Small markets at high spend (Blue Sense's example: Australia at about $300,000 a month), retargeting or existing customer campaigns, or very new ads with tiny reach.

claim: Rank Meta ad metrics by reliability: amount spent first, then ROAS or CPA, then CPC and CTR, then hook and hold rate; an ad at double the spend with a lower return is usually better.
body: Blue Sense's order surprises most people. Amount spent comes first because budget distribution is Meta telling you which creative it can actually use to find buyers. An ad taking twice the spend at a somewhat lower ROAS is usually the more valuable ad: it is often the one reaching new people, while middle and bottom-funnel ads follow up and collect the credit. When an ad takes a lot of spend, ask why: low frequency, strong hook and hold rates, high click-through rate. ROAS or CPA comes second; for these, Blue Sense removes one-day view from the attribution setting and uses seven-day click with one-day engaged view. CPC and CTR come third. Hook rate and hold rate come last: they are good diagnostics showing which part of an asset to rebuild, but often do not track with sales, so do not use them to predict winners or cut ads early. How to apply: sort ads by spend first in your weekly review, then read return; let spend distribute before judging, and use hook and hold rates only to brief fixes.
conditions: Meta accounts running CBO or broad delivery where the platform allocates spend between ads, with enough budget for spend patterns to mean something.
fails_when: Spend is forced by ABO caps or minimums, so spend reflects your settings, not Meta's choice; or a high-spend ad's return is far below break-even, where spend share does not justify it.
numbers: reliability order: spend, ROAS or CPA, CPC and CTR, hook and hold rate
attribution: 7-day click, 1-day engaged view, no 1-day view

claim: Structure Meta as a testing campaign with one concept per ad set and 10 or more ads each, an optional scaling CBO fed by post IDs, and a separate existing-customer campaign.
body: Blue Sense's baseline layout: 1) A testing campaign where each ad set is one concept (persona, angle, offer) holding 10 or more ads. Two or three ads per concept is far too few to find a winner or know if the concept works. 2) An optional scaling campaign, worth it only for larger businesses or launch and event-style pushes that need spend to rise fast; move winners in by post ID so the ad keeps its social proof and history, never rebuild the ad, and run it as a large-budget CBO. 3) In e-commerce, always a separate existing-customer campaign. Why one concept per ad set: ROAS gets less reliable the lower you read in the account, so you judge at ad set level; it avoids ad-level sequencing confusion; and delivery works a little better when ads in an ad set share a persona. Adding new ads to a winning ad set usually resets its sequencing, so launch new ad sets instead. How to apply: rename your ad sets by concept; any ad set mixing unrelated concepts should be split at the next launch.
conditions: Meta e-commerce accounts with enough budget to give each concept ad set real spend, roughly tens of thousands a month and up.
fails_when: Very small budgets that cannot feed several ad sets of 10 ads, where fewer concepts in one campaign is more practical.

claim: Treat partnership ads as a must: in some of Blue Sense's top B2B and info accounts, about 40% of spend runs through them.
body: Partnership ads run your ad through another person's profile, such as a creator, expert or founder, alongside or instead of the brand page. Blue Sense says they are a must, particularly where ads would otherwise run only from a company or personal page, and reports that in some of the top B2B and info accounts they consult on, around 40% of account spend goes through partnership ads. In their Gorilla Mind teardown they made the same point for DTC: running ads from a creator's profile brings that profile's audience signals into delivery and helps reach people the brand page does not, which matters as frequency climbs. How to apply: list the creators, customers or experts who already post about you, or whom you pay for content, and ask for partnership ad permission. Launch your proven concepts through two or three of these profiles, compare cost per purchase and reach with the same creative from your brand page, and shift spend where the profile performs better. Keep usage rights and dates written down.
conditions: Meta accounts that can get partnership permissions from creators or experts relevant to the product; the 40% figure comes from B2B and info accounts.
fails_when: The creators have small or mismatched audiences, or permissions lapse; e-commerce accounts may see a much lower ideal share than 40%.

claim: Consolidate on Meta, but split out anything that must get spend: a creator partnership ad costing $2K a week, or new arrivals dropped every two weeks into one Advantage+ campaign, often get almost no budget.
body: Nathan says roughly 60 to 70% of Blue Sense's client spend is on Meta and about 30% on Google. He agrees heavy segmentation dilutes conversion data, so the push to consolidate after Andromeda has merit, but argues for a few deliberate splits that match business goals, and says few media buyers have the business sense to choose them well. Accounts tend to fall into two camps: two campaigns and nothing else, or one campaign per category; neither is ideal. His test: an account launching 10 ads a month can live in one campaign; one launching 600 a month cannot assume the right ads get budget. Audit examples: a creator charging $2,000 a week for a partnership ad that sits inside the main Advantage+ campaign and gets almost no spend, wasting the fee; and large fashion brands dropping new arrivals every two weeks into the same campaign as the core collection, where the algorithm keeps spending on proven core lines and the new range never takes off. How to apply: list what must get spend for commercial reasons (paid creator content, launches, new arrivals, clearance), give each its own campaign or ad set and budget, and keep the rest consolidated.
conditions: Meta accounts with high creative volume, paid creator content or frequent product drops.
fails_when: Small accounts with few ads and one product line, where splitting only fragments data.

claim: For large fashion retailers, Blue Sense's incrementality studies show TikTok driving strong incremental returns while its 7-day click ROAS sits around 0.7 to 1, but most smaller brands needing cash now should skip it.
body: Nathan calls TikTok a fairly poor ad platform in general, yet for large retail fashion brands it has done very well in Blue Sense's incrementality studies, absorbing a lot of spend at a strong incremental return. Its own 7-day click ROAS on those accounts looks terrible, around 0.7 to 1. A leadership team steering by attributed ROAS, from the platform or a third-party tool, would cut it and pour money into middle and bottom of funnel. Michael's counterpoint for smaller brands: most need cash now, and top-of-funnel bets like TikTok are long-term investments they often cannot afford, so most should not be advertising on TikTok; if they do top-of-funnel at all, Meta and Instagram are the better place. How to apply: if you are a large, well-known fashion or retail brand, run a lift or geo test before judging TikTok, and fund it on incremental return. If you are smaller with tight cash, put upper-funnel money into Meta first and leave TikTok until you can afford to measure it properly.
conditions: Large retail fashion brands with high awareness and budget for lift tests.
fails_when: Smaller brands that need short-term cash returns, or categories where TikTok's audience does not match the buyer.

claim: Paid ads are for acquisition, except fashion with frequent drops, where a dedicated existing-customer campaign for new arrivals pays; target its CPA at half the new-customer CPA or lower.
body: Blue Sense once held that no ad money should go to existing customers, because acquisition compounds growth while retention makes you profitable. They changed their view for fashion. Brands dropping new products weekly cannot reach the whole customer base by email and SMS alone: people miss or ignore emails, and without stores they walk past, they never see most new arrivals. So a dedicated campaign showing new arrivals and current campaign shoots to existing customers is incremental. Judge it on a different KPI from prospecting: if new customer CPA target is $40, aim for $20 or lower on existing customers, since a warm audience should be far cheaper to convert. If existing-customer CPA is close to new-customer CPA, you are overspending on them or your ads are weak. How to apply: build an existing-customer audience from your customer list, exclude it from prospecting reporting, rotate new arrival and shoot creative, and hold it to the lower CPA target.
conditions: Fashion and other brands with frequent new product drops and a sizeable customer list on Meta.
fails_when: Brands with rare launches or small customer lists, where email and SMS already reach most buyers and paid spend on them is mostly waste.
numbers: $40 new-customer CPA versus $20 or lower existing-customer CPA

claim: Set existing-customer ad budget in dollars: frequency (4 to 7 a month) times customers times CPM divided by 1,000; cutting $1,000 a day to $700 kept 47 of 50 conversions.
body: Spending more on a small, known audience does not make it buy more, so returns fall off fast. In Blue Sense's example, $1,000 a day on existing customers brings 50 conversions; cutting to $700 a day still brings 47. The extra $300 bought only 3 conversions, about $100 each, likely far above what you would want to pay. Most brands overspend here, and the savings can go into acquisition. Do not size this budget as a percentage of total spend. Work it out in dollars: the number of times a month you want each customer to see an ad (Blue Sense uses four to seven), times the number of customers in the audience, times the CPM, divided by 1,000. As our own illustration, 50,000 customers at frequency 5 and a $15 CPM gives $3,750 a month. How to apply: compute the formula budget, cut the existing-customer campaign toward it in steps, and watch whether conversion volume holds; if it does, move the difference to prospecting.
conditions: Brands running a separate campaign or ad set aimed at existing customers.
fails_when: Audiences too small for Meta to deliver steadily, or launch weeks where a short burst of higher frequency is intended.

claim: To enter a new market, push one or two proven SKUs hard and keep reordering stock; Blue Sense would happily scale a product at 15% MER to $1M a month, then broaden the range.
body: This is Blue Sense's usual approach for taking local brands into the US: find the one or two products that sell best, put as much spend behind them as possible, and keep reordering inventory. A winner at a 15% MER (ad spend as a share of revenue) scaled to $1M a month at around a 20% net margin is a good business on its own, and it can bring your first $10 million in that country plus a customer list. Brand teams often worry the brand will become known for one product. Blue Sense's answer: once you have a large customer list and some awareness, add new product tests in the account and widen the range, while the winning ads keep running. How to apply: pick SKUs with proven ads and healthy margin; check stock depth and reorder lead times before scaling; set a review point, such as a revenue milestone, to start testing more of the range.
conditions: Brands entering a new country with at least one proven product and cash to hold enough stock.
fails_when: Products with a short trend life or long reorder lead times; brands whose position depends on range breadth.

claim: About 4% of fashion ads and products drive about 64% of revenue (the 80/20 rule applied twice), so check stock and size depth before letting a winning ad take most of the budget.
body: The 80/20 rule nests inside itself. If 20% of ads drive 80% of results, then the top 20% of that 20% drives 80% of the 80%: about 4% of ads or products producing about 64% of revenue. In a fashion account this means more than half of spend will pool into a couple of ads. Two checks follow. First, does the product in that ad have enough days of inventory, and enough of its best-selling sizes, to support that spend? If not, you either sell it out quickly, which erodes the margin you would have made anyway, or the ad dies when core sizes run out. Second, the rest of the range gets little exposure. A large retailer called this the trench coat problem: with 2,000 products live, buyers never learn the brand sells trench coats. How to apply: review the top 5% of ads by spend each week with stock and size data beside them, and plan creative for under-exposed products on purpose.
conditions: Fashion and apparel brands with a wide range of products and sizes, where one winning ad can sell through the stock behind it.
fails_when: Small catalogs where one hero product is the business and stock is replenished continuously.
numbers: about 4% of ads or products drive about 64% of revenue
example: 2,000 products live on site

claim: Budget fashion existing-customer ads as CPM times monthly frequency times customers divided by 1,000; 500,000 customers at $20 CPM and frequency 6 is $60,000 a month, kept between 3 and 7.
body: Picking a percentage of spend for existing customers is the wrong question. Work it out in dollars instead. Formula: CPM on that audience, times the frequency you want over 30 days, times the number of existing customers, divided by 1,000. Blue Sense's example: $20 CPM, frequency of 6, and 500,000 customers gives $60,000 a month. Most brands will land lower, because CPMs on customer lists are often below $20 and frequency can be trimmed. Their bands: above 7 in 30 days is wasted money, and below 3 is too little to matter. Where you sit in that band depends on how much fresh creative feeds the campaign and how often you drop new products. How to apply: pull reachable customer count from your matched list, take the last month's CPM on that audience, choose a frequency between 3 and 7, compute the budget, and then check frequency weekly in Ads Manager and adjust.
conditions: Fashion brands with frequent drops and a sizeable customer list on Meta.
fails_when: Categories where existing-customer spend tests show no lift, or very small lists where Meta cannot hold frequency steady.

claim: Fashion account structure should grow with business complexity, not spend: a $50k a month brand may drop 15 products every two weeks, a bigger one 60 to 70 products and 200 new ads weekly.
body: Above $250k a month the structure gets more detailed, but the driver is business complexity. Blue Sense's contrast: a brand spending about $50k a month might launch 10 to 20 ads a week and drop around 15 products every two weeks, so a simple setup copes. A brand at the larger tier may drop 60 to 70 products every week and launch around 200 ads a week, with more categories, markets and business units, and the account has to mirror that. How to apply: before adding campaigns, list what has changed in the business: new categories, new markets with their own stock, faster drop cadence, more creative per week. Add structure only for those changes. If spend has grown but the business has not, keep the structure and add creative volume instead.

claim: Fashion brands under $50k a month need about three Meta campaigns: testing with each product launch in its own ad set, a scaling CBO only for evergreen ads, and existing-customer retargeting.
body: Blue Sense often audits fashion accounts at $50k to $100k a month running around 21 campaigns: reach, traffic, a campaign per product, sale and extra-off campaigns. That much splitting cuts performance. Under $50k a month keep three. A testing campaign (CBO or ABO, personal choice) where every new product launch gets its own ad set, so new drops do not reset learning in working ad sets; you can also split ad sets by concept, margin or product type. A scaling CBO, only if testing runs as ABO and you have ads that can run for months. Many fashion ads show one product, so when it or its core sizes sell out the ad must stop, even if it could have held $100k of spend. Make creative that can stay live longer before bothering with a scaling campaign. Finally, an existing-customer campaign with catalog ads and new arrivals; visitor retargeting already happens inside cold campaigns.
conditions: Fashion brands spending under about $50k a month on Meta with regular product drops.
fails_when: Brands with separate business units or regions that each need their own budget control even at this spend.

claim: Fashion is the exception to near-zero Meta spend on existing customers: Blue Sense's inverse holdout tests found that spend incremental, because new product drops land every one to three weeks.
body: In most categories Blue Sense's standard practice is to put close to 0% of paid media toward existing customers, because lift tests show it is rarely incremental; those buyers come back through email and organic anyway. They carried that rule into fashion accounts until inverse holdout tests, about three years before this video, showed otherwise: in fashion, existing-customer spend did drive extra sales. The reason is product cadence. Fashion brands drop new products every one, two or three weeks, and many customers miss the email or the organic post. Paid ads put the new range on their screen. How to apply: if you sell fashion with frequent drops, run an existing-customer campaign built around new arrivals and catalog ads, keep it in its own campaign so cold campaigns can exclude customers, and size it by frequency rather than a percentage. If you are not in a frequent-drop category, test before assuming it pays.
conditions: Fashion brands with frequent new arrivals and a large customer base.
fails_when: Categories with slow product turnover (furniture, single SKU consumables), or brands that have never run a holdout to confirm it.

claim: For fashion brands spending $30k to $75k a month: 7-day click, 180-day LTGP to CAC of 2 to 3, two to three Meta campaigns, Shopping at 80% plus of Google, and 30 to 50 new ads a month.
body: Blue Sense's action list for this tier. Measurement: run all campaigns on 7-day click, and use 180-day lifetime gross profit to CAC as the health check, aiming for 2 to 3. Meta: only two or three campaigns; Australian brands should run Australia and New Zealand together rather than separately; cap spend on existing customers. Google: Shopping should take 80% or more of the Google budget, and the highest leverage work is fixing the Shopping feed (images, titles, product types). Creative: launch 30 to 50 new ads a month, use partnership ads, and keep about 80% of creative evergreen and 20% seasonal so ads can run long enough to scale. How to apply: compare your account against each line and fix the gaps in this order: attribution setting, campaign count, feed, then creative volume.

fails_when: Brands whose Google channel is mostly brand demand, or who sell mainly in one market where the AU and NZ advice does not apply.

claim: From $50k to $250k a month, split fashion campaigns by business unit (like denim at 40% of revenue) and split ad sets by the question you want answered, changing that split as questions change.
body: At this tier Blue Sense runs several Advantage+ campaigns and uses a simple rule for each level. Campaigns follow business units: anything the business forecasts, targets and reports on separately. Example: denim drives about 40% of revenue and has different LTV, so denim gets its own campaign apart from the rest of the range; basics and seasonal products might also be split if the brand chooses to advertise basics at all. Ad sets follow the question you want answered right now. If leadership wants proof that UGC beats campaign shoots so budget can move, split ad sets by format and report the result. If you want to learn which concepts work, split by concept; for product-level learning, split by product. Blue Sense does not think format splits are usually the best choice, but they are right when someone needs that data. Unlike campaigns, ad set structure should change as the questions change. How to apply: write the current question at the top of your test log and match ad sets to it.
conditions: Fashion brands spending about $50k to $250k a month with defined business units.
fails_when: Business units are too small to fund their own campaign, or nobody will act on the answer the ad set split produces.

claim: Grade fashion stock A to D by sell-through and tie paid media to clearing grade C, since millions in dead stock locks up cash even when the P&L shows profit.
body: Grade A sells fast enough that you worry about running out. Grade B moves slowly. Grade C barely moves. Grade D does not sell at all. Blue Sense has seen brands with about $10M of grade C stock: on paper the business made $10M profit, but it was all sitting in the warehouse, not in the bank. Paid media can help clear it, as a low-ROAS, low-profit exercise that improves cash and business health. Options: give grade C products priority in Shopping campaigns, make more Meta creative for them, test them on a newer channel like TikTok, or sell them in the other hemisphere where the season fits. There is a brand risk: pushing products people do not want to new customers can make the brand look like its weakest range. One middle path is to show grade C products mainly to existing customers. How to apply: share a weekly stock grade report with whoever runs ads, and set a separate, lower efficiency target for clearance spend.
conditions: Fashion and apparel brands holding seasonal stock that sells at very different speeds, with cash tied up in slow lines.
fails_when: The slow stock is off-brand or poor quality, so showing it to new buyers harms the brand more than the cash recovered helps.

claim: In fashion brands that nearly always have a sale running, cap discount and promo campaigns at about 20% to 30% of ad budget so 70% to 80% stays in evergreen campaigns.
body: Many fashion brands run some kind of offer almost constantly: a sale, an extra percentage off, a bundle. If promo ads go into the main campaigns or take an open share of budget, they keep disrupting learning and pull spend toward price-sensitive buyers. Blue Sense generally caps promo and discount campaigns at about 20% to 30% of total budget, keeping 70% to 80% in evergreen campaigns that run steadily and are not interrupted. The exact cap depends on targets and the sale calendar. How to apply: put all offer-led ads in a separate promo campaign with its own budget. At the start of each month, set its share against the cap, and judge it on contribution margin after the discount rather than on ROAS, since discounted revenue carries less profit.

claim: Skip Pinterest ads for most brands: view-through credit inflates results, click-through ROAS is much worse, and in Australia it tops out around $10k to $20k a month.
body: Pinterest shows about ten pins at once. If one is your ad and the person buys from you within a day, Pinterest claims the sale. It also tends to serve pins to existing site visitors, who were likely to buy anyway, so reported results run far ahead of reality. Look at click-through purchases or click-through ROAS and the picture is much worse. Scale is the other problem. In a small market like Australia, Blue Sense finds you can spend only about $10k to $20k a month at most. That means build and optimization time on a channel that cannot take much budget, when the same $10k added to Meta would likely bring better incremental return and keep the team focused. How to apply: if you run Pinterest, judge it only on click-through results and a holdout. Otherwise, put that budget and time into your main channels.

claim: TikTok ads pay in fashion only with a strong native organic content engine; Blue Sense's fashion lift tests were 4 of 5 strongly positive, while 4 holdouts outside fashion all failed.
body: Blue Sense sees TikTok as excellent for some fashion clients and poor for others, and the deciding factor is creative. TikTok needs native-feeling content in large volume because it fatigues fast. If a brand already posts a lot of good organic TikTok content, that content tends to work as paid too, and the channel is underused. If not, TikTok will not work. Their test record: about five lift experiments on TikTok for fashion brands, four of them very positive. Outside fashion, four holdout tests all came back poor, showing almost no incrementality, and Blue Sense pulled those clients off the platform. How to apply: before spending on TikTok, check whether you can supply native videos every week. If yes, start by running your best organic posts as ads and run a lift or holdout test before scaling. claim: When new season stock lands, do not switch off ads for older products that are still efficient; hold or raise their spend to sell through, and plan creative 1.5 to 2.5 months before products arrive.
body: Fashion creative is planned about 1.5 to 2.5 months before the product is on sale. When the new range arrives, a common reflex, especially for agencies with no stock visibility, is to turn off the older ads and move all spend to the new products. That hurts. Sell-through on last season's products only falls as they go out of season, so cutting their ads leaves more stock for markdown. If those older ads still turn over stock efficiently, even at modest spend, keep them running or raise them to clear the remainder, then move on. The same timing lets you feed learnings forward: what worked in the last drop should shape the briefs for the content shooting now. How to apply: before each drop, list older products with stock left and their current ad efficiency. Keep the efficient ones live through the transition, and put a creative review of the previous drop into the planning calendar.

claim: Above about $50,000 a month, the media buyer must manage inventory as well as ROAS: a P&L showing $2M profit with $3M of unsold stock is a business about $1M short of cash.
body: Agencies are judged on efficiency and profit, so they push spend to the best-selling products and the best ads. That can leave slow stock piling up. Blue Sense's example: $2M of reported profit but $3M sitting in unsold inventory, so the business is about $1M negative on cash because every dollar earned went into stock. The fix runs through the ad account: restructure so slow lines get their own budget and their own creative, accept lower efficiency for a while, and turn stock back into cash. That is a hard pill for teams used to chasing ROAS, but it rebalances the business. How to apply: share a monthly stock report with your buyer showing weeks of cover and aged stock by product, set sell-through goals next to ROAS targets, and ask for spend by product, not only by ad. At this spend level the buyer's job is managing risk across ads, across products and against the business plan.
conditions: Brands holding inventory, especially with wide catalogues, spending roughly $50,000 a month or more on Meta.
fails_when: Single-product or made-to-order brands with little stock risk; very small accounts where product mix cannot be steered.

claim: Aim for 70 to 90% of effort on top of funnel, about 20% middle and 5 to 10% bottom; with consolidated campaigns, set this split through the creative you produce, not campaign budgets.
body: Meta accounts used to set funnel budgets with separate campaigns for cold, warm and hot audiences. Now most accounts are consolidated into a few campaigns, perhaps with a separate one for retargeting, so Meta decides where each dollar goes based on the ads it has. That means your creative mix sets the budget mix. If most new ads are product-aware offers and DPA-style content, spend drifts to warm people and new customer growth stalls. How to apply: tag every new ad by awareness stage when you brief it, and make about 70 to 90% of new assets for unaware and problem-aware viewers, with the rest for product-aware and most-aware viewers. Use the separate retargeting campaign only for the small bottom of funnel slice, mainly existing customers and, for long purchase journeys, 90-day site visitors. Blue Sense says there is a finer way to size the bottom of funnel budget, but this split is the working rule.
conditions: Consolidated Meta accounts using broad targeting and few campaigns.
fails_when: Brands with large existing audiences, frequent drops or very long purchase cycles that justify more warm spend.

claim: Check DPA and retargeting ROAS with existing customers excluded and Meta's incremental attribution column; a reported 5x can really be about 2.5x, and moving budget into DPAs starves the top of funnel.
body: Dynamic product ads look brilliant because they mostly reach people who were already going to buy. Blue Sense's check: exclude existing customers, then in Ads Manager open Columns, choose compare attribution settings, add incremental attribution and apply. Meta estimates lift by holding back about 10% of the people it would target and comparing their purchase rate with those who saw ads. If 2% of the exposed group buy and 1% of the holdout buy, the ads caused only half the sales, so a reported 5x is closer to 2.5x. DPAs can work on cold audiences at around $1,000 a day in some accounts, but not at $50,000 a day. The spiral: high reported ROAS pulls budget from prospecting into DPAs, fewer new people enter the funnel, the DPA pool then dries up, and the whole account declines. Cap DPA budgets and judge them on incremental numbers.
conditions: Accounts running catalogue or retargeting ads alongside prospecting, especially fashion and large catalogues.
fails_when: Small accounts where DPAs are a minor line; incremental estimates are noisy at low volume, so confirm with a holdout test where possible.

claim: Choose CBO or ABO by risk appetite: in Blue Sense's data about 4% of ads end up holding roughly 64% of spend and revenue, and CBO speeds that concentration; ABO spreads risk at slightly lower return.
body: Pareto's 80/20 rule compounds: 20% of ads drive 80% of results, and within that, 20% of the 20% drive 80% of the 80%, which is about 4% of ads with about 64% of the totals. Blue Sense says it sees this in every account breakdown it runs. A CBO campaign lets Meta follow that curve, which usually gives the best short-term efficiency but leaves you over-reliant on a few ads that will fatigue. The same happens with products: put a whole catalogue in one CBO and spend piles onto a few SKUs, which can leave other stock unsold. ABO, with budgets set per ad set, forces spread across concepts and products at a small cost in return. How to choose: run ABO as the steady state when you want a derisked portfolio and even sell-through. Switch to CBO for a period when you need a quick lift in efficiency and care less about testing. The host says he would pick ABO most of the time for his own business.
conditions: Accounts with several concepts or products where portfolio risk and stock sell-through matter.
fails_when: Very small budgets that cannot fund many ad sets under ABO; single-product brands with no sell-through concerns may prefer CBO.

claim: Creative playbook by Meta spend: $4,000 to $30,000 a month, 3 core concepts and 60 to 80% of budget on testing; $30,000 to $100,000, 5 to 6 concepts; $100,000+, 8 to 10 active concepts and 100+ new assets monthly.

At $30,000 to $100,000: bring in two to three UGC creators, put about 25% of spend into production, run five to six concepts to start spreading risk, use a testing campaign plus likely a scaling campaign, launch about 30 to 100 new creatives a month, and add partnership ads. Above $100,000: a full team (scripting, an editor, four to six creators and a designer; part-time is fine) so production runs as a system; at least 10% of spend on creative; 8 to 10 active concepts; at least 100 new assets a month; and a model tracking cost per asset by source against profit contribution per ad.

claim: Give each concept its own ad set: Meta's targeting lives at the ad set level, so mixing personas confuses who to find, and a mixed ad set cannot tell you which concept worked.
body: Even with broad targeting, the ad set is where Meta works out who to reach. Put an ad for older men next to one for young women under the same ad set and it has to guess who the set is for, and results suffer. There is a second cost. Because ad-level ROAS is unreliable, the ad set result is your main read. If the set holds one persona, one angle and one offer, a good result means this concept works and you should make more like it; a bad one means it does not. If it holds three concepts, a 3x ROAS teaches you nothing you can act on. How to apply: name ad sets by concept (persona, angle, offer), keep three or more ads of that one concept in each, and when you produce a fresh batch for the same concept, launch it as a new ad set with a shoot number instead of adding to the old one.
conditions: Testing campaigns where you want a learning loop on which concepts work.
fails_when: Very small budgets that cannot fund several ad sets to a readable result; then fewer, larger concept tests are better.
numbers: at least 3 ads per concept ad set

claim: If an ad set is hitting its target, do not switch off the low-ROAS ads inside it; Meta sequences ads, and the low-ROAS opener often feeds the purchases credited to the closer.
body: Meta's reported ROAS per ad is last click, but its delivery system learns from the whole path of views and clicks before a sale. In a typical ad set one ad opens (an unaware, top of funnel piece), another warms the person up (product aware), and a third closes (very aware). The closer shows the big number, say 6x, the middle ad 2x and the opener 1.4x. Turn off the two weak ones and the closer often collapses, because the people it was converting are no longer being warmed up. Rule: judge the ad set against its KPI. If it hits target, leave every ad alone. If it misses, you are free to turn ads off or add new ones, because there is no working sequence to break. A good creative strategist can usually tell from the ads themselves which one opens and which one closes, which is a better guide than the ad-level ROAS column.
conditions: Ad sets with several ads where Meta spreads spend across them and the ad set as a whole hits KPI.
fails_when: An ad set that is missing KPI, or an ad that takes real spend with zero results over a long period; single-ad ad sets.
numbers: example ad ROAS: closer 6x, middle 2x, opener 1.4x

claim: Make the account only as complex as the business; for most small to mid brands that means a testing campaign with one concept per ad set, an optional scaling campaign, and a retargeting campaign, with existing customers excluded from cold.
body: A $10,000 a month startup with one product and one persona needs a very simple account; an $800M retailer with 50 new SKUs a week and several regions needs more structure to match its commercial goals. For small to mid brands Blue Sense's default is three parts. (1) A testing campaign, ABO or CBO by preference and risk appetite, with each concept as its own ad set holding at least three ads and up to 50 to 100 depending on spend. (2) An optional scaling campaign, where you can move winners by their post IDs so they keep their engagement; keep it only if it works in your account. (3) A retargeting campaign aimed mainly at existing customers, which lets you exclude existing customers from the other two so they stay purely cold. Add an ad set for 90-day website visitors only if the purchase journey is long and engaged people need more frequency.
conditions: Brands roughly under $100,000 a month on Meta with a few products and personas.
fails_when: Large retailers with many regions, business units or weekly drops; those need structure that matches their commercial goals.

claim: Never add new ads to an ad set that is hitting KPI, or turn a winner off to relaunch it; raise the budget instead, and put fresh ads for that concept in a new ad set.
body: Adding ads to a working ad set partly resets learning, because Meta has to relearn how to sequence ads and split spend across them. If the set is beating target and you are scaling it, that risk is not worth taking; the host says he has hurt winning ad sets this way himself. If the set is missing target, change anything you like, turn ads off or add many new ones, since there is no working sequence to protect. When a concept wins and you make 20 more ads for it, launch them as a new ad set named so it filters with the original (for example concept one, shoot two). To scale a winner, increase its budget and leave it running. Copying its post IDs into a scaling campaign is fine as an extra, but switching off the original to relaunch it elsewhere is a classic beginner error.
conditions: Meta ad sets with several ads that are meeting their CPA or ROAS target.
fails_when: Ad sets that are underperforming, where disruption costs nothing; single-ad ad sets.

claim: Pace a winning ad by stock and cash: push it hard to sell through excess inventory, or hold it near $100 a day so it lasts 6 months, not 6 weeks, when stock or cash is tight.
body: Each ad has a total spend capacity, the area under its daily spend curve from launch to switch-off. You cannot avoid the end, but you can change the shape: push budget hard and it peaks high and fatigues fast; keep it modest and it can run for months. Which is right depends on the business, not the ad. If you hold surplus stock that must turn into cash this month, squeeze the winner even at a worse MER. If stock is short, a new order is weeks away, or growth is outrunning your cash cycle, running hot makes no sense: you will stock out and waste the ad. Agencies often lack this context and push winners hard because it makes a strong 30 to 90 day case study and they report on ROAS. Tell your buyer your stock position and cash plan every month, and agree how hard to run winners.
conditions: Brands with inventory limits or seasonal stock, working with an in-house buyer or agency.
fails_when: Print-on-demand or made-to-order brands with no stock risk; small ads whose capacity is reached quickly anyway.
numbers: example: about $100 a day for 6 months versus burning out in 6 weeks
agency case study window 30 to 90 days

claim: Rank creative metrics by reliability: amount spent first, then 7-day click or incremental ROAS and CPA, then CPC and CTR as leading signals, then hook rate (3 seconds) and hold rate (15 seconds) as diagnostics.
body: Spend is the best long-run proxy because Meta pushes budget to ads that cause purchases anywhere in the sequence. If one ad shows 1.7x ROAS and another 2.2x but Meta gives the first double the spend, the first is likely the stronger top of funnel ad: it reaches new people at low frequency and feeds sales credited elsewhere. If the 2.2x ad could scale, it would get more spend. ROAS or CPA comes second, but only on 7-day click or incremental attribution. CPC and CTR do not prove an ad converts, but at the extremes they let you call ads early: if no ad above, say, a $3 CPC has ever been profitable in your account, a new ad sitting there at low spend can be cut. Hook and hold rates do not predict sales, but they show where to fix a video: a weak hook rate means swap the hook, and a weak hold rate often means the bridge failed.
conditions: Meta accounts with enough ads and history to set your own CPC and hook rate baselines.
fails_when: Campaigns with forced even budgets (strict ABO with one ad per set), where spend does not reflect Meta's choice.

hold rate: share past about 15 seconds
early cut example: CPC above $3 if none above it were profitable

claim: Run partnership (collab) ads: they target using the audience data of both your handle and the creator's, feel organic, and in some Blue Sense accounts carry up to 40% of total spend.
body: A partnership ad runs from your brand page together with a creator's handle. Meta can now test showing the brand, the creator or both on the post and keep the best mix. The edge is targeting: Meta uses the creator's audience signals to find similar new people, so a well matched creator helps you reach cold buyers, not just their followers. Viewers also see it as a creator post, so it feels less like an ad. Blue Sense calls it one of the most underused formats in 2026, while warning that the advantage may fade as more brands catch on. How to apply: pick creators whose followers look like your buyers, get partnership ad permission in Instagram, and run their posts and your scripted content through their handle in prospecting campaigns. Their spend-tier playbook adds partnership ads from about $30,000 a month.
conditions: Brands with access to relevant creators and enough spend to test them, roughly $30,000 a month and up.
fails_when: Creators whose audience does not match your buyer, which steers targeting the wrong way; the edge may shrink as the format becomes common.

claim: When a hero ad fatigues, extend it in this order: new hooks on the same body, a new format, its post ID in a scaling campaign, then a cost cap campaign; skip duplicating ad sets.
body: Once an ad fatigues there is little you can do, which is why the portfolio approach matters, but these tactics squeeze more from the tail. New hooks on the proven body are the most reliable. Format rotation comes next: turn a winning video into a static, a winning VSL into UGC, or a winning image into a long-copy unaware static, which is in effect a new strategy on the same idea. Moving the post ID into a scaling campaign keeps its likes and comments and sometimes buys more spend, but it will not save an account. A cost cap campaign can force more delivery for a while, yet it is a short-term buying move and burns the creative faster. Duplicating ad sets is an old trick Blue Sense no longer recommends. Keep producing new concepts alongside, so you never depend on rescuing a dying ad.
conditions: Meta accounts with a fatiguing hero ad and a proven body or post with social proof.
fails_when: Accounts with no other working ads, where these tactics only delay the drop; cost caps set too tight can choke delivery entirely.

claim: TikTok has been blocked in India since 29 June 2020 under Section 69A of the IT Act, so Indian brands cannot advertise to or sell to Indian buyers on TikTok.
body: On 29 June 2020 India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology blocked TikTok and 58 other apps under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act and its 2009 blocking rules, citing threats to sovereignty, defence, state security and public order and reports of user data being sent to servers outside India. Further orders blocked more apps later in 2020. The block means TikTok ads, TikTok Shop and TikTok creator programmes do not reach audiences in India. How to apply: for an Indian brand selling at home, short-form video plans go to Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts and Indian short-video apps, and TikTok cards in this library (all scoped to other markets) do not apply. An Indian brand exporting to the US, UK or EU can still use TikTok in those markets through a local seller or ad account that meets that market's rules, and should apply the US or UK TikTok cards there.

fails_when: Indian brands targeting buyers abroad, where TikTok is available; the block could be lifted by a future government order, so check before planning.

claim: Under India's E-Commerce Rules, a brand's ads must match the product's real characteristics and use conditions, it must not post reviews posing as a buyer, and vouching '100% genuine' makes it liable for authenticity.
body: Rule 7 of the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 sets three duties that reach ads and product pages for a brand selling its own stock. Rule 7(3): advertisements must be consistent with the actual characteristics, access and usage conditions of the goods. Rule 7(2): the entity must not falsely represent itself as a consumer and post reviews, or misrepresent the quality or features of goods. Rule 7(5): an entity that explicitly or implicitly vouches for, or guarantees, the authenticity of goods bears the liability in any action over their authenticity. Rule 4(6) adds that an entity selling imported goods must name the importer it bought them from. Marketplace sellers carry the same ad and review duties under rule 6. How to apply: check every ad claim against the product spec sheet before launch, never seed reviews from staff or agency accounts, and use 'genuine' or 'authentic' badges only where you can prove the chain of supply, because the badge shifts liability to you.
conditions: Ads, listings and reviews for goods sold online to consumers in India.
fails_when: ASCI's code and the CCPA's 2022 ad guidelines add further claim rules (substantiation, disclaimers); product-specific laws apply to regulated categories.
